nodes.name: Arithmetic
nodes.desc: The four operations, done reliably and with a sense of roughly what the answer should be. That estimate is the actual skill. It is what catches a mistake before it travels.

nodes.name: Order of Operations
nodes.desc: The agreed order for evaluating an expression, so one string of symbols means one thing. Small, but every algebraic error later either respects it or comes from ignoring it.

nodes.name: Fractions
nodes.desc: Parts of a whole, and arithmetic where the denominators have to agree first. Fluency here quietly decides how hard algebra feels two years later.

nodes.name: Decimals & Percents
nodes.desc: Three ways of writing the same quantity, and moving between them without thinking. Percentage change is the one people keep getting wrong, in both directions.

nodes.name: Negative Numbers
nodes.desc: Quantities below zero and what the operations do to them. Signs are the single most common source of a wrong answer in otherwise correct algebra.

nodes.name: Algebra
nodes.desc: Letters standing in for numbers, and rearranging while keeping both sides equal. The shift is from computing an answer to manipulating a relationship, which is what makes the rest of mathematics possible.

nodes.name: Linear Equations
nodes.desc: Equations whose graph is a straight line, and solving one or several at once. Slope and intercept are worth being able to read off in either direction without hesitation.

nodes.name: Inequalities
nodes.desc: Relationships that are less-than rather than equal, and the one rule that surprises everyone: multiplying by a negative flips the sign.

nodes.name: Geometry
nodes.desc: Shape, angle, area and distance, and proving something is true for every case rather than the one you drew. Drawing the diagram first is not a study tip, it is the method.

nodes.name: Coordinate Geometry
nodes.desc: Shapes described by equations on a grid, which lets algebra answer geometric questions. The bridge that makes both subjects considerably more powerful than either alone.

nodes.name: Quadratics
nodes.desc: Equations with a squared term, and the parabola they draw. Three routes to a solution (factoring, completing the square, the formula) and knowing which is quickest matters.

nodes.name: Functions
nodes.desc: A rule taking each input to exactly one output, and the graph as its picture. Domain, range, composition and inverses are the vocabulary the whole of later mathematics assumes you have.

nodes.name: Exponents & Logarithms
nodes.desc: Repeated multiplication and the operation that undoes it. Logs turn multiplication into addition, which is why they appear everywhere from complexity to acoustics.

nodes.name: Trigonometry
nodes.desc: Ratios in a right triangle that turn out to describe every wave. Derive the unit circle once rather than memorizing the table and the identities stop being arbitrary.

nodes.name: Statistics
nodes.desc: Describing data honestly: what is typical, how spread out it is, and how sure you are allowed to be. Most misuse is not bad arithmetic but a chart or an average answering a question nobody asked.

nodes.name: Counting & Combinatorics
nodes.desc: Counting arrangements without listing them. Whether order matters and whether repetition is allowed are the two questions that decide which formula applies.

nodes.name: Probability
nodes.desc: How likely something is, given what you already know. Conditional probability is where intuition fails hardest, which is why the classic paradoxes are all built from it.

nodes.name: Sequences & Series
nodes.desc: Ordered lists of numbers and what happens when you add them all up. Whether an infinite sum settles on a value is the question calculus later answers properly.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.desc: Establishing that something is true for every case, not merely the ones you tried. Induction, contradiction and construction are the three moves worth being fluent in.

nodes.name: Precalculus
nodes.desc: The last tightening of functions, graphs and algebra before limits begin. Not a subject so much as everything you will need fluently the moment calculus starts.

nodes.name: Limits
nodes.desc: What a function approaches as the input closes in on a value, whether or not it ever arrives. Every idea in calculus is defined in terms of this one, so it is worth more time than it usually gets.

nodes.name: Continuity
nodes.desc: A function with no jumps, holes or gaps. One you could draw without lifting the pen. The theorems that follow all quietly require it, which is why the exceptions matter.

nodes.name: Derivatives
nodes.desc: The rate at which something changes at a single instant, defined as a limit of average rates. Being able to say what it means for a real quantity matters more than being able to compute it.

nodes.name: Differentiation Rules
nodes.desc: Product, quotient and chain. The shortcuts that make derivatives fast once you have done a few from first principles. The chain rule is the one that keeps being the culprit.

nodes.name: Implicit Differentiation
nodes.desc: Differentiating a relationship that is not written as y equals something. The trick is remembering that y is still a function of x, so the chain rule applies every time it appears.

nodes.name: Optimization
nodes.desc: Finding the largest or smallest value something can take, by looking where the derivative is zero. The modeling is the hard half; the calculus is usually two lines.

nodes.name: Related Rates
nodes.desc: How fast one quantity changes given how fast another does, when the two are linked. Write the relationship first and differentiate with respect to time second. The reverse never works.

nodes.name: Integrals
nodes.desc: Adding up infinitely many infinitely small pieces to get an area, a total or an accumulation. Meeting it first as a Riemann sum is what stops it being an arbitrary new symbol.

nodes.name: The Fundamental Theorem
nodes.desc: That differentiation and integration undo each other. It is what turns integration from a limit you must compute into an antiderivative you can look up, and it deserves to feel surprising.

nodes.name: Integration Techniques
nodes.desc: Substitution, parts and partial fractions. The toolkit for integrals that do not yield directly. Recognizing which to reach for is pattern matching that only practice builds.

nodes.name: Areas & Volumes
nodes.desc: Using integration for the area between curves and the volume of a solid of revolution. Sketch the region and the representative slice first; the integral then writes itself.

nodes.name: Series
nodes.desc: Infinite sums, and the tests that decide whether one settles on a finite value. A rare place where the answer is a clean yes or no and the reasoning is the whole content.

nodes.name: Taylor Series
nodes.desc: Approximating any well-behaved function by a polynomial built from its derivatives. This is how a calculator computes sine, and why the approximation gets worse away from the center.

nodes.name: Differential Equations
nodes.desc: Equations relating a quantity to its own rate of change, which is how nearly every physical law is written. Solving one means finding a whole function rather than a number.

nodes.name: Curve Sketching
nodes.desc: Using the first and second derivatives to find where a graph rises, falls and bends. It's the most common free-response setup on the AP exam.

nodes.name: Linear Approximation
nodes.desc: Using the tangent line to estimate values near a point. Your calculator does a fancier version of this every time you press a button.

nodes.name: L'Hopital's Rule
nodes.desc: A shortcut for limits that come out as zero over zero or infinity over infinity. Check the form first, since using it anywhere else gives nonsense.

nodes.name: Mean Value Theorem
nodes.desc: Somewhere between two points, the instant rate equals the average rate. It sounds obvious, and it quietly powers half the proofs in the course.

nodes.name: Accumulation & Motion
nodes.desc: Position, velocity and acceleration tied together by derivatives and integrals. Say the units of each answer out loud before you write it down.

nodes.name: Parametric & Polar Calculus
nodes.desc: Slopes, arc length and area for curves drawn by a parameter or an angle. This is BC-only territory, and it shows up every year.

nodes.name: The AP Calculus Exam
nodes.desc: Free-response technique, calculator rules and justifying answers in words. Graders want your reasoning, so practice writing it out in full.

nodes.name: What a Diff Eq Is
nodes.desc: An equation that links a function to its own rate of change. The answer is a whole function, which takes some getting used to.

nodes.name: Checking a Solution
nodes.desc: Plug a candidate function in and see if both sides match. It's quick, and it catches most mistakes on homework.

nodes.name: Slope Fields
nodes.desc: Tiny arrows that show the slope at every point. You can sketch solutions before solving anything, and AP Calc BC loves asking about them.

nodes.name: Separable Equations
nodes.desc: Move every y to one side and every x to the other, then integrate. Don't drop the constant, because it's what fits the solution to the starting point.

nodes.name: Initial Value Problems
nodes.desc: Using a starting condition to pick one solution out of a family. Most real problems come with one, so practice reading it off the question.

nodes.name: Growth & Decay Models
nodes.desc: Populations, cooling coffee and radioactive decay. Each is a rate proportional to an amount, and each solves to an exponential.

nodes.name: Euler's Method
nodes.desc: Approximating a solution with small straight steps. Smaller steps give better answers, and you'll see exactly why the error builds up.

nodes.name: First-Order Linear
nodes.desc: Equations you solve with an integrating factor. It feels like a trick the first time and like a recipe by the fifth.

nodes.name: Logistic Growth
nodes.desc: Growth that slows down as it hits a limit. The carrying capacity sits right in the equation once you know where to look.

nodes.name: Exact Equations
nodes.desc: Equations that come from a hidden function of x and y. A quick partial-derivative test tells you if the method applies.

nodes.name: Second-Order Linear
nodes.desc: Equations with a second derivative, solved with a characteristic equation. Real, repeated and complex roots each give a different kind of answer.

nodes.name: Springs & Oscillation
nodes.desc: Masses on springs, with and without friction. Underdamped, critically damped and overdamped are three outcomes of one equation.

nodes.name: Forcing Terms
nodes.desc: Adding an outside push with undetermined coefficients or variation of parameters. Resonance is what happens when the push matches the natural rhythm.

nodes.name: Laplace Transforms
nodes.desc: Turning a calculus problem into an algebra problem and back. Engineers use it for circuits and control systems all the time.

nodes.name: Systems of Equations
nodes.desc: Several linked equations solved together with matrices and eigenvalues. Predator and prey models live here.

nodes.name: Phase Portraits
nodes.desc: Pictures of how a system moves over time. Stable points, spirals and saddles tell the story without solving anything.

nodes.name: Series Solutions
nodes.desc: Building a solution as a power series when nothing else works. It's slow, and it works when the conditions are right.

nodes.name: Intro to Partial Diff Eqs
nodes.desc: Equations with more than one variable, like heat spreading through a rod. A first look at what physics and engineering majors do next.

nodes.name: Kinds of Data
nodes.desc: Categories, counts and measurements, and the fact that what you may do to a number depends on which it is. Averaging a set of postcodes is arithmetic that runs and means nothing.

nodes.name: Center & Spread
nodes.desc: Mean, median and mode, then the range, quartiles and standard deviation around them. A center quoted without a spread is half a description and usually the more flattering half.

nodes.name: Reading Charts
nodes.desc: Histograms, box plots and scatter plots, and what each is capable of hiding. A truncated axis and a bin width chosen after the fact are the two edits that change a conclusion without changing a number.

nodes.name: Distributions
nodes.desc: The shape values take across a population. Symmetric, skewed, or with two peaks that mean two populations got mixed. Naming the shape is what tells you which summary is honest.

nodes.name: Probability
nodes.desc: How likely something is, on a scale from impossible to certain, and the rules for combining likelihoods. Almost every paradox in the subject comes from adding probabilities of events that can happen together.

nodes.name: Conditional Probability
nodes.desc: The chance of one thing given that another has happened, which is rarely the same as the chance the other way round. Confusing the two directions is the single most consequential error in medicine and courtrooms alike.

nodes.name: Bayes Theorem
nodes.desc: Updating a belief when evidence arrives, in one line of algebra. Its famous lesson is that a very accurate test for a very rare condition still produces mostly false positives.

nodes.name: The Normal Distribution
nodes.desc: The bell curve, and why so many measurements land on it. Standardizing to how many deviations from the mean a value is turns every normal question into the same question.

nodes.name: Sampling
nodes.desc: Learning about a population from a part of it, and the ways a part can fail to represent the whole. Random selection is not a formality; it is the entire license for what follows.

nodes.name: Sampling Distributions
nodes.desc: What the average of a sample would do if you took the sample again and again. The remarkable result is that it settles into a bell shape almost regardless of what the population looks like.

nodes.name: Confidence Intervals
nodes.desc: A range of plausible values with a stated success rate for the method that produced it. It is a claim about the procedure over many repeats, not a probability that this particular interval contains the answer.

nodes.name: Hypothesis Tests
nodes.desc: Asking whether the data would be surprising if nothing were going on. The p-value measures that surprise and nothing else, and treating it as the probability the claim is wrong is the misreading that never dies.

nodes.name: Errors & Power
nodes.desc: Two ways to be wrong: crying wolf, and missing a real effect. Power is the chance of catching an effect that is there, and a study with too few subjects fails before it starts.

nodes.name: Effect Size
nodes.desc: How big the difference is, as distinct from how confident you are that it is not zero. With a large enough sample, an utterly trivial difference becomes statistically significant.

nodes.name: Regression
nodes.desc: Fitting a line, reading its slope as a rate, and checking the residuals rather than admiring the fit. The assumptions are where the honesty lives; the coefficient is only where the story is.

nodes.name: Multiple Comparisons
nodes.desc: Test twenty things at the usual threshold and one comes up significant by luck alone. Deciding what you will test before looking is the only defense that fully works.

nodes.name: Causal Inference
nodes.desc: What it takes to say one thing caused another rather than moved with it. Randomization earns it outright; without it, you are arguing that you controlled for everything that matters, and you probably did not.

nodes.name: Bayesian Methods
nodes.desc: Carrying a prior belief into the analysis and coming out with a distribution over the answer. It says the thing people wanted the confidence interval to say, at the cost of having to state the prior out loud.

nodes.name: Non-Parametric Methods
nodes.desc: Tests that work on ranks and resampling rather than an assumed shape. Slower and less powerful when the assumptions hold, and the right answer whenever they clearly do not.

nodes.name: Study Design
nodes.desc: Deciding what to collect, from whom and how many, before any of it exists. No analysis rescues a study that was going to be ambiguous whatever the data said.

nodes.name: Vectors
nodes.desc: A quantity with direction as well as size, and equally a list of numbers. Holding both pictures at once (arrow and list) is what makes the rest of the subject readable.

nodes.name: Vector Arithmetic
nodes.desc: Adding vectors tip to tail and scaling them longer or shorter. Every later idea is built from exactly these two moves, which is why the subject is called linear.

nodes.name: Dot Product
nodes.desc: One number from two vectors, measuring how much they point the same way. Zero means perpendicular, and that single fact powers projections, similarity scores and most of graphics.

nodes.name: Span & Independence
nodes.desc: Everything you can reach by combining a set of vectors, and whether one of them was redundant. Dependence is the formal version of a column that told you nothing new.

nodes.name: Basis & Dimension
nodes.desc: A minimal set of directions that reaches the whole space, and how many you need. Choosing a different basis is choosing a different set of coordinates for the same objects.

nodes.name: Matrices
nodes.desc: A grid of numbers, best read as a list of what happens to each basis vector. That reading turns the multiplication rule from an arbitrary procedure into an obvious one.

nodes.name: Linear Transformations
nodes.desc: Functions that stretch, rotate and shear space while keeping grid lines straight and the origin fixed. A matrix is not a table of numbers; it is one of these written down.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.desc: Doing one transformation after another, which is exactly what multiplying two matrices means. It explains at once why the order matters and why the product is defined so strangely.

nodes.name: Systems of Equations
nodes.desc: Several linear constraints at once, read as one question: which input lands on this output. Elimination is the algorithm; the geometry is planes meeting in a point, a line, or nowhere.

nodes.name: Inverses
nodes.desc: The transformation that undoes another, when one exists. It fails to exist exactly when the first one flattened the space, and that is what makes a system unsolvable rather than merely hard.

nodes.name: Determinant
nodes.desc: The factor by which a transformation scales area or volume, with a sign for whether it flipped. Zero means everything collapsed onto a lower dimension, which is the same zero that blocks the inverse.

nodes.name: Rank & Null Space
nodes.desc: How many dimensions survive a transformation, and everything that gets crushed to zero. Together they account for every input and answer why a solution is unique, infinite or absent.

nodes.name: Projections
nodes.desc: The closest point in a subspace to a given vector. The shadow it casts. It is the whole idea behind fitting a line to points that do not lie on one.

nodes.name: Orthogonality
nodes.desc: Directions at right angles, and bases made entirely of them. They make coordinates trivial to compute and keep numerical work stable, which is why so much effort goes into constructing them.

nodes.name: Least Squares
nodes.desc: The best answer to a system with no exact answer, found by projecting onto what is reachable. Regression is this, and seeing that connection explains where its formula comes from.

nodes.name: Eigenvectors & Eigenvalues
nodes.desc: The directions a transformation leaves pointing the same way, and how much it stretches them. Find those and the transformation becomes a simple scaling in the right coordinates.

nodes.name: Diagonalisation
nodes.desc: Rewriting a transformation in its own eigenbasis so it becomes a diagonal matrix. Applying it a thousand times then costs one exponentiation rather than a thousand multiplications.

nodes.name: Singular Value Decomposition
nodes.desc: Any matrix at all as a rotation, a stretch and another rotation. It is the most generally useful factorization there is, and the machinery under low-rank approximation and dimensionality reduction.

nodes.name: Numerical Stability
nodes.desc: What happens to these methods in finite-precision arithmetic, where nearly-dependent columns amplify error enormously. Conditioning tells you when an answer computed correctly is still worthless.

nodes.name: Applications
nodes.desc: Graphics, search rankings, compression, quantum states and every neural network layer are the same handful of operations wearing different clothes. Recognizing them is what the subject is for.

nodes.name: Propositional Logic
nodes.desc: Statements that are true or false, joined by and, or and not. A truth table settles any argument in this fragment mechanically, which is exactly why processors can be built out of it.

nodes.name: Implication
nodes.desc: If this, then that. And the fact that it is only false when the promise is broken. Its contrapositive is equivalent and its converse is not, which is the confusion behind an enormous number of wrong arguments.

nodes.name: Sets
nodes.desc: A collection with no order and no repeats, and the three operations on them. Union, intersection and difference mirror the logic words "or", "and" and "not" exactly, which is not a coincidence.

nodes.name: Quantifiers
nodes.desc: For all, and there exists. Their order changes the meaning completely, and negating a statement correctly means swapping each one and flipping the inside.

nodes.name: Relations
nodes.desc: Which things are connected to which, as a set of pairs. Reflexive, symmetric and transitive are the three properties worth knowing by name, because together they define what it means for things to be equivalent.

nodes.name: Functions & Mappings
nodes.desc: A relation that gives exactly one output per input, and what injective and surjective actually rule out. Counting arguments later depend entirely on which of those two a mapping has.

nodes.name: Counting
nodes.desc: Multiply choices made in sequence, add choices made instead of each other. Nearly every combinatorial mistake is one of those two rules applied where the other belonged.

nodes.name: Permutations & Combinations
nodes.desc: Arrangements where order matters and selections where it does not. Getting the answer usually means deciding that one question first and doing arithmetic second.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole Principle
nodes.desc: More items than boxes means some box holds two. Trivially obvious and startlingly powerful. It proves that any lossless compressor must make some inputs larger.

nodes.name: Direct Proof
nodes.desc: Arguing from the assumption to the conclusion in steps nobody can dispute. Writing one is mostly the discipline of stating what you are allowed to use before you use it.

nodes.name: Contradiction & Contrapositive
nodes.desc: Two ways round a proof that resists the direct route: assume the opposite and break something, or prove the equivalent reversed statement instead. Irrationality and infinitude of primes both fall to the first.

nodes.name: Induction
nodes.desc: Prove it for the first case, then prove each case follows from the one before. It is the same shape as recursion, and understanding either properly makes the other obvious.

nodes.name: Recurrence Relations
nodes.desc: Defining a sequence in terms of its earlier terms, and solving for a closed form. This is where the running time of a divide-and-conquer algorithm actually comes from.

nodes.name: Graph Theory
nodes.desc: Things and the connections between them, stripped of everything else. Once a problem is stated as a graph, decades of known results become available to it at once.

nodes.name: Trees & Counting Structures
nodes.desc: Connected graphs with no cycles, and how many of them there are. The counting results here are what tell you how large a search space really is before you write the search.

nodes.name: Modular Arithmetic
nodes.desc: Arithmetic that wraps around, the way a clock does. Hashing, checksums and public-key cryptography are all built on the fact that wrapping is easy forwards and hard to undo.

nodes.name: Number Theory
nodes.desc: Divisibility, primes and the structure hiding in the integers. The oldest branch of pure mathematics, and the one every secure connection you make depends on.

nodes.name: Boolean Algebra
nodes.desc: Logic as algebra, with laws you can factor and simplify by. It is how a circuit gets smaller and how a compiler decides that two conditions were the same condition.

nodes.name: Automata & Languages
nodes.desc: The simplest machines that can recognize patterns, and what each kind of machine cannot recognize at all. This is the theory a regular expression is a practical corner of.

nodes.name: Computability & Complexity
nodes.desc: What can be computed at all, and what can be computed in reasonable time. The halting problem and the open question about P and NP are both results about limits rather than about cleverness.

nodes.name: Mental Arithmetic
nodes.desc: Fast, accurate calculation without reaching for anything. Squares to thirty, common factorizations, fraction sense. It buys back the minutes that the last five problems on a paper actually need.

nodes.name: Algebraic Manipulation
nodes.desc: Moving expressions around fluently enough that the moving is not what you are thinking about. Substitution, symmetry and factoring are the three that turn an intractable equation into an obvious one.

nodes.name: Contest Timing
nodes.desc: Reading the whole paper first, budgeting per problem, and abandoning one on purpose. Most lost AMC points are not problems that could not be solved but problems that were never read.

nodes.name: Counting
nodes.desc: Multiplying choices made in sequence and adding choices made instead of one another, plus complementary counting when the direct count is worse. Nearly every combinatorics error is one of those rules used where another belonged.

nodes.name: Angle Chasing
nodes.desc: Propagating known angles through a figure until the unknown one falls out. It is the geometry technique with the highest ratio of problems solved to theory required, and it rewards drawing the diagram large.

nodes.name: Modular Arithmetic
nodes.desc: Arithmetic that wraps, and what it lets you ignore. Working modulo a well-chosen number turns questions about enormous integers into questions about a handful of residues.

nodes.name: Probability
nodes.desc: Counting the favorable cases over counting all of them, once you are sure both counts describe the same sample space. Almost every wrong answer here is a right count of the wrong space.

nodes.name: Sequences & Series
nodes.desc: Arithmetic and geometric progressions, and the telescoping trick that collapses a sum nobody wants to compute. Recognizing which kind you are looking at is most of the work.

nodes.name: Polynomials
nodes.desc: Roots, coefficients and the relations between them. Vieta turns a question about the roots you cannot find into arithmetic on the coefficients you were given.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole & Extremal
nodes.desc: More items than boxes means a box holds two, and looking at the largest or smallest case first. Both are ways of proving something exists without ever constructing it.

nodes.name: Power of a Point
nodes.desc: One relation that holds for every line through a fixed point and a circle, whichever side the point is on. It is the first result that makes circle geometry feel like algebra rather than luck.

nodes.name: Trigonometry in Geometry
nodes.desc: Law of sines and cosines as escape hatches when the figure refuses to yield to angles alone. The cost is arithmetic, which is why it is a second choice rather than a first.

nodes.name: Recursion & Telescoping
nodes.desc: Describing the nth case in terms of the ones before it, then either solving it or summing it so that everything cancels. A great many counting problems are recurrences that have not been written down yet.

nodes.name: Inequalities
nodes.desc: AM-GM, Cauchy-Schwarz, and the discipline of tracking when equality holds. The equality case is not a footnote. It is usually what tells you whether the bound you proved is the one being asked for.

nodes.name: Diophantine Equations
nodes.desc: Equations where only whole-number solutions count, which makes them far more constrained than they look. Factoring and a well-chosen modulus between them dispose of most of what appears on a paper.

nodes.name: Invariants & Monovariants
nodes.desc: Finding the quantity a process never changes, or only ever moves one way. It is how a question about a thousand moves is answered without simulating any of them.

nodes.name: Generating Functions
nodes.desc: Encoding a counting sequence as the coefficients of a power series, so that combinatorics becomes algebra. Heavy machinery, and unreasonably effective on the problems it fits.

nodes.name: AIME Strategy
nodes.desc: Three hours, fifteen problems, integer answers and no partial credit. A completely different game from the AMC. Verification matters more than speed here, because an answer you cannot check is worth nothing.

nodes.name: Olympiad Proof Writing
nodes.desc: Writing an argument a hostile grader cannot fault, which is a separate skill from finding it. Stating what you are allowed to assume before you use it is most of the difference between full marks and two.

nodes.name: Functional Equations
nodes.desc: Deducing what a function must be from an identity it satisfies everywhere. Substituting well-chosen values is the whole technique, and proving your candidate is the only one is the half people forget.

nodes.name: Combinatorial Geometry
nodes.desc: Counting arguments applied to points, lines and regions in the plane. It is where the two halves of the subject that never speak to each other finally have to.

nodes.name: The Olympiad Round
nodes.desc: Six proof problems over two days, where one solved completely beats three half-written. Everything below this converges here, because a paper at this level never tells you which of the four subjects it is testing.

nodes.name: Angles & Degrees
nodes.desc: How far something turns, in degrees. You'll use it in every other node here, so get quick at spotting complementary and supplementary pairs.

nodes.name: Right Triangles
nodes.desc: The Pythagorean theorem and the names of the three sides. Labeling opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse right is half of every trig problem.

nodes.name: Sine, Cosine & Tangent
nodes.desc: Three ratios that link an angle to the sides of a right triangle. SOH CAH TOA gets you started. Knowing which ratio fits the sides you have is the real skill.

nodes.name: Solving Triangles
nodes.desc: Finding missing sides and angles from what you know. Draw it, label it, pick the ratio, then check that the answer makes sense for the picture.

nodes.name: Inverse Trig
nodes.desc: Going from a ratio back to an angle with arcsin, arccos and arctan. Calculators give one answer, and sometimes the triangle wants the other one.

nodes.name: Radians
nodes.desc: Angles counted in radius lengths around the circle. It looks strange at first, but calculus only works cleanly in radians, so switch now.

nodes.name: The Unit Circle
nodes.desc: Sine and cosine as the coordinates of a point on a circle of radius one. Build it from two special triangles and you'll never need to memorize the table.

nodes.name: Angles of Elevation
nodes.desc: Word problems with ladders, ramps and shadows. The math is easy once the sketch is right, so spend your time on the sketch.

nodes.name: Graphing Sine & Cosine
nodes.desc: Turning the unit circle into waves. Amplitude, period, phase shift and midline are four knobs, and each one moves the graph in its own way.

nodes.name: Tangent & Reciprocal Graphs
nodes.desc: Tangent, secant, cosecant and cotangent, with their asymptotes. Most mistakes here come from forgetting where cosine equals zero.

nodes.name: Trig Identities
nodes.desc: Equations that hold for every angle, like sin squared plus cos squared equals one. Proving them is algebra practice in disguise. Work one side until it looks like the other.

nodes.name: Sum & Double-Angle Formulas
nodes.desc: Sine and cosine of a sum, plus the double and half-angle versions. Derive the double-angle ones from the sum formulas and you'll only need to remember two.

nodes.name: Solving Trig Equations
nodes.desc: Finding every angle that works. Answers repeat around the circle, so read the interval in the question before you stop.

nodes.name: Law of Sines & Cosines
nodes.desc: Solving triangles that don't have a right angle. Use sines for matching pairs and cosines when you know two sides and the angle between them.

nodes.name: Area & the Ambiguous Case
nodes.desc: Half ab sin C, and the side-side-angle setup that can give zero, one or two triangles. Tests love the ambiguous case because most people stop at one answer.

nodes.name: Vectors & Components
nodes.desc: Splitting a force or velocity into horizontal and vertical parts with sine and cosine. This is where trig shows up in physics class.

nodes.name: Polar Coordinates
nodes.desc: Points described by a distance and an angle. Roses and spirals that are messy in x and y become one short equation.

nodes.name: Complex Numbers in Trig Form
nodes.desc: Writing complex numbers with a length and an angle, then using De Moivre's theorem to raise them to powers. It ties algebra, geometry and trig together.

nodes.name: Modeling Repeating Things
nodes.desc: Using sine curves to model tides, daylight hours and Ferris wheels. Pick the midline and amplitude from the data first, then the period.

nodes.name: Functions Review
nodes.desc: Domain, range and function notation, done fast. Precalc assumes all of this, so shore up any gaps in the first two weeks.

nodes.name: Transformations
nodes.desc: Shifts, stretches and reflections of a parent graph. Learn what each change to the equation does and you can sketch most graphs in seconds.

nodes.name: Polynomials
nodes.desc: End behavior, zeros and multiplicity. You'll be able to sketch a degree-five graph from its factored form without a calculator.

nodes.name: Polynomial Division
nodes.desc: Long division and synthetic division, plus the remainder and factor theorems. It's how you crack open a cubic once you've found one root.

nodes.name: Rational Functions
nodes.desc: Fractions of polynomials, with holes, vertical asymptotes and horizontal ones. Factor first, cancel second, and the graph tells you the rest.

nodes.name: Exponential Functions
nodes.desc: Growth and decay by a fixed percent each step. Compound interest, populations and half-life are all this one shape.

nodes.name: Logarithms
nodes.desc: The inverse of an exponential, and the laws that let you bring exponents down. Most log mistakes are the product rule used backwards.

nodes.name: Exponential & Log Equations
nodes.desc: Solving for a variable stuck in an exponent. Take a log of both sides, and always check for answers that break the domain.

nodes.name: Inverse & Composite Functions
nodes.desc: Putting one function inside another, and undoing a function. The horizontal line test tells you when an inverse even exists.

nodes.name: Piecewise & Absolute Value
nodes.desc: Functions with different rules on different intervals. Calculus teachers use them to test whether you really get limits, so get comfortable now.

nodes.name: Trig Functions
nodes.desc: The unit circle, radians and the six trig graphs as functions. If trig was shaky last year, this is your second chance.

nodes.name: Identities & Equations
nodes.desc: Simplifying and solving with trig identities. It's mostly algebra wearing a costume, so lean on your factoring.

nodes.name: Sequences & Series
nodes.desc: Arithmetic and geometric patterns and their sums. Sigma notation looks scary but it's just a compact loop.

nodes.name: Conic Sections
nodes.desc: Circles, ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas from their equations. Completing the square turns a messy equation into one you can read.

nodes.name: Vectors
nodes.desc: Quantities with size and direction, added tip to tail. Physics leans on this heavily, so it pays off twice.

nodes.name: Polar & Parametric
nodes.desc: Curves drawn by an angle or by time instead of by x. Parametric equations are how you describe something moving.

nodes.name: Matrices
nodes.desc: Grids of numbers for solving systems and moving points around. A preview of linear algebra that shows up on some precalc finals.

nodes.name: Intro to Limits
nodes.desc: What a function heads toward near a point. It's the first idea of calculus, and seeing it early makes the first month of calc much easier.

nodes.name: Calc-Ready
nodes.desc: Mixed review where you choose the tool yourself. If you can do a page of these without notes, you're ready for calculus.

nodes.name: Expressions
nodes.desc: Letters standing in for numbers, plus combining like terms. Get this smooth and every later equation gets shorter.

nodes.name: Solving Equations
nodes.desc: Doing the same thing to both sides until x stands alone. Check your answer by plugging it back in, every time.

nodes.name: Multi-Step Equations
nodes.desc: Distributing, clearing fractions and variables on both sides. Write one step per line so mistakes have nowhere to hide.

nodes.name: Inequalities
nodes.desc: Solving with less-than and greater-than, then graphing on a number line. Flip the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative.

nodes.name: Slope & Lines
nodes.desc: Rise over run, slope-intercept form and point-slope form. Read the slope as a rate, like dollars per hour, and word problems get easy.

nodes.name: Systems of Equations
nodes.desc: Two equations, two unknowns, solved by graphing, substitution or elimination. Pick the method that makes the numbers nicest.

nodes.name: Exponent Rules
nodes.desc: Multiplying powers, powers of powers and negative exponents. Most mistakes come from adding exponents that should be multiplied.

nodes.name: Polynomials
nodes.desc: Adding, subtracting and multiplying polynomials. FOIL is just the distributive property done twice.

nodes.name: Factoring
nodes.desc: Pulling out common factors, trinomials and the difference of squares. Factoring is multiplying backwards, so check by multiplying out.

nodes.name: Quadratic Equations
nodes.desc: Solving by factoring, completing the square or the quadratic formula. The discriminant tells you how many answers to expect.

nodes.name: Functions & Notation
nodes.desc: f of x, domain, range and reading graphs. A function is a machine that gives one output for each input.

nodes.name: Radicals
nodes.desc: Simplifying square roots and rationalizing denominators. Radicals are just fractional exponents wearing a hat.

nodes.name: Rational Expressions
nodes.desc: Fractions with polynomials in them. Factor everything first, then cancel, then watch for values that break the denominator.

nodes.name: Exponential Functions
nodes.desc: Growth and decay by a percent each step. Compound interest is the one example worth knowing cold.

nodes.name: Logarithms
nodes.desc: The inverse of an exponential. Logs let you solve for a variable stuck up in an exponent.

nodes.name: Complex Numbers
nodes.desc: The number i, where i squared is negative one. They show up when a quadratic has no real answers.

nodes.name: Modeling With Functions
nodes.desc: Picking linear, quadratic or exponential to fit real data. The shape of the data tells you which one to try first.

nodes.name: Algebra 2 Final Review
nodes.desc: Mixed problems where you have to choose the tool yourself. If you can do these, precalc will feel familiar.

nodes.name: Points, Lines & Planes
nodes.desc: The undefined terms and how geometry builds on them. Precise words matter here more than in any other math class.

nodes.name: Angle Relationships
nodes.desc: Vertical, supplementary and complementary angles. Mark every angle you know on the diagram before doing anything else.

nodes.name: Parallel Lines
nodes.desc: Transversals and the angle pairs they make. Alternate interior angles are equal, and proofs lean on that a lot.

nodes.name: Triangle Basics
nodes.desc: The angle sum, exterior angles and the triangle inequality. Triangles are the building block for almost everything after.

nodes.name: Logic & Reasoning
nodes.desc: If-then statements, converses and counterexamples. One counterexample is enough to sink a claim.

nodes.name: Congruent Triangles
nodes.desc: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and HL as proof shortcuts. Know which ones work and why SSA doesn't.

nodes.name: Two-Column Proofs
nodes.desc: Statements on the left, reasons on the right. Start from what you are given, and work toward what you need with every step justified.

nodes.name: Similar Triangles
nodes.desc: Same shape, different size, with proportional sides. Shadows and map scales are similar-triangle problems in disguise.

nodes.name: Right Triangles
nodes.desc: The Pythagorean theorem and the special 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles. Learn the special ones and you'll skip a lot of work.

nodes.name: Quadrilaterals
nodes.desc: Parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses, squares and trapezoids. Know which properties each one inherits from the one above it.

nodes.name: Transformations
nodes.desc: Translations, reflections, rotations and dilations on the coordinate plane. Track one point at a time when they stack up.

nodes.name: Circles
nodes.desc: Arcs, chords, tangents and inscribed angles. An inscribed angle is half the arc it cuts off.

nodes.name: Area & Perimeter
nodes.desc: Formulas for polygons and circles, and splitting odd shapes into easy ones. Write the formula before plugging in numbers.

nodes.name: Surface Area & Volume
nodes.desc: Prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres. Pyramids and cones are one third of the matching prism or cylinder.

nodes.name: Coordinate Geometry
nodes.desc: Distance, midpoint and slope to prove things with algebra. It is often easier than a classic proof.

nodes.name: Constructions
nodes.desc: Copying angles, bisecting and building shapes with only a compass and straightedge. It shows why the theorems are true.

nodes.name: Intro to Trig
nodes.desc: Sine, cosine and tangent in right triangles. This is the bridge into the full trigonometry course.

nodes.name: Geometry Final Review
nodes.desc: Mixed problems and proofs from the whole year. Draw a big, labeled diagram for every single problem.

nodes.name: The Method
nodes.desc: Turning a question into something an experiment could actually settle, with a control and a prediction that could fail. The willingness to be wrong is the part that makes it work.

nodes.name: Asking a Testable Question
nodes.desc: Narrowing an interest into something with a measurable answer. "Does this work" becomes "does this change that, by how much, compared with what" before any apparatus is touched.

nodes.name: Units & Dimensions
nodes.desc: Every quantity carries a unit, and units follow through a calculation like algebra. Checking that they come out right catches more mistakes than rechecking the arithmetic.

nodes.name: Measurement
nodes.desc: Getting a number off an instrument and knowing how much of it to believe. Precision, accuracy and uncertainty are three different things, and reporting all three honestly is the skill.

nodes.name: Uncertainty & Error
nodes.desc: Every measurement is a range rather than a value, and the ranges combine through a calculation in predictable ways. A result quoted without one is not yet a scientific result.

nodes.name: Data & Graphs
nodes.desc: Turning readings into a picture that shows the relationship. Which variable goes on which axis, and whether a line through the points is justified at all, are decisions rather than conventions.

nodes.name: Variables & Controls
nodes.desc: Changing one thing, holding the rest still, and knowing what you failed to hold still. A result from an experiment with two things changing at once cannot be attributed to either.

nodes.name: Laboratory Practice
nodes.desc: Working safely and repeatably: hazards read before starting, equipment used properly, and everything recorded as it happens rather than afterwards from memory.

nodes.name: Recording Results
nodes.desc: A notebook somebody else could repeat the work from, including the readings that went wrong. Tidying data as you record it is how the interesting anomaly gets lost.

nodes.name: Models
nodes.desc: A simplified description that predicts something. Every model is wrong in some respect on purpose, and knowing which simplification you made is what tells you where it will fail.

nodes.name: Scale & Orders of Magnitude
nodes.desc: Estimating roughly before calculating precisely, and noticing when an answer is a thousand times too large. Scientists check a result against a rough estimate before they check the arithmetic.

nodes.name: Statistics for Science
nodes.desc: Deciding whether a difference is bigger than the noise, and how large it is. The effect size answers whether it matters; significance only answers whether it is probably there.

nodes.name: Weighing Evidence
nodes.desc: One study is a data point rather than a finding. Sample size, design and whether anybody has reproduced it decide how much weight a result can carry.

nodes.name: Reproducibility
nodes.desc: Somebody else getting your result from your description. It is the mechanism that makes science self-correcting, and it works only when methods are published in enough detail to follow.

nodes.name: Scientific Writing
nodes.desc: Method, results and discussion kept strictly apart, so a reader can disagree with your interpretation while accepting your data. The separation is the discipline, not the format.

nodes.name: Reading & Reviewing Papers
nodes.desc: Reading the methods before the abstract, and the figures before the conclusion. Peer review filters rather than verifies, which is why a published paper is a claim and not a fact.

nodes.name: Research Ethics
nodes.desc: Consent, welfare, honest reporting and declaring who paid for the work. Presenting an exploratory finding as though it had been the hypothesis all along is the commonest quiet dishonesty in the field.

nodes.name: Communicating Science
nodes.desc: Explaining a result to people who will not read the paper, without overstating it. Most public misunderstanding of science is generated at exactly this step rather than in the laboratory.

nodes.name: Kinematics
nodes.desc: Describing motion without asking what causes it: position, velocity, acceleration and the equations linking them. Getting comfortable that acceleration is a change in velocity rather than a large velocity is half the battle.

nodes.name: Vectors in Physics
nodes.desc: Quantities with a direction, and splitting them into components along axes you chose. Choosing the axes well turns a two-dimensional problem into two one-dimensional ones.

nodes.name: Newton Laws
nodes.desc: Force changes motion, forces come in pairs, and a body with no net force keeps doing exactly what it was doing. The third law is the one people state correctly and apply to the wrong body.

nodes.name: Free-Body Diagrams
nodes.desc: Drawing one object and every force acting on it, and nothing else. It is not a study aid; on most problems it is where the answer comes from, and skipping it is why the algebra goes wrong.

nodes.name: Friction & Circular Motion
nodes.desc: Contact forces that resist sliding, and the fact that going round a corner at constant speed is still accelerating. Centrifugal force does not appear in any of these diagrams, and that is the point.

nodes.name: Work & Energy
nodes.desc: A bookkeeping quantity that is never created or destroyed, only moved. It answers in one line what tracking forces through a changing geometry takes ten to answer.

nodes.name: Momentum
nodes.desc: Mass times velocity, conserved in every collision whether or not energy is. That difference is exactly what separates a bounce from a crash, and it is the reason both are solvable.

nodes.name: Rotation
nodes.desc: Every linear idea again with angles: torque for force, moment of inertia for mass, angular momentum for momentum. The structure repeats exactly, which makes it far less work than it first looks.

nodes.name: Gravitation
nodes.desc: One law covering a dropped apple and a moon, falling off with the square of distance. Orbits are the first case where an object is falling continuously and never arriving.

nodes.name: Fluids
nodes.desc: Pressure, buoyancy and flow. Pressure depending only on depth rather than on the shape of the container is the counterintuitive fact that makes hydraulics work.

nodes.name: Heat & Temperature
nodes.desc: Temperature is how fast the particles jiggle; heat is energy moving because of a temperature difference. Treating them as one thing makes every later result impossible to state properly.

nodes.name: Laws of Thermodynamics
nodes.desc: Energy is conserved, and disorder in a closed system does not decrease. The second law is what forbids perpetual motion and what gives time a direction at all.

nodes.name: Waves
nodes.desc: Energy traveling without matter traveling with it. Frequency, wavelength and speed are locked together, so a wave entering a new medium must change one of them.

nodes.name: Sound & Resonance
nodes.desc: Pressure waves in a medium, and the frequencies at which a system prefers to vibrate. Resonance explains a wine glass shattering and a bridge closing for repairs.

nodes.name: Light & Optics
nodes.desc: Reflection, refraction, lenses and the fact that light bends because it changes speed. Interference is the experiment that ended the argument about whether light is a wave.

nodes.name: Electric Fields
nodes.desc: Charge, and the field describing what a charge would feel at each point. Mathematically the same shape as gravity, with the crucial difference that it can push as well as pull.

nodes.name: Circuits
nodes.desc: Current, voltage and resistance, and the two conservation rules that solve any network of them. Voltage is a difference, and forgetting that is why a bird on a power line is fine.

nodes.name: Magnetism
nodes.desc: Moving charge makes a field, a changing field makes moving charge. That loop is every motor and every generator, and it is what unified electricity and magnetism into one subject.

nodes.name: Electromagnetic Waves
nodes.desc: Fields regenerating each other and propagating at a speed the equations predict outright. That speed turning out to be the speed of light is one of the great results in physics.

nodes.name: Quantum Physics
nodes.desc: Energy arriving in lumps, particles behaving like waves, and outcomes that are probabilities rather than certainties. Strange, exactly right experimentally, and the basis of every semiconductor.

nodes.name: Relativity
nodes.desc: What follows from the speed of light being the same for everybody: time and length stop being absolute. Every satellite fix you use corrects for it, which is as practical as a revolution gets.

nodes.name: The Design Process
nodes.desc: Define the problem, brainstorm, build, test and improve. Real engineering loops through it many times.

nodes.name: Sketching Ideas
nodes.desc: Quick drawings to think and explain. A rough sketch beats a perfect one that takes an hour.

nodes.name: Requirements & Constraints
nodes.desc: Budget, size, weight, time and safety. Write them down before you design anything.

nodes.name: Units & Estimation
nodes.desc: Keeping units straight and making rough estimates. A quick estimate catches answers that are off by a thousand.

nodes.name: Forces & Statics
nodes.desc: Free-body diagrams for things that stay still, like bridges and shelves. Every force has to balance.

nodes.name: Materials
nodes.desc: Strength, stiffness and weight of wood, metal and plastic. The right material is often the cheapest fix.

nodes.name: CAD Modeling
nodes.desc: Turning sketches into 3D models with real dimensions. Models let you test fit before cutting anything.

nodes.name: Prototyping
nodes.desc: Cardboard, 3D prints and quick builds. Build cheap first so failures are cheap too.

nodes.name: Circuits Basics
nodes.desc: Voltage, current and resistance with Ohm's law. Most projects end up needing a little electronics.

nodes.name: Testing & Data
nodes.desc: Planning fair tests and recording results. Data beats opinions when picking between designs.

nodes.name: Trade-Offs & Decision Matrices
nodes.desc: Scoring options against the requirements. Every design gives up something to get something else.

nodes.name: Mechanisms
nodes.desc: Levers, gears, pulleys and linkages. Every simple machine trades force for distance.

nodes.name: Safety & Failure
nodes.desc: Factors of safety and learning from famous failures. Engineers design for what can go wrong.

nodes.name: Engineering Notebook
nodes.desc: Recording decisions, data and changes as you go. Judges and teams both rely on it.

nodes.name: Fields of Engineering
nodes.desc: Mechanical, electrical, civil, chemical, biomedical and software. Try small projects in a few before you pick.

nodes.name: A Capstone Project
nodes.desc: Solving a real problem from start to finish. It makes a strong portfolio piece for college.

nodes.name: States of Matter
nodes.desc: Solid, liquid and gas as three arrangements of the same particles with different energies. Almost every everyday chemical fact is a statement about how tightly particles are held and how fast they move.

nodes.name: Atoms & Elements
nodes.desc: Protons decide what element it is, neutrons decide the isotope, electrons decide the chemistry. Everything else in the subject is a consequence of that last one.

nodes.name: The Periodic Table
nodes.desc: The elements arranged so that a column shares behavior. It is a prediction machine rather than a reference list: position tells you reactivity, size and what charge an atom is likely to take.

nodes.name: Electron Configuration
nodes.desc: Where electrons sit around a nucleus, in shells and orbitals with room for a fixed number each. The outermost shell being full or nearly full explains why the noble gases do nothing and the halogens do everything.

nodes.name: Bonding
nodes.desc: Atoms sharing or transferring electrons to reach a stable arrangement. Ionic, covalent and metallic are three answers to one question, and which one you get is largely readable off the periodic table.

nodes.name: Molecular Shape
nodes.desc: Electron pairs pushing each other apart, giving molecules definite three-dimensional shapes. Shape decides polarity, polarity decides solubility, and that chain is why water behaves as it does.

nodes.name: The Mole
nodes.desc: A count, like a dozen, chosen so that atomic mass in grams contains one of them. It is the bridge between the mass you can weigh and the number of particles that actually react.

nodes.name: Formulae & Equations
nodes.desc: Writing what reacted and what came out, balanced so no atoms appear or vanish. The balancing is conservation of mass written down, not a puzzle convention.

nodes.name: Stoichiometry
nodes.desc: Using the equation as a recipe: how much of this makes how much of that. Finding the reagent that runs out first is the step that converts a chemical question into an arithmetic one.

nodes.name: Solutions & Concentration
nodes.desc: Dissolving, and saying how much is dissolved per unit of solution. Nearly all reactions you will meet happen in solution, because particles have to meet to react.

nodes.name: Reaction Types
nodes.desc: The handful of patterns most reactions fall into. Combination, decomposition, displacement, combustion. Recognizing the pattern lets you predict products you have never been taught.

nodes.name: Energy in Reactions
nodes.desc: Breaking bonds costs energy and making them releases it; the difference is what you feel as hot or cold. It also explains why a reaction that releases energy overall still needs a match.

nodes.name: Reaction Rates
nodes.desc: How fast, and the four things that change it: concentration, temperature, surface area and a catalyst. All four work through the same mechanism. How often particles collide hard enough.

nodes.name: Equilibrium
nodes.desc: Reactions that run both ways at once and settle where the two rates match. Nothing has stopped at equilibrium, which is why disturbing it makes the mixture visibly shift to absorb the change.

nodes.name: Acids & Bases
nodes.desc: Donating and accepting protons, measured on a scale where each step is a factor of ten. Buffers resisting change are what keep blood and seawater within the narrow band life needs.

nodes.name: Oxidation & Reduction
nodes.desc: Electrons moving from one species to another, always in pairs of half-reactions. Rusting, respiration and every battery are the same accounting done in different settings.

nodes.name: Electrochemistry
nodes.desc: Driving a redox reaction with electricity or getting electricity out of one. Cells, plating and corrosion protection all fall out of putting the two half-reactions in separate compartments.

nodes.name: Organic Chemistry
nodes.desc: The chemistry of carbon, which bonds four ways and to itself indefinitely. Functional groups are the vocabulary: learn what each one does and a million compounds become a few dozen behaviors.

nodes.name: Laboratory Practice
nodes.desc: Measuring, titrating, purifying and recording it so somebody else could repeat it. Technique is where the uncertainty in a result actually comes from, long before the arithmetic.

nodes.name: Analytical Chemistry
nodes.desc: Working out what a sample actually contains, by spectroscopy, chromatography and titration. Identification and quantification are separate problems, and most real questions need both answered.

nodes.name: Why Carbon
nodes.desc: Carbon makes four bonds and loves bonding to itself. That's why there are millions of organic compounds and why this class has its own reputation.

nodes.name: Skeletal Structures
nodes.desc: Drawing molecules as zigzag lines with the hydrogens left out. You'll draw thousands of these, so get fast and get neat.

nodes.name: Naming Compounds
nodes.desc: IUPAC names from the longest chain and its branches. Naming feels like busywork until you need to read a lab procedure.

nodes.name: Functional Groups
nodes.desc: Alcohols, ketones, amines, acids and the rest. The group decides how a molecule reacts, so knowing them on sight is the whole game.

nodes.name: Resonance
nodes.desc: One molecule, several drawings, and the real thing is a blend. Push electrons with curved arrows and leave the atoms where they are.

nodes.name: Acids & Bases in Orgo
nodes.desc: pKa tables and what makes a proton easy to pull off. Almost every mechanism starts with an acid-base step, so this pays off all year.

nodes.name: Conformations
nodes.desc: Newman projections and chair cyclohexanes. Build a model kit once and these stop being flat puzzles.

nodes.name: Stereochemistry
nodes.desc: Chirality, R and S, and molecules that are mirror images. It's the topic most students find hardest to see, so use models.

nodes.name: Curved Arrows & Mechanisms
nodes.desc: Showing where electrons go in a reaction. Memorizing reactions doesn't scale. Understanding arrows does.

nodes.name: SN1 & SN2
nodes.desc: Substitution reactions and how to tell which path wins. Look at the substrate, the nucleophile, the leaving group and the solvent.

nodes.name: E1 & E2
nodes.desc: Elimination reactions that make double bonds, and how they compete with substitution. Bulky bases change who wins, so watch for them.

nodes.name: Alkene Reactions
nodes.desc: Adding things across a double bond. Markovnikov's rule and its exceptions cover most exam questions.

nodes.name: Carbonyl Chemistry
nodes.desc: Aldehydes, ketones and the reactions at the C=O. The carbon is slightly positive, and nearly everything follows from that.

nodes.name: Multistep Synthesis
nodes.desc: Planning how to build a target from simple starting materials. Work backwards from the product, one bond at a time.

nodes.name: Aromatic Rings
nodes.desc: Benzene and why it's so stable. Electrophilic substitution and directing groups are the heart of second-semester orgo.

nodes.name: IR & NMR
nodes.desc: Reading a spectrum to work out a structure. Start with the IR for functional groups, then let the NMR count the hydrogens.

nodes.name: Orgo Lab Skills
nodes.desc: Recrystallization, distillation, extraction and TLC. Good technique is how you get a yield worth writing up.

nodes.name: Biomolecules
nodes.desc: Sugars, amino acids and fats seen as organic molecules. This is where orgo connects to biochem and the MCAT.

nodes.name: What Life Is
nodes.desc: The shared properties of living things: organization, metabolism, response, reproduction. The borderline cases are the interesting part, which is why a virus is still argued about.

nodes.name: Cells
nodes.desc: The smallest unit that is alive, and the compartments inside it that do separate jobs. Every organism is one of these or a colony of them cooperating.

nodes.name: Membranes & Transport
nodes.desc: A boundary that decides what gets in and out, some of it for free and some at a cost. Osmosis is the case worth being fluent in, because it explains wilting, swelling and why saltwater dehydrates you.

nodes.name: Biological Molecules
nodes.desc: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Four families doing nearly everything. Structure predicts function throughout, which is why a change to one amino acid can break an entire organism.

nodes.name: Enzymes
nodes.desc: Proteins that make a specific reaction fast enough to be useful at body temperature. Their shape is the whole mechanism, which is why heat and the wrong acidity destroy them permanently.

nodes.name: Respiration
nodes.desc: Releasing energy from food into a form a cell can spend. The aerobic route yields far more than the anaerobic one, which is exactly why muscles burn when the oxygen runs short.

nodes.name: Photosynthesis
nodes.desc: Building sugar out of air and water using light. Nearly every calorie in every food chain entered biology through this reaction, which makes it the most important one on the planet.

nodes.name: DNA
nodes.desc: A four-letter code that stores instructions and copies itself accurately. The pairing rule is the whole trick: each strand carries enough information to rebuild the other.

nodes.name: Protein Synthesis
nodes.desc: Copying a gene and translating it three letters at a time into a chain of amino acids. This is where a sequence stops being information and starts being a working machine.

nodes.name: Cell Division
nodes.desc: One cell becoming two identical ones for growth, or four half-loaded ones for reproduction. The second kind shuffles the deck, which is where most of the variation in a population comes from.

nodes.name: Genetics
nodes.desc: How traits pass down, and why an unexpressed variant can reappear generations later. The simple dominant and recessive cases are the exception; most traits are many genes and an environment.

nodes.name: Mutation & Variation
nodes.desc: Copying errors and damage, most of which do nothing and some of which change a protein. Variation is not a defect in the system; without it a population cannot respond to anything.

nodes.name: Evolution
nodes.desc: Heritable variation plus differential survival, repeated. It requires no foresight and no goal, which is the part that is hard to hold onto while reading about adaptation.

nodes.name: Classification
nodes.desc: Grouping organisms by shared ancestry rather than by resemblance. Convergence is why a dolphin and a shark look alike and sit nowhere near each other on the tree.

nodes.name: Organ Systems
nodes.desc: Cells into tissues into organs into systems, each solving a problem that a single cell solves by diffusion alone. Size is the reason multicellular life needs any of this machinery.

nodes.name: Homeostasis
nodes.desc: Holding internal conditions steady while the outside moves, by negative feedback. Temperature, blood sugar and water balance are three instances of one control pattern.

nodes.name: Nerves & Hormones
nodes.desc: Two signaling systems: one electrical and fast down a fixed wire, one chemical and slow but reaching everywhere. Which one a body uses for a job is decided by how quickly the answer is needed.

nodes.name: Immunity
nodes.desc: Distinguishing self from not-self, and remembering an intruder well enough to answer faster next time. Vaccination is that memory installed without the illness that would normally create it.

nodes.name: Ecology
nodes.desc: Organisms interacting with each other and with the physical world. Energy flows through and is lost at each step; matter cycles round, which is why food chains are short and nutrients are not.

nodes.name: Populations
nodes.desc: Growth, limits and the interactions that hold numbers where they are. Exponential growth meeting a ceiling is the model behind conservation, epidemics and pest control alike.

nodes.name: Biotechnology
nodes.desc: Reading, editing and building with the same molecules. The techniques are now routine enough that the interesting constraints are ethical and ecological rather than technical.

nodes.name: Water & pH
nodes.desc: Why water is such a good solvent and how pH and buffers keep cells working. Everything in a cell happens in water, so start here.

nodes.name: Bonds That Matter
nodes.desc: Covalent bonds, hydrogen bonds and the weak forces that fold molecules. Weak bonds are the ones that make life flexible.

nodes.name: Amino Acids
nodes.desc: The twenty building blocks of proteins and their side chains. Group them by charge and polarity instead of memorizing a list.

nodes.name: Protein Structure
nodes.desc: Primary through quaternary structure. Shape decides function, and one wrong amino acid can wreck the shape.

nodes.name: Enzymes
nodes.desc: Proteins that speed up reactions. Learn active sites, substrates and what heat and pH do to them.

nodes.name: Enzyme Kinetics
nodes.desc: Michaelis-Menten, Km, Vmax and the Lineweaver-Burk plot. Know exactly what each kind of inhibitor does to the graph.

nodes.name: Carbohydrates
nodes.desc: Sugars, starches and fiber, and how glucose links into chains. Cells burn them, store them and use them as name tags.

nodes.name: Lipids & Membranes
nodes.desc: Fats, phospholipids and cholesterol. Membranes form on their own because of how lipids treat water.

nodes.name: Nucleic Acids
nodes.desc: DNA and RNA as molecules, with their bases, pairing and backbone. The chemistry explains why DNA lasts and RNA is short-lived.

nodes.name: Energy & ATP
nodes.desc: How cells store and spend energy with ATP. Coupled reactions are the trick that lets uphill reactions happen.

nodes.name: Glycolysis
nodes.desc: The first steps in breaking down glucose. Know the inputs, the outputs and the steps that get regulated.

nodes.name: The Krebs Cycle
nodes.desc: Where carbon from food leaves as CO2. Track the carriers that pick up electrons more than every single intermediate.

nodes.name: Electron Transport
nodes.desc: The chain in the mitochondria that makes most of your ATP. A proton gradient across a membrane drives the whole thing.

nodes.name: Photosynthesis Chemistry
nodes.desc: The light reactions and the Calvin cycle at the molecular level. It's a lot like the electron transport chain run backwards.

nodes.name: Metabolic Regulation
nodes.desc: How hormones and feedback turn pathways up and down. Insulin and glucagon are the classic pair to know cold.

nodes.name: Cell Signaling
nodes.desc: Receptors, second messengers and cascades. One signal outside the cell can flip thousands of switches inside.

nodes.name: Biochem Lab Methods
nodes.desc: Gels, assays and spectrophotometry. Knowing how the data gets made helps you read the graphs in a paper.

nodes.name: Biochem of Disease
nodes.desc: Diabetes, sickle cell and other conditions explained at the molecular level. This is where biochem starts to feel like medicine.

nodes.name: The Microbial World
nodes.desc: Bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists and viruses, and how small they are. Most of them are harmless, and plenty are useful.

nodes.name: Using a Microscope
nodes.desc: Focusing, staining and making a wet mount. Most bad lab drawings come from rushing the focus.

nodes.name: Bacterial Cells
nodes.desc: No nucleus, a cell wall and DNA in a loop. Shape and wall type tell you a lot about a microbe.

nodes.name: Gram Staining
nodes.desc: Purple or pink tells you about the cell wall. It's still the first test in a hospital lab.

nodes.name: Aseptic Technique
nodes.desc: Working without contaminating your sample or yourself. Flame the loop, keep lids close and label everything.

nodes.name: Growing Cultures
nodes.desc: Agar plates, streaking for single colonies and incubation. One clean colony is the starting point of most experiments.

nodes.name: Microbial Growth
nodes.desc: Lag, log, stationary and death phases. Bacteria can double in twenty minutes, which is why food safety rules exist.

nodes.name: Microbial Metabolism
nodes.desc: Some microbes need oxygen, some hate it and some ferment. Bread, yogurt and cheese all depend on this.

nodes.name: Bacterial Genetics
nodes.desc: Plasmids and how bacteria swap genes. Sharing genes sideways is how resistance spreads so fast.

nodes.name: Viruses
nodes.desc: Genetic material in a protein coat that needs a host to copy itself. They're the reason flu shots change every year.

nodes.name: Fungi & Protists
nodes.desc: Yeasts, molds and single-celled eukaryotes. Some make bread rise, and one kind causes malaria.

nodes.name: Controlling Microbes
nodes.desc: Heat, disinfectants and antiseptics, and which one to use when. Sterile and clean mean very different things.

nodes.name: Antibiotics & Resistance
nodes.desc: How drugs target bacteria and how bacteria fight back. Finishing the full course of pills matters for a reason.

nodes.name: Microbes & Immunity
nodes.desc: How your body spots invaders and remembers them. Vaccines work by giving the immune system a safe practice run.

nodes.name: Infectious Disease
nodes.desc: How germs spread, cause harm and get diagnosed. Koch's postulates are the classic test for proving a microbe causes a disease.

nodes.name: Epidemiology
nodes.desc: Tracking outbreaks with data. Learn R0, contact tracing and why case counts lag behind reality.

nodes.name: Microbes in the Environment
nodes.desc: Nitrogen fixing, decomposition and the gut microbiome. The planet quietly runs on microbes.

nodes.name: Microbes in Biotech
nodes.desc: Using bacteria to make insulin, enzymes and vaccines. Most biotech starts with a microbe doing the work.

nodes.name: The Neuron
nodes.desc: Dendrites, cell body, axon and terminals. Every thought and movement runs on this one cell type.

nodes.name: Brain Regions
nodes.desc: Lobes, the brainstem, the cerebellum and the limbic system. Learn the map first, and the details hang on it later.

nodes.name: Action Potentials
nodes.desc: How a neuron fires using sodium and potassium. It's all or nothing, and the graph is a favorite test question.

nodes.name: Synapses
nodes.desc: Where one neuron talks to the next with chemicals. Most drugs do their work right here.

nodes.name: Spinal Cord & Reflexes
nodes.desc: The highway between brain and body, and reflexes that skip the brain entirely. Pulling your hand off a hot stove is a reflex arc.

nodes.name: Neurotransmitters
nodes.desc: Dopamine, serotonin, GABA and glutamate, and what each tends to do. Real brains are messier than the simple labels.

nodes.name: Senses
nodes.desc: How eyes, ears, skin, nose and tongue turn the world into signals. Your brain fills in a lot of what you think you see.

nodes.name: Vision
nodes.desc: Rods, cones and the path from retina to the back of the brain. Optical illusions show the shortcuts your visual system takes.

nodes.name: Movement
nodes.desc: The motor cortex, cerebellum and basal ganglia working together. Smooth movement takes constant correction.

nodes.name: Neuroplasticity
nodes.desc: The brain rewiring itself every time you use it. It's the science behind why practice works.

nodes.name: Memory
nodes.desc: How the hippocampus helps store memories and why sleep locks them in. Pulling things from memory makes them stick better than rereading.

nodes.name: Sleep & the Brain
nodes.desc: Sleep stages and what the brain does in each. All-nighters before tests work against you, and here's the biology why.

nodes.name: Emotion & Stress
nodes.desc: The amygdala, stress hormones and fight or flight. A little stress sharpens you, and a lot shuts thinking down.

nodes.name: The Teen Brain
nodes.desc: The brain keeps building into your mid-twenties, and the planning parts finish last. It explains a lot about being a teenager.

nodes.name: Studying the Brain
nodes.desc: EEG, fMRI and lesion studies, and what each can and can't show. Brain scans are easy to over-read.

nodes.name: Brain Disorders
nodes.desc: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, depression and epilepsy at a basic level. Each one teaches something about how a healthy brain works.

nodes.name: Drugs & the Brain
nodes.desc: Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine and medications at the synapse. Addiction is what happens when the reward system gets hijacked.

nodes.name: Reading Neuro Research
nodes.desc: Picking apart how a study was designed and what it claims. Headlines about brain science are often way bigger than the results.

nodes.name: Anatomical Terms
nodes.desc: Directions, planes and body regions, like anterior and proximal. Learning the words first makes every later chapter faster.

nodes.name: Tissues
nodes.desc: Epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue. Every organ is built from these four.

nodes.name: The Skin
nodes.desc: Layers, glands and how skin heals. It's your biggest organ and your first line of defense.

nodes.name: The Skeleton
nodes.desc: The 206 bones, how bone grows and how joints move. Group bones by region instead of memorizing a flat list.

nodes.name: Muscles
nodes.desc: How muscles contract, and the major muscles with their actions. Learn origin and insertion and the action makes sense.

nodes.name: The Nervous System
nodes.desc: Brain, spinal cord and nerves, and how signals travel. It ties every other system together.

nodes.name: Special Senses
nodes.desc: Eyes, ears, taste and smell. Dissections make these click faster than any diagram.

nodes.name: The Endocrine System
nodes.desc: Glands and hormones that work slower than nerves but last longer. Feedback loops are the key idea.

nodes.name: Blood
nodes.desc: Red cells, white cells, platelets and blood types. Know why a type O donor can give to almost anyone.

nodes.name: The Heart
nodes.desc: Chambers, valves and the path blood takes. Trace one drop of blood all the way around, out loud.

nodes.name: Blood Vessels
nodes.desc: Arteries, veins and capillaries, and how blood pressure works. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its color.

nodes.name: The Respiratory System
nodes.desc: Airways, alveoli and how gases swap. Breathing rate is driven more by carbon dioxide than by oxygen.

nodes.name: The Digestive System
nodes.desc: From mouth to colon, plus the liver and pancreas. Follow one meal through the whole path.

nodes.name: The Immune System
nodes.desc: Barriers, white blood cells and antibodies. Vaccines train this system before the real threat shows up.

nodes.name: The Urinary System
nodes.desc: Kidneys filter blood and balance water and salts. A nephron is a tiny filter worth drawing from memory.

nodes.name: The Reproductive System
nodes.desc: Anatomy, hormones and development. Treat it like any other system, with the same care for terms.

nodes.name: Homeostasis
nodes.desc: How the body keeps temperature, sugar and pH steady. Almost every test question comes back to this idea.

nodes.name: Disease & Clinical Cases
nodes.desc: Applying what you know to real cases, like diabetes or asthma. Great practice for HOSA, nursing and pre-med.

nodes.name: DNA Structure
nodes.desc: The double helix, base pairing and how DNA copies itself. A pairs with T and C pairs with G, every single time.

nodes.name: Genes & Chromosomes
nodes.desc: How DNA is packed into chromosomes and where genes sit on them. Humans have 23 pairs.

nodes.name: Meiosis
nodes.desc: The cell division that makes eggs and sperm with half the chromosomes. Crossing over is where new combinations come from.

nodes.name: Mendel's Laws
nodes.desc: Dominant and recessive traits, segregation and independent assortment. Mendel worked it all out with pea plants.

nodes.name: Punnett Squares
nodes.desc: Predicting the odds of a cross. They're probability tables, so treat them like one.

nodes.name: Dihybrid Crosses
nodes.desc: Two traits at once, and the classic 9:3:3:1 ratio. Multiplying probabilities beats drawing a sixteen-box square.

nodes.name: Beyond Simple Dominance
nodes.desc: Incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles and polygenic traits. Blood type is the go-to example.

nodes.name: Sex-Linked Traits
nodes.desc: Genes on the X chromosome, like color blindness. That is why some traits show up more in boys.

nodes.name: Pedigrees
nodes.desc: Reading family trees to work out how a trait is inherited. Start with the clues that rule options out.

nodes.name: Gene Expression
nodes.desc: Transcription and translation, from DNA to RNA to protein. The codon chart is your decoder ring.

nodes.name: Gene Regulation
nodes.desc: How cells turn genes on and off. Every cell has the same DNA, so regulation is why a skin cell is not a neuron.

nodes.name: Mutations
nodes.desc: Point mutations, frameshifts and chromosome changes. Most are harmless, and a few cause disease or new traits.

nodes.name: Population Genetics
nodes.desc: Hardy-Weinberg and how allele frequencies change. It connects genetics straight to evolution.

nodes.name: Biotech Tools
nodes.desc: PCR, gel electrophoresis and CRISPR. These are the tools behind DNA tests and gene therapy.

nodes.name: Genetic Disorders
nodes.desc: Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, Down syndrome and more. Link each one to the kind of mutation behind it.

nodes.name: Genetics & Ethics
nodes.desc: Designer babies, genetic privacy and testing. Good answers weigh real benefits against real risks.

nodes.name: Levels of Ecology
nodes.desc: Organism, population, community, ecosystem and biosphere. Know which level a question is asking about before you answer it.

nodes.name: Biomes
nodes.desc: Deserts, forests, tundra, grasslands and oceans. Temperature and rainfall decide which biome you get.

nodes.name: Energy Flow
nodes.desc: Producers, consumers and decomposers, and the ten percent rule. Energy flows through a system and leaks out as heat.

nodes.name: Food Webs
nodes.desc: Who eats whom, drawn as a web. Pull out one species and predict the ripple effects.

nodes.name: Nutrient Cycles
nodes.desc: Carbon, nitrogen and water moving through living and nonliving things. Draw each cycle from memory.

nodes.name: Population Growth
nodes.desc: Exponential and logistic growth and carrying capacity. Real populations rarely grow without limits for long.

nodes.name: Limiting Factors
nodes.desc: Food, space, predators and disease that hold populations in check. Some depend on density and some do not.

nodes.name: Species Interactions
nodes.desc: Predation, competition, mutualism and parasitism. Each one has a plus, minus or zero for each side.

nodes.name: Niches
nodes.desc: The role a species plays and the resources it uses. Two species cannot share the exact same niche for long.

nodes.name: Succession
