nodes.desc: How communities rebuild after a fire or a new island forms. Pioneer species come first and change the place for the next ones.

nodes.name: Biodiversity
nodes.desc: Why more species usually means a sturdier ecosystem. Keystone species hold more weight than their numbers suggest.

nodes.name: Field Sampling
nodes.desc: Quadrats, transects and mark-recapture. You can estimate a whole population without counting every animal.

nodes.name: Human Impact
nodes.desc: Habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and climate change. Link each threat to the ecological idea it breaks.

nodes.name: Conservation
nodes.desc: Protected areas, corridors and restoration. Saving habitat saves more species than saving one at a time.

nodes.name: An Ecology Project
nodes.desc: Studying a real local habitat over time. Great for science fair, and the data is all yours.

nodes.name: Deep Time
nodes.desc: Getting used to spans where a millimeter a year builds a mountain range. Almost every argument against these subjects is really a failure to take four billion years seriously as a number.

nodes.name: Rocks & Minerals
nodes.desc: Three families defined by how they formed: cooled, compressed or transformed. Identifying which one you are holding tells you what was happening where it was made.

nodes.name: Inside the Earth
nodes.desc: Crust, mantle and core, deduced almost entirely from how earthquake waves bend on their way through. Nobody has drilled past the crust, and we still know the structure with confidence.

nodes.name: Plate Tectonics
nodes.desc: A cracked shell moving on a slow-flowing interior. It is the one theory that explains mountains, earthquakes, volcanoes and matching fossils on opposite coasts at the same time.

nodes.name: Earthquakes & Volcanoes
nodes.desc: What happens at the edges where plates meet, and why the hazard maps look the way they do. The magnitude scale is logarithmic, so two steps up is a thousand times the energy.

nodes.name: Reading the Record
nodes.desc: Layers, fossils and radiometric dating as three independent clocks that agree. Their agreement is the evidence, far more than any one of them alone.

nodes.name: Weather
nodes.desc: Uneven heating, moving air and water changing state. Fronts, pressure and humidity between them account for nearly everything a forecast is trying to say.

nodes.name: The Atmosphere
nodes.desc: A thin layered envelope held on by gravity, with almost all the weather in the bottom slice. Its composition is what keeps the surface habitable and what makes changing it consequential.

nodes.name: Oceans & Currents
nodes.desc: A heat store that moves energy around the planet on a conveyor driven by temperature and salt. It is why one coast at a given latitude is temperate and another is not.

nodes.name: Earth Cycles
nodes.desc: Water, carbon, nitrogen and rock, each moving through reservoirs on wildly different timescales. Understanding where a cycle stores things and for how long is what makes any of it predictable.

nodes.name: Climate
nodes.desc: The statistics of weather over decades, and the balance between energy arriving and leaving. Feedbacks are the part that matters: ice reflecting sunlight it no longer reflects once it melts.

nodes.name: Resources & Hazards
nodes.desc: Where useful materials concentrate, and where living is dangerous. Both answers come from the same processes, which is why the most fertile ground is often at the foot of a volcano.

nodes.name: The Sky
nodes.desc: What moves, how often and why, from a fixed spot on a spinning tilted planet. Seasons come from the tilt rather than the distance, which is the most commonly held wrong belief in the subject.

nodes.name: The Solar System
nodes.desc: A star, eight planets and an enormous amount of empty space drawn to scale by almost nobody. Orbits, moons and the division between rocky and gas worlds all trace back to how it formed.

nodes.name: Orbits & Gravity
nodes.desc: Continuous falling that keeps missing the ground. Once that clicks, tides, satellites and why astronauts float all stop being separate facts.

nodes.name: Light from Space
nodes.desc: Almost everything known about the universe arrived as light. Splitting it reveals composition, temperature and motion, which is how a chemical analysis of a star is possible at all.

nodes.name: Stars
nodes.desc: Fusion holding gravity off for billions of years, then losing. How a star dies depends almost entirely on its mass, and the heavy elements you are made of came from those deaths.

nodes.name: Galaxies
nodes.desc: Hundreds of billions of stars bound together, rotating faster at the edges than the visible mass allows. That discrepancy is the observation that put dark matter on the table.

nodes.name: Cosmology
nodes.desc: The universe as one object with a history: expanding, cooling, and leaving a faint glow behind. Distant galaxies receding faster the further away they are is the observation the whole picture rests on.

nodes.name: Observation & Instruments
nodes.desc: Telescopes, satellites, cores and seismographs. Evidence gathered where an experiment is impossible. Every one of these subjects advances by finding a new thing to measure rather than a new thing to try.

nodes.name: Earth as a System
nodes.desc: Rock, air, water and life as four coupled parts that have shaped each other for billions of years. Oxygen in the atmosphere is biological in origin, which is the clearest case of the coupling running both ways.

nodes.name: Reading the Night Sky
nodes.desc: Constellations, bright stars and how the sky turns overnight. Learn five constellations and the rest fall into place.

nodes.name: Sky Motions
nodes.desc: Daily rotation, the seasons and why the stars shift through the year. Earth tilts, and that tilt does most of the work.

nodes.name: Moon Phases & Eclipses
nodes.desc: Why the moon changes shape and when eclipses happen. Draw the sun, earth and moon from above and it clicks.

nodes.name: Using a Telescope
nodes.desc: Aperture, magnification and finding objects. Start with the moon, then Jupiter and Saturn.

nodes.name: Gravity & Orbits
nodes.desc: Kepler's laws and Newton's gravity. Orbits are just falling and missing, forever.

nodes.name: Light & Spectra
nodes.desc: How astronomers learn what stars are made of from their light alone. Each element leaves its own barcode.

nodes.name: The Planets
nodes.desc: Rocky planets, gas giants and ice giants, and what makes each one weird. Compare them by size, distance and atmosphere.

nodes.name: Moons, Asteroids & Comets
nodes.desc: The small bodies of the solar system. Some moons may hide oceans that could hold life.

nodes.name: The Sun
nodes.desc: Fusion in the core, sunspots and solar flares. The sun is an average star that happens to be very close.

nodes.name: Star Properties
nodes.desc: Brightness, temperature, size and the HR diagram. The HR diagram is the single most useful chart in astronomy.

nodes.name: Lives of Stars
nodes.desc: Nebulae, main sequence, red giants, white dwarfs and supernovae. A star's mass decides its whole story.

nodes.name: Black Holes & Neutron Stars
nodes.desc: What is left after the biggest stars die. Gravity gets so strong that light cannot escape a black hole.

nodes.name: Galaxies
nodes.desc: Spirals, ellipticals and the Milky Way. There are more galaxies than anyone can count.

nodes.name: Cosmology
nodes.desc: The Big Bang, the expanding universe and dark matter. Looking far away means looking back in time.

nodes.name: Exoplanets
nodes.desc: Planets around other stars, found by dips in starlight and wobbles. Thousands are known, and more turn up every month.

nodes.name: Observing Projects
nodes.desc: Logging observations, astrophotography and contests like the Science Olympiad astronomy event. Keep a sky journal.

nodes.name: Minerals
nodes.desc: Identifying minerals by hardness, luster, streak and cleavage. A streak plate and a nail do a lot of the work.

nodes.name: The Rock Cycle
nodes.desc: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks and how each turns into the others. There is no start or end to the cycle.

nodes.name: Igneous Rocks
nodes.desc: Rocks cooled from magma or lava. Big crystals mean slow cooling deep underground.

nodes.name: Sedimentary Rocks
nodes.desc: Layers of sand, mud and shells pressed into rock over time. This is where fossils live.

nodes.name: Metamorphic Rocks
nodes.desc: Rocks changed by heat and pressure without melting. Marble used to be limestone.

nodes.name: Earth's Interior
nodes.desc: Crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. Earthquake waves are how we know any of this.

nodes.name: Plate Tectonics
nodes.desc: Plates moving apart, colliding and sliding past each other. Most mountains, volcanoes and quakes sit on plate edges.

nodes.name: Earthquakes
nodes.desc: Faults, seismic waves and magnitude. Each step up the scale is about 32 times more energy.

nodes.name: Volcanoes
nodes.desc: Shield, cinder cone and composite volcanoes. Thick, sticky magma makes the explosive ones.

nodes.name: Weathering & Erosion
nodes.desc: Water, ice, wind and gravity breaking rock down and moving it. Rivers carve canyons a grain at a time.

nodes.name: Fossils
nodes.desc: How fossils form and what they tell us about past life. Most living things never become fossils at all.

nodes.name: Geologic Time
nodes.desc: Eons, eras and periods, plus radiometric dating. Earth is about 4.6 billion years old, and people are a very recent arrival.

nodes.name: Reading Geologic Maps
nodes.desc: Topographic maps, contour lines and rock layers on a map. Close contour lines mean steep ground.

nodes.name: Earth Resources
nodes.desc: Ores, fossil fuels, groundwater and soil. Where they are depends on geology from millions of years ago.

nodes.name: Geologic Hazards
nodes.desc: Landslides, tsunamis and sinkholes, and how communities prepare. Mapping risk saves lives.

nodes.name: Field Geology
nodes.desc: Reading the rocks on a real hike or road cut. A hand lens and a notebook are all you need to start.

nodes.name: Reading the Question
nodes.desc: Working out what is being asked and what has quietly been given, before any formula is written down. Olympiad problems hide the given quantity in a clause, and the reach for an equation is what walks past it.

nodes.name: Units & Estimation
nodes.desc: Carrying units through an expression so a wrong one announces itself, and knowing the order of magnitude before computing. On a multiple-choice paper the estimate frequently is the answer.

nodes.name: Uncertainty
nodes.desc: How error in a measurement propagates into everything computed from it, and how many figures you are entitled to report. The lab events grade this directly and the written papers assume it.

nodes.name: Free-Body Diagrams
nodes.desc: Every force on one object and nothing else on the page. Almost every mechanics mistake at this level is a force drawn that was not acting, or one acting that was not drawn.

nodes.name: Stoichiometry
nodes.desc: Counting particles by weighing them, and the ratio a balanced equation actually asserts. The limiting reagent is where this is tested, because it is where the arithmetic stops being proportional.

nodes.name: Cell Biology
nodes.desc: Membranes, organelles and the reactions that pay for everything a cell does. Olympiad biology assumes this the way olympiad physics assumes algebra. As vocabulary rather than as content.

nodes.name: Kinematics & Dynamics
nodes.desc: Position, velocity and acceleration as one another's derivatives, and Newton's laws applied to a diagram you drew correctly. Choosing the axes well is worth more than any algebraic technique here.

nodes.name: Energy & Momentum
nodes.desc: Conservation laws, and knowing which one survives a given collision. They turn problems that are brutal in forces into two lines of arithmetic, which is exactly why the paper is written to obscure that they apply.

nodes.name: Chemical Equilibrium
nodes.desc: Reactions that arrive somewhere and stop, and what shifts them. Le Chatelier gives the direction in a sentence; the equilibrium constant is what makes it a number.

nodes.name: Redox & Electrochemistry
nodes.desc: Tracking electrons through a reaction and the voltage that transfer is worth. Balancing a half-reaction in acid is mechanical, heavily examined, and dropped by people who never practiced it under time.

nodes.name: Genetics
nodes.desc: Inheritance as probability, from a cross through linkage to population frequencies. The pedigree questions are logic puzzles wearing a lab coat, which is why they reward practice rather than reading.

nodes.name: Physiology
nodes.desc: Systems that hold a body at a set point, and what the feedback loop does when it is pushed. Homeostasis is the through-line, and an answer that does not name a feedback mechanism is usually incomplete.

nodes.name: The F=ma Exam
nodes.desc: Twenty-five mechanics problems in seventy-five minutes with no calculator, which makes it a test of setup speed rather than of depth. The estimate and the free-body diagram between them decide most of the score.

nodes.name: Thermodynamics
nodes.desc: Energy, entropy and which direction a process will go on its own. It is the one topic both the physics and the chemistry ladders examine, from opposite ends and with different notation.

nodes.name: Ecology & Evolution
nodes.desc: Populations changing over time, under selection and under each other. The quantitative half (Hardy-Weinberg, growth models) is what the olympiad rounds actually test.

nodes.name: The Lab Practical
nodes.desc: Doing the measurement, recording it honestly, and writing the uncertainty beside it under a time limit. Graded on the notebook as much as the number, which is a shock to people who only ever sat written papers.

nodes.name: Electricity & Magnetism
nodes.desc: Fields, potential and the fact that a changing one of each makes the other. The second semester exam assumes calculus fluency in a way the mechanics paper does not.

nodes.name: Chemistry Olympiad
nodes.desc: A national exam with a laboratory part, where the written half rewards breadth and the practical half rewards having actually handled glassware. Very few competitors are strong at both.

nodes.name: Biology Olympiad
nodes.desc: The broadest syllabus of the three by a distance, examined at a depth textbooks do not reach. Semifinalists are separated by reading primary literature rather than by revising harder.

nodes.name: Modern Physics
nodes.desc: Relativity and quantization, where the classical answer is confidently wrong. It appears late in the selection ladder and rewards understanding the postulates over memorizing the results.

nodes.name: Selection Camp
nodes.desc: The round after the national exam, where problems take hours rather than minutes and a partial argument is worth writing. Everything below converges here because nothing at this level announces its topic.

nodes.name: Earth Systems
nodes.desc: Air, water, land and life all feeding into each other. APES questions almost always ask how a change in one spreads to the rest.

nodes.name: Nutrient Cycles
nodes.desc: Carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water moving through the planet. Draw each cycle from memory and label where people interfere.

nodes.name: Ecosystems & Energy
nodes.desc: Food webs and the 10 percent rule. Energy flows one way through a system, and matter keeps cycling.

nodes.name: Biodiversity
nodes.desc: Why more species make ecosystems tougher. Habitat loss is the biggest threat on the list.

nodes.name: Population Growth
nodes.desc: Carrying capacity, growth curves and human population trends. The demographic transition model shows up on almost every exam.

nodes.name: Soil & Land Use
nodes.desc: How soil forms, erodes and gets used for farming. Good soil takes centuries to build and a few bad seasons to lose.

nodes.name: Water Resources
nodes.desc: Aquifers, watersheds and who gets the water. Farming uses most of it, which surprises a lot of people.

nodes.name: Food & Agriculture
nodes.desc: Industrial farming, pesticides and sustainable options. Every choice trades yield for a cost somewhere else.

nodes.name: Energy Sources
nodes.desc: Fossil fuels, nuclear and renewables, with their pros and cons. Compare them on cost, reliability and pollution.

nodes.name: Air Pollution
nodes.desc: Smog, acid rain and indoor air quality. Know the main pollutants and where each one comes from.

nodes.name: Water Pollution
nodes.desc: Runoff, dead zones and bioaccumulation. A little toxin at the bottom of a food chain becomes a lot at the top.

nodes.name: Waste & Recycling
nodes.desc: Landfills, composting and what really happens to recycling. Using less always does more good than recycling more.

nodes.name: Climate Change
nodes.desc: The greenhouse effect, feedback loops and the evidence. Be ready to explain the mechanism in plain words.

nodes.name: Climate Impacts
nodes.desc: Sea level rise, ocean acidification and shifting ranges. The impacts hit unevenly, which makes it a fairness question too.

nodes.name: Solutions & Policy
nodes.desc: Carbon pricing, regulations and international deals. Every fix has winners and losers, and good answers name both.

nodes.name: APES Free Response
nodes.desc: Calculations, experiment design and explain-the-graph questions. Show your units and explain your reasoning in full sentences.

nodes.name: Field Studies
nodes.desc: Sampling plants, testing water and counting species outside. Real data is messy, so record everything as you go.

nodes.name: A Local Project
nodes.desc: Picking a real problem in your town and studying it. A small project done well is great for college apps too.

nodes.name: Crime Scene Basics
nodes.desc: Securing the scene, walking through it and touching nothing. One careless step can ruin the evidence.

nodes.name: Documenting the Scene
nodes.desc: Photos, sketches and notes before anything gets moved. If it isn't written down, it didn't happen.

nodes.name: Chain of Custody
nodes.desc: A record of everyone who handled each piece of evidence. A broken chain can get evidence thrown out of court.

nodes.name: Fingerprints
nodes.desc: Loops, whorls and arches, and how prints get lifted. No two people share the same prints, even identical twins.

nodes.name: Trace Evidence
nodes.desc: Hair, fibers, glass and soil. Tiny bits move between people and places whenever they touch.

nodes.name: Blood Spatter
nodes.desc: Reading the shape and angle of drops to rebuild what happened. It's trig and physics, which surprises most students.

nodes.name: DNA Profiling
nodes.desc: Comparing DNA from a scene to a suspect. It's powerful, and contamination is its biggest weakness.

nodes.name: Toxicology
nodes.desc: Testing for drugs and poisons in the body. Dose and timing decide whether something is harmful.

nodes.name: Forensic Chemistry
nodes.desc: Chromatography and other tests to identify unknown substances. Ink, drugs and paint can all be matched this way.

nodes.name: Forensic Anthropology
nodes.desc: What a skeleton can tell you about age, sex and height. Bones also hold clues about injuries and cause of death.

nodes.name: Time of Death
nodes.desc: Body temperature, rigor mortis and insects as clocks. Each method gives a range, so combine them.

nodes.name: Questioned Documents
nodes.desc: Handwriting, ink and paper analysis to spot forgeries. Small habits in handwriting are hard to fake.

nodes.name: Digital Forensics
nodes.desc: Recovering data from phones and computers. Deleted files are usually still sitting there.

nodes.name: Firearms & Ballistics
nodes.desc: Matching bullets to guns and reading trajectories. It's careful comparison work under a microscope.

nodes.name: Evidence & Probability
nodes.desc: What a match really means and how likely a coincidence is. Misreading these numbers has sent innocent people to prison.

nodes.name: Expert Testimony
nodes.desc: Explaining science to a jury in plain words. Being clear and honest about limits matters more than sounding smart.

nodes.name: Forensics & Justice
nodes.desc: Wrongful convictions, junk science and reform. Good forensics protects the innocent as much as it catches the guilty.

nodes.name: Solving a Mock Case
nodes.desc: Putting every skill together on one full scenario. Build the timeline, test each theory and write up what the evidence supports.

nodes.name: Lab Safety
nodes.desc: Goggles, gloves, closed shoes and knowing where the eyewash is. Read the safety sheet before you open the bottle.

nodes.name: Glassware & Equipment
nodes.desc: Beakers, cylinders, pipettes and burettes, and what each is good for. A beaker holds liquid. A cylinder or pipette is what you trust for volume.

nodes.name: Precise Readings
nodes.desc: Reading a meniscus at eye level and recording every certain digit plus one. Sig figs start right here.

nodes.name: Units & Sig Figs
nodes.desc: Converting units and keeping the right number of significant figures. Lose the units and you lose points.

nodes.name: Lab Notebook
nodes.desc: Writing down what you did as you did it, in pen. Someone else should be able to repeat your work from it.

nodes.name: Following a Procedure
nodes.desc: Reading the whole thing before starting and prepping everything first. Most lab disasters come from improvising halfway through.

nodes.name: Variables & Controls
nodes.desc: Changing one thing at a time and keeping the rest the same. Without a control group, you can't say what caused what.

nodes.name: Data Tables
nodes.desc: Organizing raw data with units in the headers. A clean table makes the graph and the analysis easy.

nodes.name: Graphing Results
nodes.desc: Picking the right graph, labeling axes and drawing a best-fit line. The independent variable goes on the x-axis.

nodes.name: Writing a Hypothesis
nodes.desc: An if-then statement you can actually test. It should predict a direction, and it's fine if the data proves it wrong.

nodes.name: Error & Uncertainty
nodes.desc: Random error, systematic error and percent error. Blaming human error without saying what went wrong doesn't count.

nodes.name: Basic Lab Stats
nodes.desc: Averages, ranges and standard deviation for repeated trials. More trials make your result easier to believe.

nodes.name: Lab Reports
nodes.desc: Intro, methods, results and discussion. Results say what happened. The discussion says what it means.

nodes.name: Conclusions That Hold Up
nodes.desc: Claim, evidence and reasoning tied to your data. Admit the limits of what one experiment can show.

nodes.name: Designing Your Own Lab
nodes.desc: Writing a procedure from a question instead of following one. This is what AP labs and science fairs expect.

nodes.name: Core Techniques
nodes.desc: Titration, filtration, dilution and microscopy done cleanly. Clean technique means less error to explain later.

nodes.name: Reviewing Others' Reports
nodes.desc: Reading a classmate's report like a teacher would. Spotting gaps in someone else's work sharpens your own.

nodes.name: Independent Research
nodes.desc: Running a project start to finish with less help. It's the step between school labs and real research.

nodes.name: Finding a Question
nodes.desc: Starting from something you're curious about and narrowing it down. A small question you can test beats a huge vague one.

nodes.name: Background Research
nodes.desc: Reading what's already known so you don't repeat it. Keep a list of sources from day one.

nodes.name: Project Timeline
nodes.desc: Working backwards from the fair date. Leave two extra weeks, because experiments fail.

nodes.name: Hypothesis
nodes.desc: A clear prediction with a reason behind it. Judges look for a hypothesis you can actually test.

nodes.name: Variables & Controls
nodes.desc: One thing you change, one result you track and everything else held steady. Write the list before buying any supplies.

nodes.name: Materials & Budget
nodes.desc: Gathering what you need without spending a fortune. Many great projects use stuff from home or school.

nodes.name: Safety & Approval
nodes.desc: Forms for anything with people, animals or chemicals. Some fairs reject projects that skip approval, so check early.

nodes.name: Running the Experiment
nodes.desc: Doing enough trials and recording everything. Write down surprises too, since they often become the best part.

nodes.name: Project Notebook
nodes.desc: A dated log of every step, idea and mistake. Judges often ask to see it, so keep it neat.

nodes.name: Analyzing Data
nodes.desc: Averages, graphs and maybe a simple statistical test. Let the data tell its story, even if it's not the one you hoped for.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.desc: Answering your question and saying how sure you are. Include what you'd change next time.

nodes.name: Writing the Abstract
nodes.desc: Your whole project in about 250 words. Write it last, and cut every word that isn't pulling its weight.

nodes.name: The Display Board
nodes.desc: A layout people can read from a few feet away. Use a big title, clear graphs and short text.

nodes.name: Your Pitch
nodes.desc: A two-minute talk that walks a judge through the project. Practice it out loud until it sounds natural.

nodes.name: Answering Judges
nodes.desc: Handling questions you didn't expect. Saying you don't know, then how you'd find out, is a strong answer.

nodes.name: Research Paper
nodes.desc: A full write-up for higher-level fairs. It's longer than a lab report and needs real citations.

nodes.name: Regionals & State
nodes.desc: Moving up and polishing the project between rounds. Use judges' feedback to fix weak spots.

nodes.name: ISEF & Beyond
nodes.desc: Competing at the international level and turning the project into a research path. Some students publish or win scholarships from here.

nodes.name: Reading the Syllabus
nodes.desc: Grading weights, due dates and late policies are all in there. Five minutes with it on day one saves you points all term.

nodes.name: Using a Planner
nodes.desc: Every assignment written down the day you get it. Your brain is bad at remembering due dates, so don't make it try.

nodes.name: Showing Up
nodes.desc: Going to class, on time, with what you need. It's the easiest grade boost there is.

nodes.name: Class Participation
nodes.desc: Asking and answering questions in class. Even one comment a day changes how teachers see you.

nodes.name: Talking to Teachers
nodes.desc: Emailing politely, going to office hours and asking for help early. Teachers want to help, but they can't read your mind.

nodes.name: Homework Routine
nodes.desc: Same time, same place, phone away. A routine means you don't have to decide to start every night.

nodes.name: Grades & GPA
nodes.desc: How your grade gets calculated and what each assignment is worth. Know your weighted GPA and what actually moves it.

nodes.name: Big Assignments
nodes.desc: Breaking projects and papers into chunks with their own due dates. Starting early is the whole trick.

nodes.name: Group Projects
nodes.desc: Splitting the work, setting deadlines and handling the one who disappears. Write down who does what in the first meeting.

nodes.name: Test Days
nodes.desc: Sleep, breakfast, reading every question and checking your work. Small habits on test day can be worth a letter grade.

nodes.name: Bouncing Back
nodes.desc: Looking at what went wrong after a bad grade, asking about retakes and adjusting. One test doesn't define the class.

nodes.name: School-Life Balance
nodes.desc: Fitting in sports, jobs, friends and sleep. Protect sleep first, since everything else gets worse without it.

nodes.name: Choosing Classes
nodes.desc: Picking a schedule that pushes you without burying you. Ask older students which classes really take the most time.

nodes.name: AP, IB & Dual Enrollment
nodes.desc: College-level classes in high school. They can earn credit, but only take what you can keep up with.

nodes.name: Recommendation Letters
nodes.desc: Asking teachers who know you well, early and with a brag sheet. Good letters come from relationships built over time.

nodes.name: High School to College
nodes.desc: Bigger classes, less structure and more freedom. The students who do best go to office hours and plan their weeks.

nodes.name: Owning Your Education
nodes.desc: Choosing what to learn and chasing it on your own. School hands you the tools, and you decide what to build.

nodes.name: Planning Study
nodes.desc: Deciding what to study when, against the date it is needed. Working through material in the order it appears in a book is a plan by default rather than a decision.

nodes.name: Reading to Learn
nodes.desc: Previewing the structure, asking questions, then reading for the answers. Passive reading from the first line produces a feeling of familiarity that is easily mistaken for knowledge.

nodes.name: Note-Taking
nodes.desc: Notes in your own words, shorter than the source. Transcribing what was said keeps the hands busy and the understanding untested.

nodes.name: Retrieval Practice
nodes.desc: Closing the book and trying to produce the answer. Difficult, unpleasant, and by a wide margin the best-supported study technique there is.

nodes.name: Spaced Repetition
nodes.desc: Reviewing just before you would forget, at growing intervals. It converts a fact learned once into a fact you still have in June, for a fraction of the total time.

nodes.name: Interleaving
nodes.desc: Mixing problem types instead of doing thirty of one kind. Performance in the session gets worse and retention afterwards gets better, which is why almost nobody does it voluntarily.

nodes.name: Explaining It
nodes.desc: Teaching the material to somebody, or to an empty room. The point where the explanation stalls is precisely the gap that rereading would have hidden.

nodes.name: Understanding vs Memorizing
nodes.desc: Knowing why something follows, so it can be reconstructed rather than recalled. Some things just have to be memorized, and knowing which is a decision worth making explicitly.

nodes.name: Practice Problems
nodes.desc: Working problems without the solution visible, then checking. Reading a worked solution and nodding is the most reliable way to be surprised in an exam.

nodes.name: Learning from Mistakes
nodes.desc: A record of what you got wrong and why, revisited. Most people mark, feel bad and move on, which throws away the most information-dense part of the session.

nodes.name: Memory Techniques
nodes.desc: Mnemonics, stories and places for material that is arbitrary. Enormously effective on lists and sequences, and no substitute for understanding anything with a structure.

nodes.name: Summarizing & Mapping
nodes.desc: Compressing a topic onto one page and drawing what connects to what. The compression is where the learning happens; the page afterwards is mostly a souvenir.

nodes.name: Deep Study Sessions
nodes.desc: Long uninterrupted blocks on difficult material, which is what hard subjects require. Two focused hours outperform six with a phone on the desk, and it is not close.

nodes.name: Study Groups
nodes.desc: Working with others, which is excellent for explaining and testing and terrible for first exposure. It needs a stated purpose or it becomes a social event with books open.

nodes.name: Finding Material
nodes.desc: Past papers, textbooks, lectures and problem sets, chosen for the question you actually have. Past papers are consistently the most underused resource available.

nodes.name: Revision Timetables
nodes.desc: A schedule across weeks that revisits everything more than once. Building a beautiful timetable is itself a well-known form of procrastination, so keep it to twenty minutes.

nodes.name: Exam Technique
nodes.desc: Reading the question, allocating time by marks, and writing what is being asked for. A large fraction of lost marks are technique rather than knowledge.

nodes.name: Exam Nerves
nodes.desc: Practicing under timed conditions so the state is familiar, and having a plan for going blank. Preparation reduces anxiety far more effectively than reassurance does.

nodes.name: Keeping What You Learned
nodes.desc: Occasional review after the exam, which is what separates a subject you studied from one you know. Almost all of it goes within months otherwise, whatever the grade said.

nodes.name: Teaching Yourself
nodes.desc: Learning something with no course, no deadline and nobody checking. It needs every skill in this tree at once, and it is the one that keeps working for the rest of your life.

nodes.name: Why Take Notes
nodes.desc: Notes help you pay attention now and review later. Writing by hand helps you process, and typing helps you keep up.

nodes.name: Listening for Key Points
nodes.desc: Catching what the teacher repeats, writes on the board or says will be on the test. Those are your headings.

nodes.name: Notes From Reading
nodes.desc: Summarizing textbook sections in your own words. Read a section first, then write without looking.

nodes.name: Shorthand
nodes.desc: Symbols and abbreviations you'll still understand later. Make a key and stay consistent.

nodes.name: Cornell Notes
nodes.desc: Notes, a cue column and a summary on one page. The cue column turns your notes into a quiz.

nodes.name: Outline Method
nodes.desc: Main ideas with indented details under them. It works great for organized lectures.

nodes.name: Mind Maps & Diagrams
nodes.desc: Drawing the links between ideas. Good for subjects where everything connects to everything else.

nodes.name: Notes From Slides
nodes.desc: Adding what the teacher says out loud, since slides are only the outline. Copying slides word for word misses most of the lesson.

nodes.name: Digital Notes
nodes.desc: Apps like Notion, OneNote or GoodNotes. Pick one system, give every class a home and keep it organized.

nodes.name: Notes for Math & Science
nodes.desc: Worked examples with every step and the reason for it. Leave space to redo the problems later.

nodes.name: Organizing Notes
nodes.desc: Dates, titles and folders by class. If you can't find a note, it can't help you.

nodes.name: Same-Day Review
nodes.desc: Ten minutes the same day to fill the gaps. It makes a huge difference in what you remember a week later.

nodes.name: Quizzing From Notes
nodes.desc: Covering your notes and recalling the answers. Rereading feels productive, and testing yourself works far better.

nodes.name: Study Sheets
nodes.desc: Shrinking a whole unit onto one page before a test. Making the sheet is the studying.

nodes.name: Your Note System
nodes.desc: A setup that works for every class you take. Tweak it at the start of each semester.

nodes.name: How AI Chatbots Work
nodes.desc: They predict likely words from patterns in text. That's why they can sound sure and still be wrong.

nodes.name: Your School's AI Rules
nodes.desc: Every class and teacher sets their own policy. Check the syllabus and ask when it seems unclear.

nodes.name: Asking Good Questions
nodes.desc: Giving context, a clear task and the format you want. Better prompts get better answers.

nodes.name: Academic Honesty
nodes.desc: Turning in AI writing as your own is cheating, even when it's easy. Use it to learn, then do the work yourself.

nodes.name: AI as a Tutor
nodes.desc: Asking it to explain, quiz you or check your steps. Ask for hints before answers so you still do the thinking.

nodes.name: Fact-Checking AI
nodes.desc: Checking claims, numbers and sources against real references. AI makes up citations, so look up every one.

nodes.name: Making Practice Questions
nodes.desc: Turning your notes into flashcards or practice tests. Testing yourself is one of the best ways to study.

nodes.name: Feedback on Drafts
nodes.desc: Asking for comments on clarity and structure while you do the rewriting. Keep your own voice.

nodes.name: Explaining Hard Topics
nodes.desc: Asking for simpler explanations, analogies or examples. Then explain it back in your own words to see if it stuck.

nodes.name: Research With AI
nodes.desc: Using AI to find search terms and summarize what you've read. Always go to the real source before citing anything.

nodes.name: Citing AI Use
nodes.desc: Saying how you used AI when your class allows it. MLA and APA both have formats for it.

nodes.name: AI for Coding Homework
nodes.desc: Using it to explain errors and concepts. If you can't write it again without help, you didn't learn it.

nodes.name: Privacy & Your Data
nodes.desc: What happens to everything you type in. Don't share personal info or other people's work.

nodes.name: Knowing the Limits
nodes.desc: Spotting confident wrong answers, bias and old info. The better you know a topic, the easier mistakes are to catch.

nodes.name: A Study Workflow
nodes.desc: A routine where AI helps you plan, quiz and review while you do the real work. It should make you sharper.

nodes.name: AI and Your Future
nodes.desc: How these tools are changing jobs and school. The skills that last are judgment, clear writing and knowing your stuff.

nodes.name: Diagnostic Test
nodes.desc: A full practice test under real conditions before you study anything. Your score shows you where to spend your time.

nodes.name: Know the Format
nodes.desc: Sections, timing, question types and how scoring works. Surprises on test day cost points you already earned.

nodes.name: Study Plan
nodes.desc: Weekly goals working back from test day. Short daily sessions beat a few giant cram days.

nodes.name: Mistake Log
nodes.desc: Every missed question with the reason you missed it. Patterns in this log are your fastest score gains.

nodes.name: Reading Section
nodes.desc: Finding the main idea and backing answers with the passage. Every right answer has proof in the text.

nodes.name: Grammar Rules
nodes.desc: Commas, agreement, modifiers and concise wording. There are only about a dozen rules, and they repeat on every test.

nodes.name: Core Test Math
nodes.desc: Linear equations, ratios, percents and functions. Most of the math section is algebra done quickly and carefully.

nodes.name: Harder Math Topics
nodes.desc: Quadratics, exponentials, geometry and trig basics. Learn these after the core, since they're fewer questions.

nodes.name: Calculator Strategy
nodes.desc: When the calculator or Desmos saves time and when it slows you down. Graphing an equation can beat solving it by hand.

nodes.name: Words in Context
nodes.desc: Picking the word that fits the sentence. Context clues matter more than memorizing fancy words.

nodes.name: Pacing
nodes.desc: Moving on from hard questions and coming back later. Every question is worth the same, so don't let one eat five minutes.

nodes.name: Smart Guessing
nodes.desc: Crossing off wrong choices and never leaving a blank. Two eliminations make a guess a lot better than random.

nodes.name: Full Practice Tests
nodes.desc: Timed, full-length tests on a schedule. Build stamina so the last section feels like the first.

nodes.name: Reviewing Practice Tests
nodes.desc: Spending as long reviewing a test as taking it. That's where the points come from.

nodes.name: AP Exams
nodes.desc: Content review plus free-response practice with real scoring guidelines. Learn how points get awarded and write to earn them.

nodes.name: Test Anxiety
nodes.desc: Breathing, routines and practicing in test conditions. Some nerves help, and panic is something you can train down.

nodes.name: Test Day
nodes.desc: Sleep, food, ID, admission ticket and an early start. Pack the night before so the morning is boring.

nodes.name: Retakes & Superscoring
nodes.desc: Deciding when to retest and how colleges combine scores. A second try after focused review often jumps the score.

nodes.name: Building a College List
nodes.desc: Reach, target and likely schools that fit what you want. A good list has schools you'd be happy to attend at every level.

nodes.name: Researching Schools
nodes.desc: Majors, size, location, cost and culture. Visit or take virtual tours, and talk to current students.

nodes.name: Brainstorming Your Story
nodes.desc: Listing values, moments and objects that matter to you. Your best topic is often something ordinary seen in a new way.

nodes.name: Application Timeline
nodes.desc: Early decision, early action and regular deadlines. Put every date in your calendar by the end of junior summer.

nodes.name: The Common App
nodes.desc: Activities, honors, family info and where each part goes. Fill in the easy sections early so fall is for writing.

nodes.name: Activities List
nodes.desc: Ten slots with 150 characters each. Use strong verbs and numbers to show what you actually did.

nodes.name: Personal Statement
nodes.desc: A 650-word story only you could write. Small moments told well beat big dramatic topics.

nodes.name: Supplemental Essays
nodes.desc: Why this college, why this major and short answers. Name specific classes, clubs or professors you'd connect with.

nodes.name: Recommendations
nodes.desc: Asking two teachers and your counselor early. Give them a brag sheet so they can write specifics.

nodes.name: Scores & Test-Optional
nodes.desc: Deciding whether to send your scores. Compare yours to each school's middle 50 percent.

nodes.name: College Interviews
nodes.desc: Talking with an alum or admissions officer. Prepare a few stories and some real questions about the school.

nodes.name: Portfolios & Extras
nodes.desc: Art, music, research or writing samples where schools accept them. Only send extras that are strong.

nodes.name: Editing Your Essays
nodes.desc: Cutting, tightening and reading aloud. Pick one or two readers you trust, since ten readers just means ten opinions.

nodes.name: Submitting
nodes.desc: Checking every section, paying fees or getting waivers and hitting submit. Go a few days early in case the site crashes.

nodes.name: Decisions & Waitlists
nodes.desc: Reading acceptances, rejections and waitlists calmly. A letter of continued interest can help on the waitlist.

nodes.name: Comparing Offers
nodes.desc: Putting aid packages side by side and visiting admitted student days. The cheapest good fit is often the smartest choice.

nodes.name: Committing
nodes.desc: Sending your deposit by May 1 and closing out the rest. Thank the people who helped you get there.

nodes.name: Gap Years & Transfers
nodes.desc: Other paths that work out fine. Plenty of people take a year off or transfer and end up exactly where they want.

nodes.name: Trying Things
nodes.desc: Joining a few clubs, teams or programs to see what clicks. Freshman year is for sampling.

nodes.name: Picking Your Focus
nodes.desc: Dropping what you don't care about to go deep on what you do. Two or three real commitments beat ten names on a list.

nodes.name: Volunteering
nodes.desc: Service hours that actually help someone. Pick one cause you care about and stick with it for years.

nodes.name: Summer Programs
nodes.desc: Camps, courses, jobs and research over the summer. Free and local options count just as much as pricey ones.

nodes.name: Fitting It In
nodes.desc: Balancing practices and meetings with school. Put every commitment in one calendar so you can see the whole week.

nodes.name: Showing Up Every Week
nodes.desc: Steady effort over years, even in the boring weeks. Colleges and employers notice long-term commitment.

nodes.name: Taking on a Role
nodes.desc: Volunteering for the jobs nobody wants, like treasurer, setup or social media. That's how you earn trust and bigger roles.

nodes.name: Showing Impact
nodes.desc: Counting what changed, like money raised, people helped or events run. Numbers make your work concrete.

nodes.name: Competitions
nodes.desc: Contests, tournaments and showcases. They give you deadlines, feedback and something to aim for.

nodes.name: Jobs & Family Duties
nodes.desc: Working or caring for siblings counts as an activity. Colleges really do want to know about it.

nodes.name: Leading a Club
nodes.desc: Running meetings, setting goals and keeping members coming back. Leading is about making the group better.

nodes.name: Starting Something
nodes.desc: Founding a club, project or event. Start small, find two co-founders and solve a real need.

nodes.name: Awards & Honors
nodes.desc: Recognition that shows the level you reached. Apply for awards, since plenty go unclaimed.

nodes.name: Finding Mentors
nodes.desc: Advisors, coaches and older students who can guide you. Ask specific questions and follow up.

nodes.name: Handing Off
nodes.desc: Training the next leaders before you graduate. A club that keeps going after you leave is real impact.

nodes.name: Telling the Story
nodes.desc: Turning your activities into a clear story for apps and interviews. Show what you did, what changed and what you learned.

nodes.name: Activities Resume
nodes.desc: A one-page summary of everything you do. Update it every semester so nothing gets forgotten.

nodes.name: Something That Lasts
nodes.desc: A project, club or tradition that keeps going after you're gone. It's the best proof you made a difference.

nodes.name: Why Medicine
nodes.desc: Being honest about why you want to be a doctor. Shadowing early helps you find out before you spend years on it.

nodes.name: Health Careers
nodes.desc: Doctor, PA, nurse, pharmacist, dentist and more. Each path has different training, cost and lifestyle.

nodes.name: High School Prep
nodes.desc: Strong biology, chemistry and math, plus volunteering in a health setting. You're building habits you'll need in college.

nodes.name: Shadowing
nodes.desc: Following doctors around to see the real job. Aim for a few different specialties.

nodes.name: Pre-Med Prereqs
nodes.desc: Bio, general chem, orgo, physics, biochem, stats and English. Map out when you'll take each one in your first semester.

nodes.name: Science GPA
nodes.desc: Med schools look at your science grades on their own. Protect them with good study habits from day one.

nodes.name: Clinical Experience
nodes.desc: Hands-on time with patients as an EMT, scribe, CNA or volunteer. Schools want to see you've been around sick people and still want this.

nodes.name: Community Service
nodes.desc: Helping people outside of hospitals. It shows you care about people even when nobody's checking.

nodes.name: Research
nodes.desc: Working in a lab or on a project. It helps a lot at research-heavy schools, even where it isn't required.

nodes.name: The MCAT
nodes.desc: A long exam on bio, chem, physics, psych and reading. Most people study for three to six months.

nodes.name: MCAT Reading (CARS)
nodes.desc: Reading dense passages and reasoning about them. Reading hard articles every day is the best prep.

nodes.name: Leadership & Teamwork
nodes.desc: Leading a club, team or project. Medicine is teamwork, and schools want proof you can do it.

nodes.name: Letters of Rec
nodes.desc: Strong letters from science professors and people who've seen you work. Build those relationships early.

nodes.name: Handling Setbacks
nodes.desc: A bad grade or a rejection doesn't end the path. Lots of doctors applied twice or took extra years.

nodes.name: Applying (AMCAS)
nodes.desc: The primary application, your personal statement and the activity list. Submit early in June, since schools review as apps come in.

nodes.name: Secondary Essays
nodes.desc: School-specific essays that come right after. Prewrite common prompts so you can turn them around fast.

nodes.name: Med School Interviews
nodes.desc: Traditional and MMI formats. Practice ethical scenarios and talking about your own experiences.

nodes.name: Getting In
nodes.desc: Acceptances, waitlists and choosing the school that fits. Then the real training starts, and it's a long one.

nodes.name: What College Costs
nodes.desc: Tuition, housing, food, books and travel. The sticker price and what families actually pay can be very different.

nodes.name: Net Price Calculators
nodes.desc: Every college has one on its website. Run it with your family before you apply so the offers hold no surprises.

nodes.name: Types of Aid
nodes.desc: Grants, scholarships, work-study and loans. Grants and scholarships don't get paid back.

nodes.name: The FAFSA
nodes.desc: The federal form that unlocks most aid. File as soon as it opens, since some aid runs out.

nodes.name: Gathering Documents
nodes.desc: Tax returns, bank info and an FSA ID. Getting these together is the slowest part, so start early.

nodes.name: The CSS Profile
nodes.desc: An extra form many private colleges use. It asks for more detail, so start early with your family.

nodes.name: Your SAI
nodes.desc: The Student Aid Index from your FAFSA. Colleges use it to decide how much need-based aid you get.

nodes.name: Merit Scholarships
nodes.desc: Aid for grades, scores or talents. Some schools give big merit awards to students near the top of their pool.

nodes.name: Work-Study
nodes.desc: A part-time campus job paid for by aid. Pick one that fits around your class schedule.

nodes.name: Finding Scholarships
nodes.desc: Local, school, community and national awards. Small local scholarships get fewer applicants, so apply widely.

nodes.name: Scholarship Essays
nodes.desc: Writing about goals, service and challenges. Reuse and adapt your strongest essays across applications.

nodes.name: Reading Aid Letters
nodes.desc: Separating free money from loans in an offer. Some letters list loans in a way that looks like free aid.

nodes.name: Appealing an Offer
nodes.desc: Asking for more aid when your situation changes or another school offers more. A polite, specific letter often works.

nodes.name: Student Loans
nodes.desc: Federal and private loans, interest and repayment. Borrow federal first and only what you need.

nodes.name: Keeping Your Aid
nodes.desc: GPA rules, credit loads and refiling the FAFSA every year. Losing a scholarship over a missed form really hurts.

nodes.name: A College Budget
nodes.desc: Planning your money for each semester before it starts. Books, food and trips home add up fast.

nodes.name: Choosing Without Debt Stress
nodes.desc: Picking a school with a cost your family can handle. Graduating with little debt gives you more choices later.

nodes.name: Reading Fluently
nodes.desc: Getting through a page without decoding it word by word, so attention is free for the meaning. Everything else in this tree assumes it, and it is built by volume rather than by exercises.

nodes.name: Vocabulary
nodes.desc: Words known well enough to use, not merely to recognize. Learning them inside a sentence you met them in beats a list, because the connotation is most of what a word actually carries.

nodes.name: Spelling & Sound
nodes.desc: The patterns behind English spelling, which is far more regular than its reputation once you know where the borrowings came from. Knowing the pattern beats memorizing the exception.

nodes.name: Parts of Speech
nodes.desc: What each word is doing in a sentence rather than what it means. It is the vocabulary you need to talk about why a sentence is broken instead of only feeling that it is.

nodes.name: Sentences
nodes.desc: Subject, verb and the clauses hanging off them. Most bad writing is not a vocabulary problem; it is sentences with too many things going on and no clear main action.

nodes.name: Punctuation
nodes.desc: Marks that show a reader how the parts fit together. The comma splice and the misused apostrophe are the two errors that cost credibility fastest, and both take an afternoon to fix for good.

nodes.name: Tense & Agreement
nodes.desc: Keeping time consistent and making the parts of a sentence match. Drifting between past and present mid-paragraph is invisible while writing and glaring on the second read.

nodes.name: Paragraphs
nodes.desc: One idea, developed, with a sentence that says what it is. A paragraph that changes subject halfway is two paragraphs, and splitting them is the cheapest structural improvement there is.

nodes.name: Summarizing
nodes.desc: Saying in three sentences what took three pages, without smuggling in your own view. It is the most reliable test of whether something was actually understood.

nodes.name: Note-Taking
nodes.desc: Capturing meaning rather than transcribing words, in a form your later self can use. Notes that are shorter than the source and rewritten in your own phrasing are the ones that survive.

nodes.name: Close Reading
nodes.desc: Reading for how something is said as well as what it says: word choice, structure, what is left out. It is the difference between having an opinion about a text and having evidence.

nodes.name: Argument
nodes.desc: A claim, reasons and the evidence under them, arranged so a skeptical reader follows. Anticipating the strongest objection rather than the weakest is what separates persuasion from assertion.

nodes.name: Tone & Register
nodes.desc: Matching how formal, warm or direct the writing is to who is reading it. The same content in the wrong register reads as rude, unserious or evasive, none of which was meant.

nodes.name: Editing
nodes.desc: Cutting, reordering and tightening after the draft exists. Nearly every first draft loses a fifth of its words with no loss of meaning, and finding them is a separate sitting from writing them.

nodes.name: Research & Sources
nodes.desc: Finding material, judging whether it is any good, and tracking where each fact came from. Recording the source at the moment you use it costs seconds and saves an evening.

nodes.name: Citation & Integrity
nodes.desc: Attributing ideas and quotations in a consistent style. The rule underneath the formatting is simple: a reader should always be able to tell which thoughts are yours.

nodes.name: Speaking & Discussion
nodes.desc: Making a point aloud, listening to the reply, and changing your mind in public when it is warranted. Structure helps more than confidence: one claim, one reason, one example.

nodes.name: Listening
nodes.desc: Following an argument you did not construct, including the part you disagree with. Being able to restate a position you disagree with, to the satisfaction of the person holding it, to their satisfaction is the test worth applying.

nodes.name: Style
nodes.desc: The choices that make prose yours: rhythm, sentence length, how much you leave to the reader. It arrives from reading widely and imitating deliberately, not from adjectives.

nodes.name: A Writing Habit
nodes.desc: Words on a schedule rather than when inspired. Every professional writer describes the same discovery: the sitting down produces the ideas, not the other way round.

nodes.name: Drafting
nodes.desc: Writing badly on purpose to get something to work with. Editing while drafting is the most common way a piece takes four times as long and comes out worse.

nodes.name: Audience & Purpose
nodes.desc: Who reads this and what they should be able to do afterwards. Almost every question about tone, length and how much to explain answers itself once those two are written down.

nodes.name: Outlining
nodes.desc: Deciding the order before committing sentences to it. Even a five-line outline prevents the commonest structural failure, which is a piece that arrives at its point in the last paragraph.

nodes.name: The Central Claim
nodes.desc: The one sentence the whole piece is defending. If it cannot be written in one sentence, the piece is not ready to be written, however much research is behind it.

nodes.name: Openings
nodes.desc: Earning the second paragraph. Written last, almost always, because you do not know what you were introducing until the piece exists.

nodes.name: Flow & Transitions
nodes.desc: Each paragraph picking up something the last one put down. When writing feels choppy the cause is usually order rather than sentence quality.

nodes.name: Clarity
nodes.desc: Making the subject do the action and putting the important thing at the end of the sentence. Two habits that fix more prose than any amount of vocabulary.

nodes.name: Concision
nodes.desc: Removing words that are doing nothing. It is a mechanical pass rather than a talent, and it is the fastest visible improvement any writer makes.

nodes.name: Revision
nodes.desc: Rewriting at the level of structure, not commas. That means being willing to cut a section you like, which is why it is easier a day later than an hour later.

nodes.name: Taking Feedback
nodes.desc: Hearing where a reader got lost without arguing that they should not have. Readers are reliable about where the problem is and unreliable about what would fix it.

nodes.name: Essays
nodes.desc: An argument built in public, with the evidence shown. The form rewards conceding the strongest counter-argument early rather than pretending it does not exist.

nodes.name: Reports & Documentation
nodes.desc: Writing that people navigate rather than read: headings, summaries and a structure that survives being skimmed. The conclusion goes first, which reverses everything essay writing taught.

nodes.name: Professional Writing
nodes.desc: Emails and messages that get a decision instead of a thread. Ask for one thing, say when it is needed, and put both in the first two lines.

nodes.name: Narrative
nodes.desc: Somebody wanting something and having trouble getting it. Scene by scene, with tension that changes rather than repeats, is most of what makes a story readable.

nodes.name: Character & Dialogue
nodes.desc: People who want incompatible things, talking past each other. Dialogue that only exchanges information is the most common thing that makes fiction feel flat.

nodes.name: Description & Image
nodes.desc: One precise detail rather than three vague ones. The rule that outlives every workshop is to give the reader something to see and let them supply the adjective.

nodes.name: Poetry
nodes.desc: Compression, line breaks and sound doing work that sentences alone cannot. Reading it aloud is not optional; the ear catches what the eye forgives.

nodes.name: Long-Form Projects
nodes.desc: Holding something together across months, when momentum matters more than any single day. Finishing badly and revising beats stalling in pursuit of a perfect chapter three.

nodes.name: Voice
nodes.desc: Writing that could not be by anybody else. It comes from imitating deliberately until the imitations stop fitting, rather than from trying to be original at the start.

nodes.name: Publishing
nodes.desc: Submitting, being rejected, and sending it out again the same week. The manuscript is half the work; the other half is the unglamorous business of putting it in front of people.

nodes.name: Writing Often
nodes.desc: A little every day, even when it comes out bad. Volume is how you get better, so lower the bar and show up.

nodes.name: Reading Like a Writer
nodes.desc: Noticing how authors open, pace and end their scenes. Borrow their tricks and make them yours.

nodes.name: Getting Ideas
nodes.desc: Prompts, what-ifs and stuff that happened to you. Write ideas down the second you have them.

nodes.name: Show With Details
nodes.desc: Specific, concrete details instead of summary. One sharp detail does more than a paragraph of description.

nodes.name: Characters
nodes.desc: People who want something and can't easily get it. Want plus obstacle is where every story starts.

nodes.name: Dialogue
nodes.desc: Talk that sounds real and moves the story forward. Cut the hellos and get to the point.

nodes.name: Point of View
nodes.desc: First person, close third or something stranger. Pick the one that gives you the best secrets to keep.

nodes.name: Plot & Structure
nodes.desc: A beginning, rising tension, a turn and an ending. Every scene should change something.

nodes.name: Writing Scenes
nodes.desc: A scene has a goal, a conflict and an outcome. If nothing changes, it's probably a summary.

nodes.name: Setting & World
nodes.desc: Places that feel lived in. Use all five senses, and stick to what the character would notice.

nodes.name: Voice
nodes.desc: The sound that makes your writing yours. It shows up when you stop trying to sound like a writer.

nodes.name: Flash Fiction
nodes.desc: Complete stories in under 1,000 words. Great practice for cutting and for nailing endings.

nodes.name: Short Stories
nodes.desc: A full story with an arc in a few thousand words. Most writers learn the craft right here.

nodes.name: Revising Fiction
nodes.desc: Big changes first, like plot, character and structure. Polishing sentences comes last, once the story works.

nodes.name: Workshopping
nodes.desc: Giving and taking feedback in a group. Pay the most attention to notes that several readers agree on.

nodes.name: Genre Writing
nodes.desc: Fantasy, sci-fi, mystery and horror each have rules readers expect. Know them before you break them.

nodes.name: Submitting Your Work
nodes.desc: Literary magazines, contests and the Scholastic Awards. Rejections are normal, so keep a list and keep sending.

nodes.name: A Longer Project
nodes.desc: A novella, novel or story collection. Finishing a long draft teaches you things nothing else can.

nodes.name: What Makes News
nodes.desc: Timely, local, important or unusual. Ask why your readers should care right now.

nodes.name: Journalism Ethics
nodes.desc: Accuracy, fairness and independence. Get it right before you worry about getting it first.

nodes.name: The Lede
nodes.desc: The first sentence that pulls readers in. Lead with the most important or most interesting fact.

nodes.name: Interviewing
nodes.desc: Asking open questions and listening for the follow-up. The best quotes come after the planned questions run out.

nodes.name: Notes & Recording
nodes.desc: Getting quotes exactly right. Record with permission and double-check every name.

nodes.name: Inverted Pyramid
nodes.desc: The most important info first and the details after. Readers can stop anytime and still get the story.

nodes.name: AP Style
nodes.desc: Rules for numbers, titles, dates and abbreviations. Consistency makes a paper look professional.

nodes.name: Sources & Verification
nodes.desc: Confirming facts with more than one source. Anonymous sources need a really good reason.

nodes.name: Sports Writing
nodes.desc: Game recaps, previews and athlete profiles. Find the one moment that decided the game.

nodes.name: Writing News Stories
nodes.desc: Straight reporting on events, meetings and decisions. Keep your opinion out of it.

nodes.name: Feature Stories
nodes.desc: Longer stories about people and trends. Use scenes and details like fiction, and make sure every fact is true.

nodes.name: Opinion & Editorials
nodes.desc: Taking a clear stand and backing it with evidence. Respect the other side's best argument.

nodes.name: Photos & Captions
nodes.desc: Pictures that tell the story and captions that name everyone. A good photo can carry a whole page.

nodes.name: Editing & Fact-Checking
nodes.desc: Cutting, checking every name and number and writing headlines. Editors protect the paper's reputation.

nodes.name: Press Law
nodes.desc: Libel, privacy and student press rights. Know what you can publish and how to defend it.

nodes.name: Digital & Social
nodes.desc: Web stories, newsletters and social posts. Headlines and visuals matter even more online.

nodes.name: Investigative Reporting
nodes.desc: Digging into records and asking hard questions over weeks. It's slow, and it's what holds powerful people to account.

nodes.name: Running a Publication
nodes.desc: Leading a staff, planning issues and hitting deadlines. Student editors learn real management fast.

nodes.name: Reading the Prompt
nodes.desc: Underlining the task words like analyze, compare and argue. Answering a different question than the one asked is the most common way to lose points.

nodes.name: A Clear Thesis
nodes.desc: One arguable sentence that answers the prompt. If nobody could disagree with it, it's too weak.

nodes.name: Outlining
nodes.desc: Topic sentences and evidence planned before you draft. Ten minutes of outlining saves an hour of rewriting.

nodes.name: Introductions
nodes.desc: A hook, some context and your thesis. Skip dictionary definitions and huge vague openers about all of human history.

nodes.name: Choosing Evidence
nodes.desc: Quotes, data and examples that really prove your point. A few strong pieces do more than lots of weak ones.

nodes.name: Body Paragraphs
nodes.desc: Claim, evidence, analysis and a link back to the thesis. Each paragraph does one job.

nodes.name: Analysis
nodes.desc: Explaining how the evidence proves your claim. This is where most of the grade lives.

nodes.name: Quoting Well
nodes.desc: Short quotes woven into your own sentences. Always set a quote up before you drop it in.

nodes.name: Transitions
nodes.desc: Words and sentences that link ideas logically. They show how each point builds on the last.

nodes.name: Conclusions
nodes.desc: Showing why your argument matters. Restating the thesis word for word wastes the space.

nodes.name: Counterarguments
nodes.desc: Raising the other side and answering it. Doing this makes your own argument look stronger.

nodes.name: MLA & APA Citations
nodes.desc: In-text citations and a works cited page. Free citation tools help, but double-check what they spit out.

nodes.name: Timed Essays
nodes.desc: Planning, writing and checking in 40 minutes. Spend five minutes planning, even under pressure.

nodes.name: Rhetorical Analysis
nodes.desc: Explaining how an author persuades. Focus on the author's choices and their effects on the reader.

nodes.name: Synthesis Essays
nodes.desc: Combining several sources into one argument of your own. AP Lang loves this one.

nodes.name: Revising Essays
nodes.desc: Rereading for argument first, then clarity, then grammar. Reading aloud catches clunky sentences.

nodes.name: Research Papers
nodes.desc: Longer papers with real sources and a strong question. Manage your notes and citations from the very start.

nodes.name: Your Writing Style
nodes.desc: Clear, confident and specific prose. Teachers notice writing that sounds like a real person.

nodes.name: Reading Widely
nodes.desc: Enough books, across enough kinds, that comparisons become available. Every later skill here is a way of noticing, and noticing needs something to notice against.

nodes.name: Plot & Structure
nodes.desc: What happens, in what order, and why that order. Noticing where a book withholds information is the first step from summarizing a story to reading one.

nodes.name: Character
nodes.desc: People built from what they want, what they do about it, and what they say instead. A character who changes is the engine of most fiction, and the change is usually smaller than the plot.

nodes.name: Narrator & Point of View
nodes.desc: Who is telling this, how much they know, and whether they can be trusted. Recognizing an unreliable narrator changes everything a book appeared to be saying.

nodes.name: Setting & Atmosphere
nodes.desc: Where and when, and what that does to what is possible. Setting is rarely decoration; it is usually the constraint the whole conflict depends on.

nodes.name: Imagery & Figurative Language
nodes.desc: Metaphor, simile and the images a book keeps returning to. A repeated image is a claim the book is making without stating it.

nodes.name: Theme
nodes.desc: What the book is about underneath what happens in it. A theme is an argument rather than a topic, which is why "love" is not one and "what love costs" might be.

nodes.name: Form & Genre
nodes.desc: The conventions a work is written inside, and what breaking one signals. Genre is a set of expectations shared with the reader, and the interesting books know exactly which one they are refusing.

nodes.name: Reading Poetry
nodes.desc: Line, sound, compression and what the break at the end of a line does to a phrase. Read aloud twice before deciding what it means, and expect the first reading to be wrong.

nodes.name: Reading Drama
nodes.desc: Text written to be performed, where nobody narrates and everything must be shown or said. What a character conceals is doing as much work as what they announce.

nodes.name: Close Reading
nodes.desc: Building a reading of a whole work out of a paragraph of it. The discipline is that every claim points at specific words, which is what makes it an argument rather than an impression.

nodes.name: Historical Context
nodes.desc: What the book was answering, and what its first readers took for granted. Context explains choices that look like flaws from here and stops anachronistic readings.

nodes.name: Movements & Tradition
nodes.desc: The conversations books have with each other across centuries. Most famous works are replies, and knowing what they are replying to is half the meaning.

nodes.name: Comparative Reading
nodes.desc: Two texts side by side, chosen so the comparison produces something neither would alone. The pairing is the argument, and a lazy pairing cannot be rescued by good analysis.

nodes.name: Critical Approaches
nodes.desc: Deliberate lenses (historical, psychological, political, formal) each making some features visible and others invisible. The point is choosing one knowingly rather than having one by default.

nodes.name: The Literary Essay
nodes.desc: A claim about a text, defended with quotation and analysis rather than plot summary. The commonest failure is retelling the book to a reader who has read it.

nodes.name: Literature in Translation
nodes.desc: Reading work whose sentences somebody else chose. Comparing two translations of one paragraph is the fastest lesson in how much of style is decision.

nodes.name: Canon & Its Critics
nodes.desc: How a set of books came to be the set everybody studies, and who decided. The argument about what was left out is itself one of the more interesting things in the subject.

nodes.name: Literary Research
nodes.desc: Finding what has already been argued, and locating the gap your reading fills. Knowing the existing scholarship is what turns an opinion into a contribution.

nodes.name: Your Own Reading
nodes.desc: An interpretation you can defend that is really yours, held loosely enough to revise. That is the whole point of the apparatus, and it is easy to lose sight of behind the apparatus.

nodes.name: Reading Poems Aloud
nodes.desc: Poems are meant to be heard. Read slowly and let yourself pause where the lines break.

nodes.name: Images
nodes.desc: Pictures made of words that hit the senses. Strong poems show you things and trust you to feel them.

nodes.name: Sound & Rhyme
nodes.desc: Rhyme, alliteration and assonance. Sound can make a line feel soft, sharp or fast.

nodes.name: Line Breaks
nodes.desc: Where a line ends changes how it reads. Breaks add pause, surprise and double meanings.

nodes.name: Metaphor & Simile
nodes.desc: Comparing two things to show something new about one of them. The best ones are surprising and exact.

nodes.name: Writing Your Own
nodes.desc: Drafting poems from prompts and memories. Write first and judge later, much later.

nodes.name: Meter
nodes.desc: Patterns of stressed and unstressed syllables. Iambic pentameter is the heartbeat of Shakespeare.

nodes.name: Fixed Forms
nodes.desc: Sonnets, haiku, villanelles and more. Rules can push you to ideas you wouldn't find on your own.

nodes.name: Free Verse
nodes.desc: Poems without set rhyme or meter. Every choice still counts, since there's no pattern to hide behind.

nodes.name: Tone & Speaker
nodes.desc: Who's talking, who they're talking to and how they feel. The speaker isn't always the poet.

nodes.name: Analyzing a Poem
nodes.desc: Linking techniques to meaning for an essay or an AP question. Every claim needs a quote and an explanation.

nodes.name: Revising Poems
nodes.desc: Cutting weak words and sharpening images. Read each draft aloud to hear what's off.

nodes.name: Spoken Word & Slam
nodes.desc: Poems built for the stage and an audience. Performance adds rhythm, pauses and eye contact.

nodes.name: Poetry Through Time
nodes.desc: Romantic, modern and contemporary voices. Each era argued with the one before it.

nodes.name: Comparing Poems
nodes.desc: Putting two poems side by side for a timed essay. Find a shared theme, then show how each one handles it.

nodes.name: A Chapbook
nodes.desc: A small collection of your best poems in an order that works. Contests and small presses publish these.

nodes.name: Publishing Poems
nodes.desc: Magazines, contests and student anthologies. Read what a journal publishes before you send it anything.

nodes.name: Sounds & Script
nodes.desc: The sounds the language uses and the marks it writes them with, learned before any vocabulary. A word learned with the wrong sounds has to be unlearned, and that is far more expensive than a slow start.

nodes.name: Core Vocabulary
nodes.desc: The first thousand words, which cover most of ordinary speech. Frequency order is not a preference here; it is the difference between six months and three years to a first conversation.

nodes.name: Survival Phrases
nodes.desc: Greetings, asking for things, and the sentences that keep a conversation alive when you are lost. "Say that again slowly" is worth more than fifty nouns.

nodes.name: Basic Grammar
nodes.desc: Word order, and how verbs change for who is doing what and when. Enough structure to build sentences you have never heard, which is the point at which phrases become a language.

nodes.name: Listening
nodes.desc: Making out words in speech at full speed, where they run together and nothing is enunciated. It lags behind reading for everybody, and the only fix is hours of it.

nodes.name: Speaking
nodes.desc: Producing sentences aloud, badly, in front of somebody. The willingness to be wrong out loud is the single largest predictor of how fast anybody learns a language.

nodes.name: Reading
nodes.desc: Text you can work through with a dictionary, then text you can follow without one. Graded material first: reading something too hard teaches vocabulary and destroys the habit.

nodes.name: Tenses & Aspect
nodes.desc: Talking about what happened, what will, and what was ongoing when something else interrupted. Languages divide time differently, and the divisions rarely map onto the ones you grew up with.

nodes.name: Cases & Agreement
nodes.desc: How a language marks who did what to whom. Endings, particles, or strict word order. Whichever system it uses, it is doing a job your first language does some other way.

nodes.name: Comprehensible Input
nodes.desc: Large amounts of material just above your level, understood mostly from context. This is where most real acquisition happens, and it does not feel like studying, which is why it gets skipped.

nodes.name: Spaced Review
nodes.desc: Reviewing each item just before you would forget it. Twenty minutes daily beats three hours weekly by a wide margin, and cards made from sentences you met beat cards bought in a deck.

nodes.name: Conversation
nodes.desc: Real exchanges at real speed, including the part where you did not catch it. Learning to repair a conversation without switching to English is a skill of its own.

nodes.name: Writing
nodes.desc: Producing text with time to think, which exposes exactly the gaps speaking lets you skate over. Getting a sentence corrected teaches more than getting a paragraph praised.

nodes.name: Idiom & Collocation
nodes.desc: Which words go together, which is mostly arbitrary and entirely noticeable. Grammatically perfect sentences that no native speaker would say are the last thing to disappear.

nodes.name: Register & Politeness
nodes.desc: Formal and casual, and who gets which. Some languages encode it in the verb itself, and getting it wrong reads as rudeness rather than as a learner error.

nodes.name: Cultural Context
nodes.desc: What is assumed, what is impolite to say directly, and the references everybody shares. Language separated from this produces sentences that are correct and land wrongly.

nodes.name: Native Media
nodes.desc: Film, news and books made for native speakers rather than for you. The first ones are exhausting; the transition from subtitles to none is the milestone most learners remember.

nodes.name: Fluency
nodes.desc: Speaking without translating in your head, and thinking in the language for stretches. It arrives gradually and is usually noticed in retrospect, often by somebody else.

nodes.name: Translating
nodes.desc: Carrying meaning across rather than words, and deciding what to lose. Being fluent in both languages is a prerequisite and nowhere near sufficient.

nodes.name: Maintenance
nodes.desc: Keeping a language you stopped studying. Without regular contact it fades faster than anything else you have learned, and reading twenty minutes a week holds most of it.

nodes.name: Handling Nerves
nodes.desc: Everyone gets nervous. Slow breathing and lots of practice turn panic into energy.

nodes.name: Voice & Volume
nodes.desc: Speaking loud enough for the back row and slowing down. Most nervous speakers talk way too fast.

nodes.name: Structuring a Speech
nodes.desc: An opening, three main points and a close. Tell them what you will say, say it, then sum it up.

nodes.name: Body Language
nodes.desc: Standing tall, using your hands and keeping your feet still. Your body should match your words.

nodes.name: Eye Contact
nodes.desc: Looking at real people, one at a time. It feels like a conversation instead of a speech.

nodes.name: Notes & Cue Cards
nodes.desc: Short keywords instead of a full script. Reading word for word kills your connection with the room.

nodes.name: Strong Openings
nodes.desc: A story, a question or a surprising fact. You have about thirty seconds to grab people.

nodes.name: Slides That Help
nodes.desc: Big images, few words and one idea per slide. Your slides should back you up and stay out of the way.

nodes.name: Telling Stories
nodes.desc: Short, specific stories make points stick. People remember stories long after they forget facts.

nodes.name: Rehearsing
nodes.desc: Practicing out loud, standing up and timing yourself. Record yourself once and watch it back.

nodes.name: Persuasive Speaking
nodes.desc: Using logic, emotion and credibility to move people. Know exactly what you want the audience to do.

nodes.name: Impromptu Speaking
nodes.desc: Speaking with little prep time. A quick structure like point, reason, example saves you.

nodes.name: Handling Q&A
nodes.desc: Listening fully, pausing and answering briefly. It's fine to say you'll find out and get back to them.

nodes.name: Class Presentations
nodes.desc: Hitting the rubric and the time limit, and sharing the stage in group talks. Plan the handoffs between speakers.

nodes.name: Speaking on Video
nodes.desc: Looking at the camera, decent lighting and clear audio. Your energy needs to be a little bigger on screen.

nodes.name: Speech Contests
nodes.desc: Oratory, extemp and declamation events. Judges reward clear structure and real presence.

nodes.name: A Talk You're Proud Of
nodes.desc: One polished talk on something you care about. TEDx youth events and school assemblies are great stages.

nodes.name: Pronunciation
nodes.desc: Classical sounds, like a hard c, w for v and long and short vowels. Reading aloud helps the endings stick.

nodes.name: Verbs & Conjugations
nodes.desc: Person, number and tense packed into one ending. Learn the four conjugations and the principal parts.

nodes.name: Nouns & Cases
nodes.desc: Nominative, genitive, dative, accusative and ablative. In Latin, the ending shows a word's job, so word order is loose.

nodes.name: The Five Declensions
nodes.desc: Noun families that share the same set of endings. Chant the charts out loud until they're automatic.

nodes.name: Core Vocabulary
nodes.desc: The thousand words that cover most texts. Loads of English words come from them, so look for the links.

nodes.name: Adjectives & Agreement
