nodes.desc: Adjectives match their nouns in gender, number and case. That's how you pair them up when they sit far apart.

nodes.name: Latin in English
nodes.desc: Roots and prefixes behind half the words on the SAT. Latin students tend to crush vocab sections.

nodes.name: Roman Life & History
nodes.desc: Daily life, the Republic and the Empire. Knowing the world makes the texts make sense.

nodes.name: All Six Tenses
nodes.desc: Present, imperfect, future, perfect, pluperfect and future perfect. The perfect stem unlocks three of them.

nodes.name: Pronouns
nodes.desc: Personal, demonstrative and relative pronouns. Relative clauses are where sentences start to get long.

nodes.name: Translating Sentences
nodes.desc: Finding the verb, then the subject, then everything else. Read the whole sentence before you write a word.

nodes.name: Passive Voice
nodes.desc: Things being done to someone. The endings change, and the ablative tells you who did it.

nodes.name: Participles
nodes.desc: Verb adjectives that pack a whole clause into one word. The ablative absolute is the classic one.

nodes.name: The Subjunctive
nodes.desc: The mood for wishes, purposes and what-ifs. Its forms are simple once you spot the vowel swap.

nodes.name: Indirect Speech
nodes.desc: Reported statements and questions. Latin uses an infinitive where English would say that.

nodes.name: Reading Caesar
nodes.desc: Real prose from the Gallic War. It's clear and military, and AP Latin builds right on it.

nodes.name: Reading Vergil
nodes.desc: The Aeneid in dactylic hexameter. Poetry scrambles word order, so the endings matter even more.

nodes.name: Scansion
nodes.desc: Marking long and short syllables to find the rhythm. It helps you read the poetry out loud the way it was meant.

nodes.name: AP Latin & Contests
nodes.desc: Sight reading, the National Latin Exam and the AP. Timed translation with no dictionary is the final test.

nodes.name: Fingerspelling
nodes.desc: The handshape for each letter. Practice reading it too, which is way harder than signing it.

nodes.name: Numbers
nodes.desc: Counting, ages, time and money each have their own rules. Palm direction can change the meaning.

nodes.name: Parts of a Sign
nodes.desc: Handshape, location, movement, palm direction and facial expression. Change one and you can change the word.

nodes.name: Everyday Signs
nodes.desc: Greetings, family, school and feelings. These are the signs you'll use in your first real conversations.

nodes.name: Facial Grammar
nodes.desc: Eyebrows and mouth shapes are part of the grammar. Raised brows mark a yes-or-no question.

nodes.name: Deaf Culture
nodes.desc: Deaf community values, history and etiquette. Getting attention with a wave or a tap is normal and polite.

nodes.name: Asking Questions
nodes.desc: WH-questions with lowered brows and yes-no questions with raised ones. The face does the work that word order does in English.

nodes.name: Using Space
nodes.desc: Placing people and things in the space around you and pointing back to them. It's how ASL keeps track of who's who.

nodes.name: Time & Tense
nodes.desc: ASL sets the time at the start of a sentence instead of on every verb. Past sits behind you and the future sits ahead.

nodes.name: Directional Verbs
nodes.desc: Verbs that move between people to show who's doing what to whom. Give and help work this way.

nodes.name: Number Systems
nodes.desc: Numbers built right into signs for time, age and money. Three weeks and five years each pack the number into one sign.

nodes.name: Classifiers
nodes.desc: Handshapes that stand for kinds of objects and show how they move. They make descriptions vivid.

nodes.name: Understanding Signers
nodes.desc: Watching the face and the whole picture at once. Watch Deaf creators and native signers on video every week.

nodes.name: Conversations
nodes.desc: Taking turns, checking understanding and keeping eye contact. Looking away can mean you've stopped listening.

nodes.name: Storytelling
nodes.desc: Role shifting and classifiers bring a story to life. ASL storytelling is an art form of its own.

nodes.name: Intro to Interpreting
nodes.desc: What interpreters do and how hard it is. Fluency takes years, and certification takes more.

nodes.name: Fluency & Community
nodes.desc: Signing comfortably with Deaf people in real settings. Community events teach more than any class can.

nodes.name: Asking a Question
nodes.desc: Turning an interest into something that could actually be answered with evidence. "Was the revolution inevitable" is a topic; "what did the people who joined it say they wanted" is a question.

nodes.name: Sources
nodes.desc: Primary material made at the time, and secondary work written about it afterwards. Knowing which you are holding decides what it can be used to prove.

nodes.name: Source Criticism
nodes.desc: Who made this, for whom, and what they wanted the reader to believe. A biased source is not a useless source; it is excellent evidence about the person who produced it.

nodes.name: Evidence & Inference
nodes.desc: The gap between what a document shows and what you want to conclude, crossed explicitly. Most weak arguments in these subjects are a hidden step in that crossing.

nodes.name: Context
nodes.desc: What was normal, sayable and possible at the time. Judging a decision by what everybody knows now is the error that makes the past look stupid rather than different.

nodes.name: Bias & Perspective
nodes.desc: Every account is from somewhere, including yours. The useful move is naming the position rather than hunting for a source that has none, because there are none.

nodes.name: Constructing an Argument
nodes.desc: A claim, the evidence, and why the evidence supports that claim rather than another. Handling the counter-example directly is what makes an argument stand up.

nodes.name: Reasoning & Fallacies
nodes.desc: The common ways an argument fails while sounding fine. Naming a fallacy is not a refutation on its own, and treating it as one is itself a habit worth losing.

nodes.name: Comparison
nodes.desc: Putting two cases side by side so the differences say something. Choosing cases that are similar enough for the difference to mean anything is most of the work.

nodes.name: Continuity & Change
nodes.desc: What actually shifted, how fast, and what stayed the same underneath. Periods are labels applied afterwards, and people living through them rarely noticed the boundary.

nodes.name: Cause & Consequence
nodes.desc: Distinguishing what made something possible, what made it likely, and what set it off. Single-cause explanations of large events are almost always a shortened version of a real argument.

nodes.name: People & Societies
nodes.desc: Groups, institutions and the rules that hold them together. Sociology as a habit rather than a subject: asking what a structure is doing rather than only what a person decided.

nodes.name: Place & Geography
nodes.desc: Rivers, mountains, distance and climate as constraints on what people could do. It is not determinism to notice that the map made some outcomes much cheaper than others.

nodes.name: Power & Politics
nodes.desc: Who decides, how they keep the ability to decide, and who is excluded. Formal institutions are half of it; the informal half is where most of it actually happens.

nodes.name: Economy & Society
nodes.desc: How people made a living, and what that allowed and prevented. Following the material constraints explains a surprising amount of what looks like pure ideology.

nodes.name: History of Ideas
nodes.desc: Where beliefs came from and what they were reacting against. Most ideas that feel obvious now were once a minority position with a specific opponent in mind.

nodes.name: Writing in the Humanities
nodes.desc: An essay that advances a position and shows its evidence, rather than surveying what others said. The literature review is background; the argument is the piece.

nodes.name: Ethical Reasoning
nodes.desc: Working out what should be done, with reasons somebody who disagrees can engage with. It is a discipline rather than an opinion, and the disagreements are usually about which principle wins.

nodes.name: Chronology
nodes.desc: A rough frame of what came before what, across more than one part of the world. Not an end in itself, and impossible to argue about causes without it.

nodes.name: Periods & Labels
nodes.desc: Ancient, medieval, modern and the rest are conveniences invented afterwards. Knowing they are arguments rather than facts is what stops them quietly doing your thinking.

nodes.name: Working with Sources
nodes.desc: Documents, objects, images and testimony, and what survived by accident rather than by importance. Absence of evidence is usually a fact about record-keeping rather than about the past.

nodes.name: Dating & Evidence
nodes.desc: Working out when something happened when nobody wrote it down: layers, materials, cross-references, radiocarbon. Independent methods agreeing is what turns a guess into a date.

nodes.name: Building a Narrative
nodes.desc: Turning fragments into an account, and being honest about the joins. Every narrative chooses a start point, and the choice is already an argument about causes.

nodes.name: Social History
nodes.desc: Ordinary lives: work, food, family, illness. Harder to research because ordinary people left fewer documents, and the part that changes how the period actually felt.

nodes.name: Political History
nodes.desc: States, rulers, laws and wars. The traditional spine of the subject. Best read as one thread among several rather than the frame everything else fits into.

nodes.name: Economic History
nodes.desc: Trade, prices, harvests and who owned the land. Long series of dull numbers explain more political upheaval than most political documents do.

nodes.name: Cultural History
nodes.desc: Belief, ritual, art and what people found funny or shameful. It is the fastest route to the fact that the past was a foreign place rather than us in worse clothes.

nodes.name: Empires & Encounter
nodes.desc: Expansion, conquest and what happened where two societies met. The sources are overwhelmingly from one side, and reading against them is a technique in itself.

nodes.name: Revolutions
nodes.desc: Moments when the arrangement of power broke rather than bent. They look inevitable afterwards and looked impossible a year before, which is the thing worth explaining.

nodes.name: War & Its Aftermath
nodes.desc: Causes, conduct and the settlements that set up the next one. Battles are the least explanatory part; logistics, finance and what happened afterwards do most of the work.

nodes.name: Technology & Change
nodes.desc: Printing, steam, rail, antibiotics and the internet. Inventions that reorganized what was possible. Adoption is usually slower and stranger than the invention story suggests.

nodes.name: Global Connections
nodes.desc: Following goods, diseases, people and ideas across borders instead of inside them. Many national histories stop making sense the moment you look at the shipping.

nodes.name: Memory & Commemoration
nodes.desc: How a society remembers, forgets and argues about its own past. What gets a statue is evidence about the people who put it up rather than about the person on it.

nodes.name: Quantitative History
nodes.desc: Censuses, tax rolls and parish records treated as data. It answers questions no chronicle can and inherits every bias in who was counted.

nodes.name: Oral History
nodes.desc: Testimony gathered from people who were there, decades later. Memory reshapes itself over time, and that reshaping is itself a subject rather than only a limitation.

nodes.name: Public History
nodes.desc: History outside the academy: museums, documentaries, curricula and heritage. What the public believes about the past is decided here far more than in journals.

nodes.name: Historiography
nodes.desc: The history of the writing of history: what each generation thought worth explaining and what it could not see. Reading it makes the current consensus visible as a position rather than as the truth.

nodes.name: Doing Research
nodes.desc: A question, an archive, months of material that answers something else, and an argument at the end. The gap between reading history and producing it is mostly patience.

nodes.name: Arguments
nodes.desc: Premises, a conclusion, and the claim that the second follows from the first. Separating whether the reasoning is valid from whether the premises are true is the first move and the one people skip.

nodes.name: Formal Logic
nodes.desc: Rules of inference that hold regardless of subject matter. Symbolizing an argument strips the rhetoric off it and shows what was actually being claimed.

nodes.name: Fallacies
nodes.desc: Standard ways of reasoning badly while sounding persuasive. Useful for reading your own drafts, and overused as a way of dismissing arguments without answering them.

nodes.name: Concepts & Definitions
nodes.desc: Being precise about what a word is being used to mean here. A surprising number of long disagreements dissolve the moment both sides define the central term.

nodes.name: Thought Experiments
nodes.desc: Impossible cases built to isolate one intuition. They are instruments rather than stories, and complaining that the scenario is unrealistic usually misses what it is for.

nodes.name: Epistemology
nodes.desc: What knowledge is and when a belief is justified. Scepticism is not the answer here; it is the pressure test every account of knowledge has to survive.

nodes.name: Metaphysics
nodes.desc: What exists and what kind of thing it is: objects, properties, time, identity over change. Abstract until it turns out that most disputes elsewhere depend on an answer here.

nodes.name: Philosophy of Mind
nodes.desc: How thought relates to matter, and what conscious experience even is. The hard question is not how brains process information but why any of it is like something from the inside.

nodes.name: Free Will
nodes.desc: Whether choices could have been otherwise, and whether it matters for responsibility. Most of the interesting work argues that determinism and responsibility are compatible, which is less obvious than either extreme.

nodes.name: Ethics
nodes.desc: What makes an action right. Consequences, duties, or the character it expresses. The three main answers each get some cases obviously right and one case famously wrong.

nodes.name: Applied Ethics
nodes.desc: Medicine, animals, war, technology and the environment, argued case by case. It is where the theories earn their keep or turn out to be unusable.

nodes.name: Political Philosophy
nodes.desc: What makes authority legitimate and what a just distribution would look like. Every actual political argument is standing on an unstated answer to one of these.

nodes.name: Aesthetics
nodes.desc: What art is, and whether a judgment of beauty claims anything beyond a preference. The interesting cases are the ones where taste feels like it should be arguable.

nodes.name: Philosophy of Science
nodes.desc: What makes a claim scientific, how theories are chosen, and what happens when one is overturned. It takes the method seriously enough to ask what it actually guarantees.

nodes.name: Philosophy of Language
nodes.desc: How words attach to things, and how a sentence gets to be about anything at all. A great deal of twentieth-century philosophy runs through this question.

nodes.name: Ancient Philosophy
nodes.desc: The Greek beginnings, where the questions were set and several answers still stand. Reading the dialogues is also the best available demonstration of what an argument in good faith looks like.

nodes.name: Modern Philosophy
nodes.desc: The turn to the knowing subject: rationalists, empiricists, and the synthesis that tried to end the argument. Most contemporary debates are still using vocabulary settled here.

nodes.name: Contemporary Traditions
nodes.desc: The split into analytic and continental approaches, and the traditions outside Europe that were doing this all along. Knowing what each is trying to achieve makes the mutual dismissals less confusing.

nodes.name: Writing Philosophy
nodes.desc: One claim, defended, with the strongest objection answered rather than avoided. Clarity is the whole style: obscurity in this subject is nearly always a sign the thought is not finished.

nodes.name: The Examined Life
nodes.desc: Actually applying any of it to how you live and what you believe. The subject is famously capable of being studied for years with no such contact, which was never the intention.

nodes.name: Research Methods
nodes.desc: Experiments, observation and self-report, and what each can and cannot establish. Almost every disagreement in the field is really about whether the design supports the claim.

nodes.name: Measuring the Mind
nodes.desc: Turning something internal into a number: reaction times, scales, physiological signals. Validity is the whole question. Whether the thing you measured is the thing you meant.

nodes.name: Statistics in Psychology
nodes.desc: Effect sizes, confidence and the difference between significant and important. A field studying small effects in noisy samples has to be unusually careful here, and historically was not.

nodes.name: Replication
nodes.desc: Whether a result appears again when somebody else runs it. A large fraction of famous findings did not, and knowing which is now part of basic literacy in the subject.

nodes.name: Research Ethics
nodes.desc: Consent, deception, debriefing and the right to withdraw. The rules exist because several of the most cited studies of the last century would not be approved today.

nodes.name: Brain & Behavior
nodes.desc: Which structures do what, and the limits of inferring a mental process from a bright patch on a scan. Localization is real and far less tidy than popular accounts suggest.

nodes.name: Perception
nodes.desc: Sensation arriving and being turned into an experience of a world. Illusions are the standard tool because they show the construction happening rather than a fault in it.

nodes.name: Attention
nodes.desc: What gets processed out of everything arriving, and what does not. The reliable finding is that people miss far more than they believe they do, including in plain sight.

nodes.name: Memory
nodes.desc: Encoding, storing and reconstructing. And it really is reconstruction. Confident memories can be entirely false, which is a fact with consequences well outside the laboratory.

nodes.name: Learning
nodes.desc: Conditioning, reinforcement and how practice changes behavior. Spacing and retrieval beat repetition and rereading, which is one of the best-replicated results in the field.

nodes.name: Thinking & Reasoning
nodes.desc: Problem solving, judgment and the shortcuts that usually work. Biases are not stupidity; they are heuristics being applied outside the conditions they were good for.

nodes.name: Language & Thought
nodes.desc: How language is acquired so fast, and how much it shapes what can be thought. The strong version of that second claim has not survived; the weak version keeps producing results.

nodes.name: Development
nodes.desc: How thinking, attachment and moral reasoning change from infancy onward. Stage theories are useful frames and less rigid than their diagrams imply.

nodes.name: Social Psychology
nodes.desc: How the presence of others changes what people do. Situation beats disposition far more often than intuition allows, and that finding survived the replication crisis better than most.

nodes.name: Personality
nodes.desc: Stable differences between people, and the five dimensions that keep reappearing across cultures. Popular type indicators are not among the things that replicated.

nodes.name: Emotion & Motivation
nodes.desc: What emotions are for, how they are regulated, and why people persist at some things and not others. Reward that undermines existing interest is the finding worth knowing first.

nodes.name: Clinical Psychology
nodes.desc: How disorders are classified, and what the evidence says about treating them. Diagnosis is a working description rather than a discovered category, and the manual is revised for exactly that reason.

nodes.name: Health & Stress
nodes.desc: The routes between mind and body: stress, sleep, pain and adherence. Chronic activation of a system built for short emergencies explains a large share of it.

nodes.name: Applied Psychology
nodes.desc: Psychology in workplaces, classrooms, courts and interfaces. It is also where findings get oversold, so the method nodes at the top of this tree stay relevant.

nodes.name: Reading the Literature
nodes.desc: Reading a paper for its sample, its design and its analysis before its abstract. The whole tree points here: being able to tell a solid finding from a well-publicised one.

nodes.name: Claim, Warrant, Impact
nodes.desc: What you say, why it is true, and why anybody should care. An argument missing the warrant is an assertion and an argument missing the impact is trivia, and judges discount both without saying so.

nodes.name: Speaking Clearly
nodes.desc: Being understood at whatever rate you have chosen, with the emphasis landing on the words that carry the argument. Speed that costs comprehension is negative value however impressive it sounds.

nodes.name: Flowing
nodes.desc: Recording both sides of the round in columns so every argument can be tracked to whoever last answered it. A dropped argument you had a response to reads exactly like a concession, which is why this is a foundation.

nodes.name: Research & Evidence
nodes.desc: Finding sources that say what you need and cutting them without misrepresenting them. The cards that win rounds are qualified, recent, and say the thing in their own words rather than in your paraphrase.

nodes.name: Active Listening
nodes.desc: Hearing what was actually argued rather than the argument you prepared for. Most novice rebuttals answer a case the opponent did not run, which costs the speech and hands the judge a reason to discount you.

nodes.name: Citing Sources
nodes.desc: Author, qualification and date, said out loud, every time. It is mechanical, it is checkable, and an evidence challenge you cannot answer loses more than the card was ever worth.

nodes.name: Case Building
nodes.desc: A constructive that is internally consistent, fits the time, and anticipates the three responses everybody runs. Writing the blocks to those responses while you write the case is what makes the second speech survivable.

nodes.name: Time Allocation
nodes.desc: Deciding before you stand which arguments get ninety seconds and which get ten. Spending four minutes on the contention you enjoy and running out of time on the one that decides the round is the classic loss.

nodes.name: Refutation
nodes.desc: Naming the argument, saying why it fails, and saying what follows. Rather than reading a card at it and moving on. The third part is the one that gets skipped and the one a judge writes down.

nodes.name: Cross-Examination
nodes.desc: Asking questions with a destination, and getting the concession on the record so you can use it later. Cross is not scored directly, which is why the answers matter more than looking clever while asking.

nodes.name: Spotting Fallacies
nodes.desc: Recognizing the move rather than merely disliking the conclusion. Correlation offered as cause, a burden quietly shifted, a term redefined mid-round. Naming it is worth less than showing what it lets the opponent skip.

nodes.name: Weighing Impacts
nodes.desc: Explaining why your impact decides the round even if theirs is also true. On magnitude, probability or timeframe. This is the hinge of the whole tree: below it you win arguments, above it you win rounds.

nodes.name: Framework & Theory
nodes.desc: Arguing about how the round should be judged before arguing inside it. A framework nobody contests decides everything downstream, which is why conceding one early is so much more expensive than it feels.

nodes.name: The Rebuttal Speech
nodes.desc: The last speech, where you stop covering everything and tell the judge the two things that decide it. Going for everything is the most common way to lose a round you were winning on the flow.

nodes.name: Value Debate
nodes.desc: Rounds decided on a criterion rather than on consequences, where the moral framework is the contested ground. It demands actual familiarity with the philosophy, because a judge who knows it will notice a name used as decoration.

nodes.name: Policy Rounds
nodes.desc: Plans, disadvantages, counterplans and solvency, at speed and at volume of evidence. The research burden is unlike any other event, and organization of the files is a real competitive advantage rather than tidiness.

nodes.name: Reading the Judge
nodes.desc: Adjusting speed, jargon and what you go for based on the paradigm in front of you. Running a technical round in front of a lay judge is a strategy error that no amount of argument quality recovers from.

nodes.name: The Tournament
nodes.desc: Six preliminary rounds in a day, both sides of a resolution you may not agree with, against cases you have never seen. Everything below converges here, and stamina turns out to be a competitive skill in its own right.

nodes.name: Prep Time
nodes.desc: Using the minutes before a speech to pick your best two arguments. Prep is where rounds get won, so practice it under the clock.

nodes.name: Public Forum
nodes.desc: Two-on-two debate on current events, judged by everyday people. Clear words and real-world impacts beat jargon in this format.

nodes.name: Extemp & Speech Events
nodes.desc: Short-prep speeches on current events and the other speech categories. Great cross-training, since they force fast structure.

nodes.name: Coaching Novices
nodes.desc: Teaching younger debaters to flow, refute and weigh. Explaining it to someone else sharpens your own rounds.

nodes.name: How the UN Works
nodes.desc: The General Assembly, Security Council and specialized agencies. Know what each body can and can't do.

nodes.name: Rules of Procedure
nodes.desc: Motions, points and how voting works. Knowing the rules cold lets you steer the room.

nodes.name: Researching Your Country
nodes.desc: Your country's history, allies, economy and voting record. Represent its view, even when it isn't yours.

nodes.name: Researching the Topic
nodes.desc: Past resolutions, key players and what's been tried. The background guide is only the starting point.

nodes.name: Position Papers
nodes.desc: A one or two page summary of your country's stance and ideas. Plenty of awards depend on it.

nodes.name: Opening Speeches
nodes.desc: A sixty-second speech on your stance. Be clear and confident, and end with a call to work together.

nodes.name: Caucusing
nodes.desc: Moderated and unmoderated debate. Speeches get attention, and the real work happens in unmods.

nodes.name: Building a Bloc
nodes.desc: Finding allies with shared goals early on. Be the delegate who brings people together.

nodes.name: Negotiation
nodes.desc: Trading ideas and finding compromises. Listen for what other countries really need.

nodes.name: Writing Resolutions
nodes.desc: Preambulatory and operative clauses in proper format. Make each clause specific and doable.

nodes.name: Merging Papers
nodes.desc: Combining draft resolutions into one. It's where your diplomacy really gets tested.

nodes.name: Amendments
nodes.desc: Changing a resolution on the floor. Friendly amendments are easy. Unfriendly ones need the votes.

nodes.name: Crisis Committees
nodes.desc: Fast-moving committees with surprise updates. Write directives fast and think a few moves ahead.

nodes.name: Impressing the Chair
nodes.desc: Leadership, diplomacy and staying in character. Chairs notice who moves the room.

nodes.name: Running a Conference
nodes.desc: Chairing a committee or running a whole conference. Students who run conferences learn a ton about leading.

nodes.name: Best Delegate
nodes.desc: Putting it all together at big conferences. Preparation and kindness both win awards.

nodes.name: Why Government Exists
nodes.desc: People giving up some freedom for order and protection. Locke and Hobbes disagreed about how much.

nodes.name: The Constitution
nodes.desc: The Preamble, seven articles and how it can change. It's short enough to read in one afternoon.

nodes.name: Three Branches
nodes.desc: Congress makes laws, the president enforces them and courts interpret them. Each one can check the others.

nodes.name: Federalism
nodes.desc: Power split between the national and state governments. Lots of fights in the news are really about this split.

nodes.name: The Bill of Rights
nodes.desc: The first ten amendments and what they protect. Speech, religion, press and fair trials are the big ones.

nodes.name: Local Government
nodes.desc: City councils, school boards and mayors. Local decisions affect your daily life the most.

nodes.name: Congress
nodes.desc: The House, the Senate and how a bill becomes a law. Most bills die in committee.

nodes.name: The Presidency
nodes.desc: Formal powers, executive orders and the cabinet. Presidents have more room in foreign policy than at home.

nodes.name: The Courts
nodes.desc: Judicial review, precedent and how cases reach the Supreme Court. Landmark cases are favorite test questions.

nodes.name: Elections
nodes.desc: Primaries, the Electoral College and how campaigns work. Voting rules vary a lot from state to state.

nodes.name: Landmark Cases
nodes.desc: Marbury, Brown, Miranda, Tinker and more. Know the facts, the ruling and why it mattered.

nodes.name: Civil Rights & Liberties
nodes.desc: Equal protection and the movements that fought for it. Rights grew through struggle and court battles.

nodes.name: Parties & Interest Groups
nodes.desc: How groups organize to win power and shape policy. Know how lobbying and PACs work.

nodes.name: Media & Public Opinion
nodes.desc: Polls, news coverage and social media. Learn to spot bias and check claims before you share them.

nodes.name: How Policy Gets Made
nodes.desc: From a problem to a law to how it gets carried out. Agencies write a lot of the actual rules.

nodes.name: Economic Policy
nodes.desc: Taxes, spending and what the Federal Reserve does. Budget fights shape every other issue.

nodes.name: AP Gov Essays
nodes.desc: Argument essays and Supreme Court comparisons. Cite a founding document and a case in every answer.

nodes.name: Getting Involved
nodes.desc: Registering to vote, contacting officials and showing up at meetings. Young voters can swing local elections.

nodes.name: Maps & Projections
nodes.desc: Latitude, longitude and why every flat map stretches something. Greenland isn't really the size of Africa.

nodes.name: Countries & Capitals
nodes.desc: Knowing where places are. It makes every news story and history lesson easier to follow.

nodes.name: Landforms & Water
nodes.desc: Mountains, rivers, plains and coasts. Rivers decided where most old cities got built.

nodes.name: Climate Zones
nodes.desc: Why some places are hot, cold, wet or dry. Latitude, ocean currents and mountains explain most of it.

nodes.name: Population
nodes.desc: Where people live, how fast populations grow and population pyramids. The demographic transition model is a test favorite.

nodes.name: Migration
nodes.desc: Why people move, with push and pull factors. Most migrants move within their own country.

nodes.name: Culture & Language
nodes.desc: How languages, religions and customs spread. Ideas travel along trade routes just like goods do.

nodes.name: Cities
nodes.desc: How cities grow, their layouts and urban sprawl. Over half the world now lives in cities.

nodes.name: Agriculture & Land Use
nodes.desc: Farming types, the Green Revolution and where food comes from. Climate and money both decide what grows where.

nodes.name: Political Geography
nodes.desc: Borders, states, nations and conflicts over territory. Many borders were drawn by people who never visited.

nodes.name: Economic Development
nodes.desc: Why some countries are richer than others, and how that changes. Measure development with more than one number.

nodes.name: Globalization
nodes.desc: Trade, supply chains and connected cultures. Your phone has parts from dozens of countries.

nodes.name: People & Environment
nodes.desc: How people change the land and how the land limits people. Deforestation and dams are classic case studies.

nodes.name: GIS & Data Maps
nodes.desc: Making maps from data with layers. GIS is used everywhere from city planning to disaster response.

nodes.name: AP Human Geography
nodes.desc: Models, vocabulary and free-response practice. Learn each model, then learn where it breaks down.

nodes.name: Sociological Imagination
nodes.desc: Seeing how personal troubles connect to bigger social patterns. Unemployment for one person is a story, and for millions it is a trend.

nodes.name: Big Theories
nodes.desc: Functionalism, conflict theory and symbolic interactionism. Each one is a lens, and each sees something the others miss.

nodes.name: Research Methods
nodes.desc: Surveys, interviews, observation and experiments. Every method trades depth for breadth somewhere.

nodes.name: Culture
nodes.desc: Norms, values, symbols and language. You notice your own culture most when you leave it.

nodes.name: Socialization
nodes.desc: How family, school, friends and media teach us who to be. It never really stops.

nodes.name: Groups & Networks
nodes.desc: In-groups, out-groups and peer pressure. Even the size of a group changes how people act.

nodes.name: Deviance & Crime
nodes.desc: Who decides what counts as breaking the rules. What is deviant changes from place to place and decade to decade.

nodes.name: Social Class
nodes.desc: Wealth, income, status and mobility. Where you start shapes where you are likely to end up.

nodes.name: Race & Ethnicity
nodes.desc: How race is a social idea with real effects. Look at data on housing, schooling and health.

nodes.name: Gender
nodes.desc: How expectations about gender are learned and enforced. Compare them across cultures and over time.

nodes.name: Family
nodes.desc: How families form and change. The typical family looks very different than it did fifty years ago.

nodes.name: Education
nodes.desc: What schools teach on purpose, and what they teach without meaning to. Tracking and funding shape outcomes.

nodes.name: Religion, Economy & Politics
nodes.desc: The big institutions that organize society. Each one sets rules most people follow without thinking.

nodes.name: Social Change & Movements
nodes.desc: How movements form, grow and win change. Steady organizing does more than a burst of outrage.

nodes.name: A Sociology Study
nodes.desc: Designing and running a small study of your own school or town. Protect the privacy of everyone you ask.

nodes.name: Variables
nodes.desc: A name bound to a value the program can read and change later. The whole idea is that the name stays put while what it holds moves, which is what lets you write one instruction that works on data you have not seen yet. Most early confusion is really about when the value changes, not about the name.

nodes.name: Types
nodes.desc: What kind of thing a value is. A number, a piece of text, a true-or-false. The type decides what the operators actually do, which is why adding two numbers and adding two strings look identical and mean completely different things.

nodes.name: Operators
nodes.desc: Arithmetic, comparison and logic: the small set of symbols that combine values into new ones. Precedence is the part worth learning properly, because a wrong assumption there produces an answer rather than an error.

nodes.name: Input & Output
nodes.desc: Getting information in from a person, a file or another program, and sending something back. It is the first point where your code meets the world, so it is also the first place your assumptions about what arrives get tested.

nodes.name: Conditionals
nodes.desc: Choosing between paths based on whether something is true. Writing the branch is easy; writing a condition that says exactly what you meant, including at the edges, is the actual skill.

nodes.name: Loops
nodes.desc: Doing the same work repeatedly. Over a range, over a collection, or until something becomes true. The two questions that matter are what changes each time round and what makes it stop.

nodes.name: Lists & Collections
nodes.desc: Holding many values under one name and working through them. Once you can build, filter and transform a list, most programs stop being about single values entirely.

nodes.name: Text & Strings
nodes.desc: Text as data you can slice, search, split and rebuild. It looks simple because you can read it, but encoding, whitespace and the cost of joining in a loop catch nearly everyone once.

nodes.name: Functions
nodes.desc: A named piece of work with inputs and a result, callable from anywhere. This is the first real tool for managing size: it lets you stop holding the whole program in your head and think about one job at a time.

nodes.name: Readable Code
nodes.desc: Naming, shape and structure chosen so the next reader (usually you, months later) understands it without running it. Not decoration: unreadable code is where most bugs hide.

nodes.name: Debugging
nodes.desc: Finding out what the program is really doing instead of what you assumed. The method is the skill: reproduce it reliably, form one hypothesis, test that hypothesis, and only then change a line.

nodes.name: Error Handling
nodes.desc: Deciding in advance what should happen when something fails. A missing file, bad input, a network that vanished. The hard judgment is which errors to handle where, and which should be allowed to stop the program loudly.

nodes.name: Data Structures
nodes.desc: Choosing the shape that fits the work: a list for order, a map for lookup, a set for membership. The choice is usually the difference between a fast program and a slow one, long before any clever algorithm is involved.

nodes.name: Objects & Classes
nodes.desc: Bundling data together with the operations that belong to it, so a thing knows how to look after itself. Powerful and easy to overuse. Plenty of code is clearer as plain functions over plain data.

nodes.name: Modules & Packages
nodes.desc: Splitting a program across files with deliberate boundaries, and pulling in code other people wrote. What to expose and what to keep private is the decision that keeps a growing project navigable.

nodes.name: Files & Persistence
nodes.desc: Storing data so it survives the program exiting, and reading it back intact. Most of the difficulty is not writing the bytes but handling the cases where the file is missing, half-written or being changed by something else.

nodes.name: Version Control
nodes.desc: Keeping every version of the work, with the ability to see what changed, why, and to go back. Branching turns it from a backup into a way of trying things without risk.

nodes.name: Testing
nodes.desc: Code that checks your code, so a change that breaks something old tells you immediately. The value is not proving correctness. It is the freedom to change things without fear.

nodes.name: Refactoring
nodes.desc: Changing the shape of code without changing what it does. Done in small steps behind tests, it is how a program that grew badly becomes one you can keep working in.

nodes.name: Asynchronous Code
nodes.desc: Work that starts now and finishes later (a download, a timer, a database call) without freezing everything else. The mental shift is that the order lines appear in stops being the order they run in.

nodes.name: Performance
nodes.desc: Making a program fast enough, starting by measuring rather than guessing. Almost all real gains come from doing less work, not from micro-optimising the work you are already doing.

nodes.name: Program Design
nodes.desc: Deciding what the pieces of a system are and how they should depend on each other, before there is much code. This is the skill that separates a program that survives its second year from one that gets rewritten.

nodes.name: HTML
nodes.desc: The structure of a page: what is a heading, a list, a button, a form. Choosing the tag that means the right thing is what gives you working keyboard support and screen-reader behavior for free.

nodes.name: CSS
nodes.desc: How the page looks, written as rules that match elements. The cascade and specificity decide which rule wins when several apply, and not knowing those two is why CSS feels random before it feels precise.

nodes.name: Layout & Flexbox
nodes.desc: Arranging boxes along a row, a column or a grid. Flexbox handles one direction and grid handles two; picking the wrong one is the usual reason a layout needs a fight to behave.

nodes.name: Responsive Design
nodes.desc: One page that works from a phone to a wide monitor. The good version comes from flexible units and content that reflows naturally, with breakpoints as a last resort rather than the plan.

nodes.name: The DOM
nodes.desc: The live tree of the page as a program can see it: find an element, read it, change it, listen for what a person does. Everything interactive on the web is ultimately this.

nodes.name: Forms & Validation
nodes.desc: Collecting input and telling someone clearly when it is wrong. Validate in the browser for speed and on the server for safety. The browser copy is a courtesy, never the guarantee.

nodes.name: JSON & Data Shapes
nodes.desc: The format almost every web API speaks, and the habit of knowing exactly what shape you expect back. Most fetch bugs are shape bugs rather than network bugs.

nodes.name: Accessibility
nodes.desc: Making the page usable by keyboard, screen reader and anyone not using it the way you do. Most of it is choosing correct HTML and keeping focus visible, not adding extra machinery.

nodes.name: HTTP & Fetch
nodes.desc: How a browser asks another machine for something: method, path, headers, status, body. Knowing what a 401 means as distinct from a 403 saves hours you would otherwise spend guessing.

nodes.name: Client State
nodes.desc: Everything the page currently knows, and keeping it true as things change. The discipline is to store each fact once and derive the rest, because two copies eventually disagree.

nodes.name: Components
nodes.desc: Building an interface from small pieces that own their own markup, style and behavior. The payoff is that you can reason about, test and reuse one piece without loading the whole page into your head.

nodes.name: Props & Composition
nodes.desc: Passing data down and composing small components into bigger ones. Getting the boundaries right (who owns which piece of state) is most of what makes a component tree pleasant or painful.

nodes.name: Routing
nodes.desc: One address per screen, so the back button, a refresh and a pasted link all do what a person expects. It is what makes an app feel like part of the web rather than a page that swallowed one.

nodes.name: Build Tools
nodes.desc: The step that turns the source you write into files a browser can load quickly. Worth understanding rather than copying: the config is where most mysterious failures live.

nodes.name: Effects & Lifecycles
nodes.desc: Running work when something appears, changes or goes away. And cleaning up after it. Almost every stubborn interface bug is an effect that ran too often or never got torn down.

nodes.name: Talking to APIs
nodes.desc: Loading real data into a real interface, including while it is still loading and when it fails. An empty result and an error are different states and a good screen never confuses them.

nodes.name: Auth & Sessions
nodes.desc: Knowing who is asking and keeping that true for the rest of the visit. The rule that matters: the browser decides what to show, the server decides what is allowed.

nodes.name: Web Performance
nodes.desc: Making a page load and respond quickly on a normal connection and a normal phone. Measure first: the biggest wins are usually shipping less code and not blocking the first paint.

nodes.name: Testing the UI
nodes.desc: Checking that a screen does what a person needs, driven the way a person drives it. Test behavior rather than internals, or every refactor breaks a hundred tests that were describing the wrong thing.

nodes.name: Deploying
nodes.desc: Getting it onto a machine that is not yours and keeping it running. The goal is that shipping is boring: one command, repeatable, and reversible when it goes wrong.

nodes.name: Web Security
nodes.desc: The handful of attacks every web app faces (injected scripts, forged requests, leaked tokens) and the specific habits that prevent each. Assume every byte from the browser is hostile until proven otherwise.

nodes.name: App Ideas
nodes.desc: Solving a small problem you or your friends actually have. A homework tracker for your school is a great start.

nodes.name: Picking a Platform
nodes.desc: iOS, Android or both at once with React Native or Flutter. Cross-platform lets you reach everyone with one codebase.

nodes.name: Dev Setup
nodes.desc: Installing tools and simulators, then running on your own phone. Expect setup to eat a full afternoon.

nodes.name: Building Screens
nodes.desc: Layouts, buttons, text and images. Design for thumbs, small screens and people in a hurry.

nodes.name: Navigation
nodes.desc: Tabs, stacks and moving between screens. Keep it simple so nobody ever feels lost.

nodes.name: App State
nodes.desc: Keeping track of data as people tap around. Most bugs come from state getting out of sync.

nodes.name: Lists & Scrolling
nodes.desc: Showing long lists without lag. Virtualized lists only draw what's on screen right now.

nodes.name: Saving Data
nodes.desc: Storing data on the device so it survives closing the app. Plan for the app getting killed at any moment.

nodes.name: Talking to APIs
nodes.desc: Fetching data from the internet and dealing with slow connections. Always show loading and error states.

nodes.name: Sign-In
nodes.desc: Accounts, passwords and signing in with Google or Apple. Use a trusted service instead of building your own.

nodes.name: Mobile Design
nodes.desc: Platform conventions, touch targets and dark mode. People expect apps to feel at home on their phone.

nodes.name: Camera, GPS & Sensors
nodes.desc: Using phone hardware with permissions. Explain why you need access before you ask for it.

nodes.name: Notifications
nodes.desc: Push and local notifications. Send too many and people turn them all off, then delete the app.

nodes.name: Accessible Apps
nodes.desc: Screen readers, text size and contrast. Accessible apps work better for everyone.

nodes.name: Testing on Real Phones
nodes.desc: Trying old phones, small screens and slow networks. Simulators hide a lot of problems.

nodes.name: App Store Release
nodes.desc: Developer accounts, screenshots, review rules and launch day. Your first submission may get rejected, and that's normal.

nodes.name: Growing & Updating
nodes.desc: Reading reviews, fixing crashes and shipping updates. Apps are never really finished.

nodes.name: Arrays
nodes.desc: A block of values in order, reachable instantly by position. Everything else is built on understanding why reading by index is free and inserting in the middle is not.

nodes.name: Strings
nodes.desc: Arrays of characters with their own set of classic problems. Most string questions are really array questions wearing different clothes, which is worth noticing early.

nodes.name: Big-O Notation
nodes.desc: A way of describing how the work grows as the input does, ignoring constants and hardware. It is the only comparison between two approaches that survives a faster machine.

nodes.name: Sets
nodes.desc: A collection with no duplicates and instant membership tests. Reaching for one is the single most common way an accidental n-squared loop becomes linear.

nodes.name: Linked Lists
nodes.desc: Values joined by references rather than by position, so inserting and removing are cheap but reaching the tenth item is not. Mostly valuable now as the place where pointer thinking is learned.

nodes.name: Stacks & Queues
nodes.desc: Two disciplines of access: last-in-first-out, and first-in-first-out. Which one a problem wants usually decides the whole shape of the solution, as with depth-first against breadth-first search.

nodes.name: Hash Maps
nodes.desc: Storing and finding values by key in roughly constant time. The trade is memory for speed, and the assumption underneath is that your keys hash evenly. Which is why collisions are worth understanding.

nodes.name: Two Pointers
nodes.desc: Walking a sequence with two indices that move under different rules. Turns a great many quadratic scans into a single pass, especially on sorted data.

nodes.name: Sliding Window
nodes.desc: Keeping a running view of a contiguous stretch, growing and shrinking it instead of recomputing. The pattern behind almost every "longest substring such that" problem.

nodes.name: Recursion
nodes.desc: A function defined in terms of a smaller version of the same problem. Write the base case first and trust the recursive call. Trying to trace every level in your head is what makes it feel hard.

nodes.name: Sorting
nodes.desc: Putting things in order, and the reason n log n is the floor for comparison-based methods. In practice you call the built-in one; knowing how it works is for choosing keys and predicting cost.

nodes.name: Binary Search
nodes.desc: Halving the search space each step on ordered data. The real power is searching over an answer rather than an array. The version most people meet years after the basic one.

nodes.name: Bit Manipulation
nodes.desc: Working directly with the binary digits of a number. Niche but occasionally decisive, and the fastest way to represent a small set of on-or-off facts.

nodes.name: Heaps & Priority Queues
nodes.desc: A structure that always hands you the smallest or largest item next, without keeping everything sorted. The engine inside scheduling, streaming top-k, and shortest-path algorithms.

nodes.name: Trees
nodes.desc: Branching structures with a single root and no cycles. Nearly every operation is naturally recursive, which makes them the place recursion finally feels obvious rather than clever.

nodes.name: Binary Search Trees
nodes.desc: A tree that keeps its values ordered, so search, insert and delete are logarithmic. As long as it stays balanced. What happens when it does not is the whole reason self-balancing trees exist.

nodes.name: Tries
nodes.desc: A tree keyed by the characters of a word, so shared prefixes are stored once. The structure behind autocomplete and fast dictionary lookups.

nodes.name: Union-Find
nodes.desc: A structure for tracking which things are in the same group as merges happen. Tiny to implement, surprisingly fast, and exactly what connectivity and spanning-tree problems need.

nodes.name: Backtracking
nodes.desc: Building a solution one choice at a time and undoing a choice when it leads nowhere. Systematic brute force. And the skill is pruning branches early enough to make it finish.

nodes.name: Greedy
nodes.desc: Taking the locally best option each step and having that be globally right. It works far less often than it appears to, so the real skill is proving the greedy choice is safe.

nodes.name: Dynamic Programming
nodes.desc: Solving overlapping subproblems once and reusing the answers. Every DP is a recursion plus memory; write the recurrence in words before writing any code and most of the difficulty disappears.

nodes.name: Representations
nodes.desc: Storing a graph as adjacency lists or a matrix, and knowing which the problem wants. Lists for sparse graphs, a matrix when you need instant edge lookup. The choice sets the cost of everything after it.

nodes.name: Breadth-First Search
nodes.desc: Exploring a level at a time with a queue. Because it reaches every node at distance one before distance two, it hands you shortest paths for free on unweighted graphs.

nodes.name: Depth-First Search
nodes.desc: Following one route as far as it goes before backing up. Natural to write recursively, and the base for cycle detection, topological order and component finding.

nodes.name: Connected Components
nodes.desc: Finding the separate islands in a graph that is not fully joined up. One traversal per unvisited node, and a surprising number of grid puzzles are exactly this.

nodes.name: Cycle Detection
nodes.desc: Deciding whether a graph contains a loop. Which differs between directed and undirected graphs. In a dependency graph a cycle is the thing that makes an ordering impossible.

nodes.name: Topological Sort
nodes.desc: An order in which dependencies always come before what needs them. This page lays its own nodes out with exactly this idea, and a cycle is what makes it fail.

nodes.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
nodes.desc: Shortest paths with weighted edges, using a priority queue to always settle the nearest unfinished node. Correct only while every weight is non-negative, which is exactly what the next node fixes.

nodes.name: Bellman-Ford
nodes.desc: Shortest paths that tolerate negative edges, by relaxing every edge repeatedly. Slower than Dijkstra, and the only one of the two that can also tell you a negative cycle exists.

nodes.name: Minimum Spanning Tree
nodes.desc: Connecting every node for the least total edge weight. Kruskal sorts edges and uses union-find; Prim grows outward from one node. Same answer, different shape of problem to suit.

nodes.name: A* Search
nodes.desc: Dijkstra with a heuristic nudging the search toward the goal. As long as the heuristic never overestimates, the answer stays optimal and the search visits far fewer nodes.

nodes.name: Bipartite Matching
nodes.desc: Pairing two sets so as many pairs as possible are matched. Scheduling, assignment and rota problems are usually this in disguise.

nodes.name: Network Flow
nodes.desc: How much can be pushed through a capacitated network, and where the bottleneck is. The max-flow min-cut theorem tying those two together is one of the most beautiful results in the subject.

nodes.name: Weighted Graphs
nodes.desc: Edges that carry a cost, like distance or time. Most real problems are weighted, and once they are, plain BFS stops finding the best path.

nodes.name: Grids as Graphs
nodes.desc: A maze or a game board is a graph where each cell links to its neighbors. Seeing that turns a scary problem into a BFS you already know.

nodes.name: 0-1 BFS
nodes.desc: Shortest paths when every edge costs zero or one, using a deque. Faster than Dijkstra for that special case and a favorite contest trick.

nodes.name: Union-Find
nodes.desc: A structure that merges groups and checks whether two items share one, in nearly constant time. It's the engine inside Kruskal's algorithm.

nodes.name: Trees & Ancestors
nodes.desc: Rooted trees, depths, parents and the lowest common ancestor of two nodes. Binary lifting answers each ancestor question in log time.

nodes.name: Floyd-Warshall
nodes.desc: Shortest paths between every pair of nodes in three nested loops. Simple to write, and fine whenever the graph has a few hundred nodes.

nodes.name: Strongly Connected Components
nodes.desc: Groups of nodes in a directed graph that can all reach each other. Tarjan's and Kosaraju's algorithms both find them in linear time.

nodes.name: Euler Paths
nodes.desc: A walk that uses every edge exactly once. Counting degrees tells you if one exists before you start searching.

nodes.name: Memory
nodes.desc: Where values actually live and what it costs to reach them. Once you can picture memory as one long addressable strip, a lot of otherwise arbitrary performance advice becomes obvious.

nodes.name: Stack & Heap
nodes.desc: Two places a program keeps things: a fast, automatically managed stack for call frames, and a flexible heap you allocate from. Which one a value lives on explains its lifetime and most of its cost.

nodes.name: Pointers & References
nodes.desc: A value that is the address of another value. Every "why did changing this change that" surprise in any language traces back to whether you copied the thing or a reference to it.

nodes.name: Processes
nodes.desc: A running program as the operating system sees it, with its own memory and its own view of the machine. Isolation is the point: one crashing process should not take the others with it.

nodes.name: File Systems
nodes.desc: How bytes are named, found and kept between runs. Paths, permissions and the fact that a write is not durable until it is flushed account for most surprises here.

nodes.name: Threads
nodes.desc: Several lines of execution inside one process, sharing its memory. The sharing is what makes threads fast and what makes them dangerous.

nodes.name: Concurrency
nodes.desc: Getting correct results when things happen at once or in an unpredictable order. Race conditions are the defining hazard: the bug is real, intermittent, and disappears when you look at it.

nodes.name: Locks & Deadlock
nodes.desc: Protecting shared state, and the new failure that protection creates: two holders each waiting on the other forever. Consistent lock ordering is the cheapest cure.

nodes.name: Buffered I/O
nodes.desc: Why reading a file one byte at a time is thousands of times slower than reading it in blocks. Buffering is the general trick of paying a large fixed cost rarely instead of a small one constantly.

nodes.name: Networking
nodes.desc: Two machines agreeing how to say something to each other, in layers. Knowing what DNS, TCP and TLS each did before your request left is what makes network debugging tractable.

nodes.name: Sockets
nodes.desc: The actual programming interface behind every network call. Open, write, read, close. Speaking HTTP by hand over one is the fastest way to stop treating the web as magic.

nodes.name: Servers
nodes.desc: A program that waits for requests and answers many of them at once. How it handles that concurrency (threads, processes or an event loop) shapes everything about how it scales.

nodes.name: Databases
nodes.desc: Storing data so it can be queried flexibly and survives a crash halfway through a write. Transactions are the promise that a group of changes either all happen or none do.

nodes.name: Indexes & Query Plans
nodes.desc: Why one query returns instantly and an almost identical one takes a minute. Reading the plan tells you what the database decided to do, which is usually not what you assumed.

nodes.name: Caching
nodes.desc: Keeping a copy of an expensive answer close by. Easy to add and hard to retire. Deciding when a cached copy stops being true is the entire difficulty.

nodes.name: Scaling
nodes.desc: Serving far more load than one machine can, and accepting the trade-offs that forces. Almost every hard distributed-systems problem starts the moment a second copy of the data exists.

nodes.name: C for Systems
nodes.desc: Writing code where you manage memory yourself. C shows you what higher-level languages hide, which is why every systems course starts here.

nodes.name: Compiling & Linking
nodes.desc: How source code turns into machine code, and why linker errors look so strange. Knowing the steps makes build failures way less mysterious.

nodes.name: Virtual Memory
nodes.desc: Every process gets its own pretend address space, mapped onto real memory in pages. Page faults and swapping explain a lot of slow programs.

nodes.name: Scheduling
nodes.desc: How the operating system decides which thread runs next. Fairness, priority and context switches all cost something.

nodes.name: Debugging With gdb
nodes.desc: Stepping through code, reading the stack and catching a crash in the act. A debugger beats guessing with print statements every time.

nodes.name: The Layers
nodes.desc: The stack of agreements that turns a click into electricity and back: link, network, transport, application. Each layer only talks to the one under it, which is what lets the whole internet change one layer at a time.

nodes.name: Packets
nodes.desc: Data cut into small pieces, each carrying its own address and finding its own way. Nothing on the internet travels as one long stream, which is why arriving out of order is normal rather than a fault.

nodes.name: Addressing
nodes.desc: The numbers that name a machine, and the mask that says which part of the number is the network. Subnetting is the one bit of arithmetic here worth doing by hand until it is automatic.

nodes.name: Routing
nodes.desc: How a packet is passed hop by hop toward a network nobody has a full map of. No router knows the whole route; each only knows the next step, which is what makes the system survive parts of it disappearing.

nodes.name: DNS
nodes.desc: The lookup that turns a name people can remember into an address a machine can route to. Caching is why a change takes hours to spread, and why "it works for me" is often a stale answer somewhere.

nodes.name: TCP
nodes.desc: A reliable ordered conversation built on an unreliable unordered one, using acknowledgements and retries. The handshake at the start is what makes a connection a thing that can be refused rather than ignored.

nodes.name: UDP
nodes.desc: Send it and hope, with no ordering and no retries. That sounds worse until the payload is a video frame that is useless late, which is why real-time media almost never uses the reliable option.

nodes.name: Ports & Sockets
nodes.desc: The number that says which program on the machine a packet is for, and the pairing of two addresses that makes a connection unique. Almost every "connection refused" is nothing listening on the port you chose.

nodes.name: NAT & Private Networks
nodes.desc: Many machines behind one public address, with a table translating the traffic back. It is why your laptop can reach the world but the world cannot start a connection to your laptop.

nodes.name: HTTP
nodes.desc: Request, status, headers, body. The application protocol most of the web is made of. Knowing that it is stateless explains cookies, tokens and half the design of every web framework.

nodes.name: TLS
nodes.desc: Encryption and identity for a connection, negotiated at the start of it. Certificates answer who is on the other end, and expired ones cause more outages than attacks do.

nodes.name: Proxies & Gateways
nodes.desc: Something in the middle that terminates one connection and starts another, to cache, filter, route or hide. Every unexplained header and mangled IP address in a log has a proxy behind it.

nodes.name: Load Balancing
nodes.desc: Spreading traffic across identical machines and taking the sick ones out of rotation. The health check is the real design decision: one that only proves the process is alive keeps sending traffic to a broken one.

nodes.name: Wireless
nodes.desc: The same layers over a shared medium where anybody in range can hear everything and two senders can talk over each other. It is why the bandwidth on the box is a ceiling nobody reaches.

nodes.name: VPNs & Tunnels
nodes.desc: Wrapping traffic for one network inside a connection over another, so a machine behaves as though it were somewhere else. Useful, and routinely mistaken for anonymity, which is a different property entirely.

nodes.name: Firewalls & Filtering
nodes.desc: Rules about which traffic is allowed where, applied at a boundary. Default-deny with narrow exceptions is the only version that stays correct as the number of services grows.

nodes.name: Diagnosing a Network
nodes.desc: Working down the layers with the standard tools until the failing one is named. The discipline is to ask which layer failed rather than which application, because the answer is almost never where the error appeared.

nodes.name: Latency & Throughput
nodes.desc: How long one thing takes versus how much fits through per second, which are different problems with different fixes. Distance is a hard floor: nothing negotiates with the speed of light in fiber.

nodes.name: Content Delivery
nodes.desc: Copies of your content held close to the people asking for it. Beating latency by shortening the distance is the only trick that works, and cache invalidation is what you trade for it.

nodes.name: Network Design
nodes.desc: Laying out addresses, segments, redundancy and failure domains for something that has to keep working while parts of it do not. The question is always what happens when this link goes, not whether it will.

nodes.name: Data & Datasets
nodes.desc: What a dataset actually is: rows that are observations, columns that are variables, and a definition of what one row means. Most confusion later traces back to nobody writing that definition down at the start.

nodes.name: Tabular Thinking
nodes.desc: Working on whole columns at once instead of looping over rows. Filter, group, aggregate, join. Four operations that cover most analysis, and thinking in them is what makes a dataset of ten million rows no harder than one of ten.

nodes.name: Cleaning Data
nodes.desc: Missing values, duplicates, three spellings of one category, a date column stored as text. This is where most of the time goes, and skipping it does not save the time. It moves it to after you have published the wrong number.

nodes.name: Notebooks & Reproducibility
nodes.desc: An analysis anybody can re-run from the raw file and get your numbers back. A notebook run out of order produces results that exist nowhere but in that session, which is the failure this is written against.

nodes.name: Exploratory Analysis
nodes.desc: Looking at the data before asking anything of it: shapes, ranges, oddities, what is missing and where. The goal is to find the surprises while they are still cheap.

nodes.name: Visualization
nodes.desc: Choosing the picture that shows the relationship rather than the one that looks impressive. A scatter plot answers a different question from a bar chart, and a chart that needs a paragraph to read is a chart that failed.

nodes.name: Descriptive Statistics
nodes.desc: Mean, median, spread and quantiles. A handful of numbers standing in for thousands. The median and the mean disagreeing is information, not a rounding problem, and the reason to always report the spread.

nodes.name: Distributions
nodes.desc: The shape the values take, and the handful of shapes that keep appearing. Recognizing a long tail matters more than naming it: on a skewed distribution the average describes almost nobody.

nodes.name: Sampling & Bias
nodes.desc: Who ended up in the data and who quietly did not. No amount of modeling recovers from a sample that never contained the people you are trying to say something about.

nodes.name: Joining Datasets
nodes.desc: Combining tables on a shared key, and checking the row count afterwards. A join that silently duplicated or dropped rows is the classic invisible error, because the result still looks like a valid table.

nodes.name: Querying at Source
nodes.desc: Asking the database for the slice you need instead of downloading everything and filtering later. Beyond a certain size that is not a preference, it is the difference between an analysis that runs and one that does not.

nodes.name: Hypothesis Testing
nodes.desc: Deciding whether a difference is bigger than the noise. The p-value answers a narrower question than most people want it to, and the effect size is the number that actually says whether anybody should care.

nodes.name: Correlation
nodes.desc: How strongly two variables move together, and the fact that a coefficient near zero rules out only a straight line. Always plot it: four famously different datasets share the same correlation.

nodes.name: Regression
nodes.desc: Fitting a relationship you can read out in words: how much the outcome moves per unit of an input, holding the rest still. The coefficients are the point, which is why it stays useful long after fancier models exist.

nodes.name: Feature Engineering
nodes.desc: Turning raw columns into things that carry signal. Ratios, differences, dates split into their parts. A good feature usually beats a better algorithm, and a leaked one beats everything until it meets reality.

nodes.name: Time Series
nodes.desc: Data where the order matters and yesterday predicts today. Trend, season and noise pull apart into three readable pieces, and any evaluation that shuffles the rows has already cheated.

nodes.name: Experiments & A/B Tests
nodes.desc: Making the comparison fair by deciding at random who gets what. Randomization is what buys you the word "caused"; peeking at the result daily and stopping when it looks good sells it straight back.

nodes.name: Data Pipelines
nodes.desc: The scheduled path from raw source to the table everyone reads, with the failures handled. The hard part is not moving the data but noticing on the morning it silently stopped.

nodes.name: Communicating Results
nodes.desc: Saying what you found, how sure you are, and what should happen next. To people who will not read the notebook. An analysis nobody acts on has the same value as one never run.

nodes.name: Data Ethics
nodes.desc: Consent, privacy and the harm a model can do at scale to people who never agreed to be in it. Anonymized data is rarely as anonymous as it sounds, and aggregation is not a defense on its own.

nodes.name: What Learning Is
nodes.desc: Fitting a function to examples so it works on new ones, instead of writing the rule by hand. The whole field is that one trade: enough flexibility to capture the pattern, little enough to not memorize the noise.

nodes.name: Supervised & Unsupervised
nodes.desc: Whether the examples come with the answer attached. With labels you are predicting; without them you are describing structure, and the two are judged by completely different standards.

nodes.name: Train, Validate, Test
nodes.desc: Three separate slices: one to fit on, one to tune against, one you look at once. The test set stops being a test set the moment you make a second decision after seeing it.

nodes.name: Metrics
nodes.desc: Accuracy, precision, recall and the ones that survive imbalance. On a problem where one class is 1% of the data, a model that always says "no" scores 99%, which is why the metric has to match the cost of each mistake.

nodes.name: Linear Models
nodes.desc: A weighted sum, and a threshold for classification. Still the right first model on most problems: it trains in seconds, tells you what it is using, and sets the bar anything heavier has to clear.

nodes.name: Overfitting
nodes.desc: A model that learned the training set rather than the pattern in it, and falls apart on anything new. The gap between training and validation score is the symptom you watch for the rest of your career.

nodes.name: Cross-Validation
nodes.desc: Rotating which slice is held out, so the score is not an accident of one split. Anything computed from the data (scaling, imputation, feature choice) has to happen inside each fold, or the leak comes back.

nodes.name: Regularization
nodes.desc: Penalizing complexity so the fit prefers the simpler explanation. One flavor shrinks weights toward zero and another sets them exactly there, which is why the second doubles as feature selection.

nodes.name: Trees & Forests
nodes.desc: Splitting the data on one question at a time, then averaging hundreds of such splitters. On ordinary tabular data an ensemble of trees is still the model to beat, and it needs almost no preprocessing to work.

nodes.name: Gradient Boosting
nodes.desc: Building trees in sequence, each fixing what the last got wrong. The strongest general answer for tables, and the one most sensitive to being tuned honestly against a validation set.

nodes.name: Clustering
nodes.desc: Grouping points that resemble each other when nobody has said what the groups are. The catch is that there is no score to appeal to. You have to argue the grouping means something.

nodes.name: Dimensionality Reduction
nodes.desc: Squeezing many correlated columns into a few that carry most of the variation. Useful for seeing high-dimensional data at all, and a reminder that most wide datasets are narrower than they look.

nodes.name: Gradient Descent
nodes.desc: Walking downhill on the error surface, one small step in the steepest direction. Nearly everything modern is trained this way, and the learning rate is the single knob that decides between converging, crawling and exploding.

nodes.name: Neural Networks
nodes.desc: Layers of weighted sums with a non-linearity between them, which is what lets them represent curves a linear model cannot. Depth buys expressiveness and buys an appetite for data along with it.

nodes.name: Backpropagation
nodes.desc: The chain rule applied backwards through the network to find the share of the error belonging to each weight. Worth deriving once by hand. After that the frameworks stop being magic and the failures start being readable.

nodes.name: Vision Models
nodes.desc: Networks that exploit the fact that meaning in a picture is local and repeats across the frame. The same filter slid over the image is why they need a fraction of the parameters a dense layer would.

nodes.name: Sequence Models
nodes.desc: Models for data where order carries the meaning. Text, audio, anything over time. The problem they all solve is how far back to remember, and how much of the past to weigh.

nodes.name: Attention & Transformers
nodes.desc: Letting every position look at every other and decide what matters, instead of passing a summary along a chain. That one change is what made models trainable at the scale everything since has been built at.

nodes.name: Transfer & Fine-Tuning
nodes.desc: Starting from a model somebody else trained and adapting it to your problem with a fraction of the data. In practice this is what most applied work is, and knowing what to freeze is most of the craft.

nodes.name: Models in Production
nodes.desc: Serving predictions to real traffic, and watching the inputs drift away from what you trained on. A model is not finished when it scores well; it is finished when somebody is monitoring it.

nodes.name: Fairness & Interpretability
nodes.desc: Being able to say why a model decided what it decided, and checking it does not decide differently for groups it should not. Removing the sensitive column does not remove the effect. The rest of the data usually reconstructs it.

nodes.name: Cells & Data Entry
nodes.desc: Rows, columns and entering data cleanly. One fact per cell keeps everything easy later on.

nodes.name: Formatting
nodes.desc: Number formats, borders and colors that make a sheet easy to read. Keep it simple and consistent.

nodes.name: Formulas
nodes.desc: Starting with an equals sign and pointing at other cells. Change one number and everything updates.

nodes.name: Absolute References
nodes.desc: Locking cells with a dollar sign when you copy formulas. It's the fix for most copied-formula bugs.

nodes.name: Common Functions
nodes.desc: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MIN and MAX. These cover most of what school and clubs need.

nodes.name: Sorting & Filtering
nodes.desc: Finding what you need in a big list. Filters hide rows without deleting them, so don't panic.

nodes.name: IF & Logic
nodes.desc: IF, AND, OR and nested conditions. They are perfect for grade calculators and checklists.

nodes.name: Lookups
nodes.desc: XLOOKUP and VLOOKUP to pull data from other tables. They save hours of copying and pasting.

nodes.name: Charts
nodes.desc: Bar, line and pie charts that make a point. Label the axes and pick the chart that fits the data.

nodes.name: Cleaning Data
nodes.desc: Removing duplicates, fixing typos and splitting text into columns. Clean the data first, then analyze it.

nodes.name: Text & Date Functions
nodes.desc: Combining names, pulling parts of text and doing date math. Dates are secretly just numbers.

nodes.name: Data Validation
nodes.desc: Dropdowns and rules that stop bad entries before they happen. Great for sheets the whole club edits.

nodes.name: Pivot Tables
nodes.desc: Summarizing thousands of rows in seconds. Drag fields around until the answer pops out.

nodes.name: Budgets & Trackers
nodes.desc: Personal budgets, grade trackers and club finances. Real projects make the skills stick.

nodes.name: Sharing & Collaboration
nodes.desc: Sharing, comments and version history in Google Sheets. Protect the important ranges from accidental edits.

nodes.name: Dashboards
nodes.desc: One page that shows the key numbers at a glance. Fewer charts make a clearer story.

nodes.name: Automation
nodes.desc: Macros and Apps Script for the stuff you repeat. If you do it every week, automate it.

nodes.name: What a Database Is
nodes.desc: A program whose whole job is storing data safely and answering questions about it faster than a file could. What you are buying over a folder of files is concurrent access, guarantees when things crash, and indexes.

nodes.name: Tables & Rows
nodes.desc: A table is one kind of thing, a row is one of them, a column is one fact about it. Deciding what one row means before writing any SQL prevents most of the trouble that follows.

nodes.name: Column Types
nodes.desc: Choosing what a column is allowed to hold, which is the cheapest validation there is. Dates stored as text and money stored as floating point are the two mistakes that are hardest to walk back later.

nodes.name: Keys & Relationships
nodes.desc: A primary key names a row uniquely and a foreign key points at one in another table. Together they are how a database stops holding the same fact in two places and starts holding it once.

nodes.name: Querying
nodes.desc: Asking for the rows and columns you want, filtered and sorted. SQL describes the result rather than the steps, which is the shift that makes it feel strange for about a week and obvious afterwards.

nodes.name: Joins
nodes.desc: Answering a question that spans two tables by matching rows on a key. Inner and outer differ only in what happens when there is no match, and that difference is usually the whole answer.

nodes.name: Grouping & Aggregates
nodes.desc: Collapsing many rows into counts, sums and averages per group. The rule that trips everyone once: filtering before grouping and filtering after it are different clauses and different questions.

nodes.name: Normalization
nodes.desc: Splitting tables so each fact is stored exactly once. Third normal form is far enough for almost everything, and knowing the rules is what lets you break them deliberately later rather than by accident.

nodes.name: Indexes
nodes.desc: A second structure that finds rows without reading the table. They make reads fast and writes slower, which is why indexing every column is not the answer even though it is tempting.

nodes.name: Query Plans
nodes.desc: What the engine decided to actually do with your query. Reading a plan turns "it is slow" into "it is scanning four million rows because this index does not cover the filter", which is a fixable statement.

nodes.name: Constraints
nodes.desc: Rules the database refuses to break. Not null, unique, foreign key, check. Application code that enforces the same rules will eventually have a path that forgets; the database never does.

nodes.name: Transactions
nodes.desc: A group of changes that all happen or none do. The classic case is moving money between two rows, and the reason to care is that every system eventually crashes exactly between them.

nodes.name: Isolation Levels
nodes.desc: How much two transactions running at once are allowed to see of each other. Each level trades a class of anomaly for throughput, and picking one is a decision about correctness, not performance.

nodes.name: Migrations
