nodes.desc: Changing the schema of a database that already has data and traffic in it. Every change wants a forward path and a way back, and the ones that lock a big table are the ones that take a site down.

nodes.name: Views & Procedures
nodes.desc: A saved query that behaves like a table, and logic that runs inside the database itself. Both hide complexity well and both hide it from your version control unless you are deliberate about it.

nodes.name: Document & Key-Value Stores
nodes.desc: Stores that drop the fixed schema in exchange for flexibility and easy horizontal growth. They do not remove the modeling work, they move it into your application, where nothing checks it for you.

nodes.name: Backups & Recovery
nodes.desc: Copies you could actually restore from, tested by restoring from them. An untested backup is a belief, and the moment you find out it was wrong is the worst possible one.

nodes.name: Replication & Sharding
nodes.desc: More machines: copies for reading, and splitting the data when one machine will not hold it. Both introduce the question of what a client sees when the copies briefly disagree.

nodes.name: Analytical Stores
nodes.desc: Databases arranged by column instead of by row, because analysis reads three columns of everything rather than everything of three rows. The same SQL, an entirely different set of trade-offs underneath.

nodes.name: Schema Design
nodes.desc: Choosing the shape of the data for the questions the system will actually be asked, years before most of them exist. This is the decision the rest of the application is built on top of and the hardest one to reverse.

nodes.name: Threat Modeling
nodes.desc: Asking who would attack this, what they want, and where the soft edge is. Before writing defenses. Security spending without a threat model reliably buys the wrong thing, thoroughly.

nodes.name: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
nodes.desc: The three things an attack takes away: secrecy, correctness, or access. Naming which one a given risk threatens is what stops every conversation about security collapsing into the word "hacking".

nodes.name: Authentication
nodes.desc: Establishing who is asking. Passwords are the weak version and a second factor is most of the fix, because it turns a stolen secret from a full compromise into a nuisance.

nodes.name: Authorization
nodes.desc: Deciding what an identified person is allowed to do, checked on every request rather than once at login. Least privilege is the rule: the account that only reads cannot be used to delete.

nodes.name: Cryptography Basics
nodes.desc: What encryption, hashing and signing each promise, which is three different promises. The practical rule is to use the library everyone reviews, because homemade cryptography fails silently and looks fine.

nodes.name: Password Storage
nodes.desc: Storing something you can check a password against but never read back, using a slow salted hash built for the job. The threat is not a clever attacker, it is a leaked table and a rented graphics card.

nodes.name: Untrusted Input
nodes.desc: Treating everything from outside as hostile until it has been checked against what you expected. Nearly every famous vulnerability class is one program handing another program text it did not read carefully.

nodes.name: Injection
nodes.desc: Data that gets read as instructions. A query, a shell command, a template. The fix is structural rather than a filter: keep the code and the data in separate arguments so no amount of quoting can move the boundary.

nodes.name: Cross-Site Scripting
nodes.desc: A script from somewhere else, running on your page inside the session of whoever is reading it. Escaping on output rather than on input is the reliable direction, because the same string is safe in one context and dangerous in the next.

nodes.name: Sessions & Tokens
nodes.desc: Keeping somebody signed in without asking again, and being able to end that trust instantly. Where the token lives decides which attacks reach it, and how long it lives decides how bad a theft is.

nodes.name: Transport Security
nodes.desc: Encrypting the wire so the network cannot read or alter what passes over it, and certificates as the answer to who you are talking to. A warning clicked through is the whole guarantee thrown away.

nodes.name: Network Defenses
nodes.desc: Firewalls, segmentation and the principle that a machine should only be reachable from where it needs to be. Segmentation is what turns one compromised laptop into one compromised laptop instead of an estate.

nodes.name: Social Engineering
nodes.desc: Attacks on people rather than software: a convincing email, an urgent phone call, a badge held for a stranger. It remains the most successful route in, and no amount of patching touches it.

nodes.name: Malware & Endpoints
nodes.desc: How hostile code arrives on a machine, persists, and is spotted. Most of the defense is unglamorous: patch quickly, do not run as administrator, and log enough to reconstruct what happened.

nodes.name: Dependencies & Supply Chain
nodes.desc: Every package you install is code you are running with your privileges. Pinning versions, reviewing what updates, and knowing what you actually depend on is the whole of the practical defense.

nodes.name: Secrets Management
nodes.desc: Keys and credentials kept out of source control, scoped narrowly, and rotatable without a deploy. A secret committed once is a secret forever, whatever the next commit removes.

nodes.name: Authorization to Test
nodes.desc: Written permission, an agreed scope and a defined window. The difference between security work and a crime. Everything below this node assumes a system you have been asked in writing to attack.

nodes.name: Penetration Testing
nodes.desc: Finding out what an attacker could actually reach, inside an agreed scope, and writing it up so it gets fixed. The report is the deliverable; the exploit is only evidence that the finding is real.

nodes.name: Incident Response
nodes.desc: What you do in the first hour: contain, preserve evidence, communicate, then recover. Rehearsed beforehand, because nobody invents a good process while the system is on fire.

nodes.name: Digital Forensics
nodes.desc: Reconstructing what happened from logs, disks and memory, without destroying the evidence while you look at it. The chain of custody matters as much as the finding if anybody will ever act on it formally.

nodes.name: Security Programs
nodes.desc: Turning all of it into something an organization does continuously: reviews, training, patch cycles and measured risk. Security as a permanent practice rather than an audit that happens once a year.

nodes.name: Fast Input & Output
nodes.desc: Reading a hundred thousand lines without the reading being the bottleneck, and printing without flushing every line. It is the one piece of boilerplate worth memorizing, because it is the same in every problem you will ever solve.

nodes.name: Reading the Constraints
nodes.desc: The bound on n is the problem telling you which complexity it will accept. Two hundred thousand rules out quadratic, twenty admits exponential, and reading that line first saves writing the wrong solution twice.

nodes.name: Complete Search
nodes.desc: Trying everything, when the constraints say everything is small enough. It is the correct answer to more Bronze problems than anybody expects, and it is the baseline every cleverer solution gets checked against.

nodes.name: Sorting & Two Pointers
nodes.desc: Putting things in order so a second pass can walk them once instead of comparing every pair. A great many quadratic solutions become linear the moment the input is sorted first.

nodes.name: Prefix Sums
nodes.desc: Precomputing running totals so any range sum is one subtraction. The first technique that trades memory for time explicitly, and the mental model every later range structure is built on.

nodes.name: Binary Search
nodes.desc: Halving the space each step, and (more usefully) binary searching on the answer itself when the check is monotonic. The second use solves problems that look nothing like searching.

nodes.name: Bronze
nodes.desc: Where the technique is rarely the difficulty and the statement usually is. Bronze problems are won by reading carefully, handling the edge case at n equals one, and not over-engineering a search that was meant to be complete.

nodes.name: Greedy
nodes.desc: Taking the locally best option and being able to argue it is globally optimal. The argument is the skill. An unproven greedy that passes the samples is the most common way to fail a whole problem.

nodes.name: DFS & BFS
nodes.desc: Walking a graph deep-first or level-first, and knowing that the second gives shortest paths when every edge costs the same. Flood fill, connected components and cycle detection are all one of these two wearing a hat.

nodes.name: Union-Find
nodes.desc: Keeping track of which things are in the same group, under merges, in almost constant time. Twenty lines that turn a class of connectivity problems into a single pass over the edges.

nodes.name: Silver
nodes.desc: The division where recognizing the shape becomes the whole game. A Silver problem is usually a graph, a sort, a prefix sum or a binary search in disguise. The plateau here is diagnostic, not technical.

nodes.name: Dynamic Programming
nodes.desc: Defining a state, a transition and a base case, then filling the table in an order where everything you need is already there. Naming the state precisely is ninety percent of it; the code is usually four lines.

nodes.name: Weighted Shortest Paths
nodes.desc: Dijkstra with a priority queue when the weights are non-negative, and knowing which algorithm to reach for when they are not. The graph is frequently not given as a graph, which is the actual difficulty.

nodes.name: Trees & Rerooting
nodes.desc: Dynamic programming where the state is a subtree, and the trick of recomputing every root from one traversal instead of n. Lowest common ancestor and binary lifting live here too.

nodes.name: Segment Trees
nodes.desc: Range queries with updates in logarithmic time, which prefix sums cannot do. Lazy propagation is where it stops being a data structure you copy and starts being one you understand.

nodes.name: Gold
nodes.desc: Where dynamic programming and real graph algorithms become the assumption rather than the achievement. Problems stop being one technique and start being two composed, which is the step most competitors find hardest.

nodes.name: Contest Number Theory
nodes.desc: Sieves, modular inverses, fast exponentiation and combinatorics under a prime modulus. A small, fixed toolkit that appears constantly and is almost never the interesting part of the problem.

nodes.name: Flows & Matching
nodes.desc: Maximum flow, minimum cut and bipartite matching. And the fact that a startling range of problems reduce to them. Spotting the reduction is far harder than running the algorithm.

nodes.name: String Algorithms
nodes.desc: Hashing, Z-function and suffix structures, for the problems where the input is text and the naive comparison is quadratic. Hashing is easiest and carries a collision risk you should be able to quantify.

nodes.name: Debugging Under Time
nodes.desc: Finding the wrong answer on test 14 with no test 14 in front of you. Stress testing against a brute force, and checking overflow and bounds before anything cleverer. It is the skill that converts near-misses into points.

nodes.name: Platinum
nodes.desc: Heavy machinery, composed, against a clock, where a full solve may take the whole contest. The division stops rewarding breadth and starts rewarding the ability to hold one hard problem in your head for four hours.

nodes.name: Shop Safety
nodes.desc: Eye protection, tethered tools, and knowing which machines you are checked out on. It is the root of this tree because every node under it involves something that can injure you or destroy the robot.

nodes.name: Mechanisms
nodes.desc: Gears, belts, linkages and the trade between speed and torque that every one of them makes. Most first-year design failures are a mechanism asked to do a job a different mechanism does easily.

nodes.name: Power & Batteries
nodes.desc: What a match actually draws, why voltage sags under load, and what a brownout does to a match you were winning. Teams lose more matches to power management than to any single mechanical failure.

nodes.name: Wiring
nodes.desc: Gauge, fusing, strain relief and connectors that survive being hit. A wiring job that works on the bench and fails on impact is the most expensive kind, because it fails intermittently at competition.

nodes.name: CAD
nodes.desc: Designing the thing before cutting it, and discovering the interference on a screen rather than in aluminum. A full-robot assembly is what tells you two subsystems want the same eight cubic inches.

nodes.name: Materials & Fabrication
nodes.desc: What each stock shape is good at, what your shop can actually cut, and the tolerances you can hold. Designing a part nobody on the team can make is a design failure rather than a manufacturing one.

nodes.name: Prototyping
nodes.desc: Building the ugly version out of wood and tape to answer one question, then throwing it away. Weeks of argument about whether an intake will work are settled in an afternoon by a prototype nobody was precious about.

nodes.name: Drivetrains
nodes.desc: The one subsystem that matters in every match regardless of the game. Tank, mecanum and swerve trade capability against complexity, and a reliable simple drive beats an ambitious one that is still being fixed on Friday.

nodes.name: Sensors
nodes.desc: Encoders, gyros and limit switches. The robot finding out where it actually is rather than where it was told to go. Every one of them is noisy, and treating a reading as truth is how mechanisms get destroyed.

nodes.name: Robot Code
nodes.desc: Subsystems, commands and a loop that must never block. Code that is fine in a unit test and stalls the main loop for forty milliseconds is code that makes the robot unsteerable.

nodes.name: Engineering Notebook
nodes.desc: Recording what was tried, what it measured and why the decision went the way it did. As you go, not the week before judging. It is separately awarded, and it is the only thing that survives a graduating team.

nodes.name: Feedback Control
nodes.desc: Closing the loop so a mechanism reaches a setpoint and stays there under load. PID is four lines and two weeks of tuning, and understanding what each term answers for is what shortens the two weeks.

nodes.name: Autonomous Routines
nodes.desc: Fifteen seconds with no driver, where dead reckoning drifts and the field is never quite where the drawing said. A short routine that works every time outscores an ambitious one that works at home.

nodes.name: Computer Vision
nodes.desc: Finding a target in a camera frame and turning that into a heading, under venue lighting nobody warned you about. Latency is the constraint that surprises teams. A perfect pose estimate arriving late is a wrong one.

nodes.name: Match Strategy
nodes.desc: Reading the game manual for where the points actually are, and designing for a role rather than for everything. Most rookie robots attempt every scoring method and are mediocre at all of them.

nodes.name: Scouting & Data
nodes.desc: Recording what every robot at the event can do, so alliance selection is a decision rather than a reputation contest. The teams that win districts are usually the ones whose scouting data was trusted.

nodes.name: Pit & Repair
nodes.desc: Diagnosing and fixing between matches, with six minutes and a queue. Spare parts made during build season and a robot designed to be taken apart are what turn a broken gearbox into a missed match rather than a lost event.

nodes.name: Competition Season
nodes.desc: Six weeks to a bag date and then an event that tests all of it at once. The robot that wins is rarely the most capable one on the field. It is the one that played every match it was scheduled for.

nodes.name: Team Roles
nodes.desc: Build, programming, design, outreach and the drive team. Knowing who owns what keeps a season from turning into chaos.

nodes.name: Driver Practice
nodes.desc: Hours driving the real robot through real match routines. Smooth, consistent drivers win more matches than fast ones.

nodes.name: Outreach & Awards
nodes.desc: Running demos, mentoring younger teams and telling your story to judges. Judged awards can matter as much as winning matches.

nodes.name: Electrical Safety
nodes.desc: Low voltage only, no wall outlets and never short a battery. Lithium batteries can catch fire if you abuse them.

nodes.name: Voltage, Current & Resistance
nodes.desc: The three quantities behind every circuit. Picturing water flowing through pipes gets you started.

nodes.name: Ohm's Law
nodes.desc: V equals I times R, and you will use it constantly. If you know any two values, you can find the third.

nodes.name: Breadboards
nodes.desc: Building circuits without soldering anything. Learn which holes connect underneath before you plug in parts.

nodes.name: Series & Parallel
nodes.desc: How resistors and batteries combine. Holiday lights and house wiring use different setups for a reason.

nodes.name: Using a Multimeter
nodes.desc: Checking voltage, current and continuity. Most debugging starts with a meter in your hand.

nodes.name: Components
nodes.desc: LEDs, capacitors, diodes, transistors and switches. Read the datasheet before you plug something in.

nodes.name: Soldering
nodes.desc: Making permanent joints that are shiny and solid. Heat the pad and let the solder flow onto it.

nodes.name: Arduino Basics
nodes.desc: Programming a microcontroller to blink, read and react. It's where code meets the real world.

nodes.name: Sensors
nodes.desc: Light, temperature, distance and motion sensors. Analog readings almost always need calibrating.

nodes.name: Motors & Drivers
nodes.desc: DC, servo and stepper motors. A motor needs more current than a pin can give, so use a driver.

nodes.name: Power Supplies
nodes.desc: Batteries, regulators and keeping voltages steady. Power dips cause the weirdest bugs.

nodes.name: Digital Logic
nodes.desc: Logic gates, binary and how computers work at the lowest level. Everything digital is built from these.

nodes.name: Talking Between Chips
nodes.desc: Serial, I2C and SPI, the ways chips pass data around. Most sensors you buy speak one of these three.

nodes.name: Designing a PCB
nodes.desc: Turning a breadboard into a printed circuit board. Free tools like KiCad put this in reach for students.

nodes.name: Debugging Circuits
nodes.desc: Checking power, ground and one thing at a time. Loose wires cause a lot of mystery bugs.

nodes.name: Build a Gadget
nodes.desc: A full project from idea to working device. Science fairs and robotics teams love these.

nodes.name: Setting Up Python
nodes.desc: Installing Python, picking an editor and running your first file. Getting set up is half the battle for beginners.

nodes.name: Variables & Types
nodes.desc: Numbers, strings, booleans and how Python decides what type a value is. Loose typing is easy at first and tricky later.

nodes.name: Input & Print
nodes.desc: Getting input from the user and printing results. f-strings make your output clean and readable.

nodes.name: If Statements & Loops
nodes.desc: if, elif, else, for and while. Python's indentation is the structure, so be careful with your spaces.

nodes.name: Functions
nodes.desc: def, parameters, return values and scope. Small functions make your code way easier to fix.

nodes.name: Lists & Tuples
nodes.desc: Ordered collections and slicing. Most beginner programs live inside a list or two.

nodes.name: Dictionaries & Sets
nodes.desc: Key-value lookups and collections of unique items. Dictionaries are Python's most useful tool.

nodes.name: String Tricks
nodes.desc: Split, join, strip and format. Working with text is half of real Python work, so learn these by heart.

nodes.name: Comprehensions
nodes.desc: Building lists and dicts in one line. They read great when short and turn painful when long.

nodes.name: Errors & Exceptions
nodes.desc: Reading tracebacks and using try and except. The last line of a traceback is the most useful one.

nodes.name: Files
nodes.desc: Reading and writing text and CSV files. A with block closes the file for you, even when something breaks.

nodes.name: Modules & pip
nodes.desc: Importing the standard library and installing packages. Virtual environments keep each project separate.

nodes.name: Classes & Objects
nodes.desc: Bundling data and behavior together. Get comfy with simple classes before you touch inheritance.

nodes.name: Debugging
nodes.desc: Print statements, the debugger and explaining your code out loud. Find where what you expected and what happened split.

nodes.name: Popular Libraries
nodes.desc: requests, pandas, matplotlib and more. Libraries let you build real projects fast.

nodes.name: Testing With pytest
nodes.desc: Writing tests that check your code for you. Tests make changes a lot less scary.

nodes.name: Projects
nodes.desc: Games, bots, scrapers and data tools. Building something you care about is the fastest way to learn.

nodes.name: Python for Contests
nodes.desc: Fast input, smart algorithms and USACO problems. Python runs slower, so the algorithm matters even more.

nodes.name: Java Setup
nodes.desc: Installing the JDK and running a class with a main method. Java is strict, and that strictness catches bugs early.

nodes.name: Primitive Types
nodes.desc: int, double, boolean and char. Integer division and casting trip up almost everyone at first.

nodes.name: Strings
nodes.desc: String methods and why you compare with .equals. Using == on strings is a classic AP CS A trap.

nodes.name: Conditionals & Loops
nodes.desc: if, while and for, plus boolean logic. Off-by-one errors live in your loop bounds.

nodes.name: Methods
nodes.desc: Parameters, return types and static methods. Breaking code into methods makes it easy to test.

nodes.name: Arrays
nodes.desc: Fixed-size lists and walking through them. Know how to find a max, a sum and a count in one pass.

nodes.name: Writing Classes
nodes.desc: Fields, constructors and methods. A class is a blueprint, and objects are what you build from it.

nodes.name: Encapsulation
nodes.desc: Private fields with getters and setters. It keeps objects from getting changed in weird ways.

nodes.name: ArrayList
nodes.desc: Resizable lists and removing items while looping. Removing while looping forward skips elements.

nodes.name: 2D Arrays
nodes.desc: Rows, columns and the nested loops that walk them. Row-major order shows up on every AP exam.

nodes.name: Inheritance
nodes.desc: extends, super and overriding. A subclass gets everything the parent has, plus its own stuff.

nodes.name: Polymorphism
nodes.desc: One reference type, many object types. Which method runs depends on the actual object.

nodes.name: Recursion
nodes.desc: Methods that call themselves, with a base case to stop. Trace small examples by hand until it clicks.

nodes.name: Searching & Sorting
nodes.desc: Linear and binary search, plus selection, insertion and merge sort. Know how each one works step by step.

nodes.name: AP CS A Multiple Choice
nodes.desc: Tracing code by hand, quickly and without a computer. Write down the value of every variable as you go.

nodes.name: AP CS A Free Response
nodes.desc: Four handwritten coding questions. Practice writing Java on paper, since there's no compiler to help.

nodes.name: Java Projects
nodes.desc: Games, apps and tools beyond the exam. Android apps and Minecraft mods both run on Java.

nodes.name: Game Ideas
nodes.desc: Small ideas you can actually finish. Start with a clone of a simple classic like Pong or Snake.

nodes.name: Picking an Engine
nodes.desc: Scratch, Godot, Unity, GameMaker or Roblox Studio. Pick one and stick with it for your first few games.

nodes.name: Game Jams
nodes.desc: Making a whole game in 48 hours. Jams teach you to cut scope fast, and they are a blast.

nodes.name: The Game Loop
nodes.desc: Input, update, draw and repeat, many times a second. Every game ever made runs on this loop.

nodes.name: Sprites & Art
nodes.desc: Images, sprite sheets and simple pixel art. Placeholder boxes are totally fine while you build.

nodes.name: Player Input
nodes.desc: Keyboard, mouse, controller and touch. Responsive controls are what make a game feel good.

nodes.name: Movement & Physics
nodes.desc: Velocity, gravity and jumping. Game physics is about how it feels more than how real it is.

nodes.name: Collisions
nodes.desc: Detecting when things touch and what happens next. Hitboxes don't have to match the art.

nodes.name: Sound & Music
nodes.desc: Sound effects and background music. Good sound makes every action feel more powerful.

nodes.name: Menus & HUD
nodes.desc: Health bars, scores, pause screens and menus. Players should always know what's going on.

nodes.name: Level Design
nodes.desc: Teaching the player without using words. Introduce one idea, test it, then twist it.

nodes.name: Game States
nodes.desc: Title screen, playing, paused and game over. Managing states keeps your code from turning into spaghetti.

nodes.name: Enemies & AI
nodes.desc: Patrols, chasing and simple decision rules. Fun enemies are predictable enough to learn.

nodes.name: Game Feel
nodes.desc: Screen shake, particles and little bounces. Small effects make a game feel alive.

nodes.name: Playtesting
nodes.desc: Watching people play without helping them. Wherever they get stuck becomes your to-do list.

nodes.name: Polish & Bugs
nodes.desc: Fixing bugs and smoothing out rough edges. The last 10 percent takes half the time.

nodes.name: Publishing a Game
nodes.desc: Releasing on itch.io, Steam or an app store. A finished small game is worth more than an unfinished big one.

nodes.name: Game Portfolio
nodes.desc: A collection of finished games for school or job applications. Show what you made and what you learned.

nodes.name: Budgeting
nodes.desc: Knowing what comes in, what goes out and what is left before the month decides for you. Almost every money problem that is not an income problem is solved at this node.

nodes.name: Tracking Spending
nodes.desc: Recording where it actually went rather than where you assumed. Two months of honest records changes more behavior than any amount of resolve.

nodes.name: Saving & Buffers
nodes.desc: Money set aside before it can be spent, starting with enough to absorb a broken boiler. The buffer is what stops a small emergency from becoming an expensive debt.

nodes.name: Debt & Interest
nodes.desc: What borrowing costs, and why compounding runs against you exactly as hard as it runs for you. The rate and the term together decide the total, and the monthly payment hides both.

nodes.name: Credit
nodes.desc: How lenders decide what you can borrow and at what price. Boring habits build it, and the score is a summary of your record rather than a judgment about you.

nodes.name: Taxes
nodes.desc: What is owed, when, and which reliefs exist. Marginal rates are the piece most people have wrong: earning more never leaves you with less overall.

nodes.name: Income & Earning
nodes.desc: Salary, self-employment and everything irregular, seen after tax and after the costs of earning it. Comparing offers on gross pay alone is how people take a pay cut by accident.

nodes.name: Value & Price
nodes.desc: What something costs to make, what it is worth to a buyer, and why those two rarely meet in the middle. Pricing from cost alone leaves money on the table or prices you out entirely.

nodes.name: Bookkeeping
nodes.desc: Every transaction recorded twice, so the books have to balance. Four hundred years old, still the standard, and the reason an error announces itself rather than hiding.

nodes.name: Financial Statements
nodes.desc: Three views of one business: what it owns, what it earned, and what actually moved. Reading them together is the skill, because each one alone can be made to look fine.

nodes.name: Cash Flow
nodes.desc: Money in the account by the date it is needed, which is not the same as being profitable. Profitable businesses fail from running out of cash more often than from anything else.

nodes.name: Business Models
nodes.desc: Who pays, for what, how often, and what it costs to serve them. Most failed ventures had a product and never had an answer to the second half of that sentence.

nodes.name: Customers
nodes.desc: Who has the problem, how badly, and what they do about it today. Talking to twenty of them beats a year of planning, and is the step that gets skipped for being uncomfortable.

nodes.name: Unit Economics
nodes.desc: What one customer earns and what one customer costs to win and serve. If the second is bigger, growth makes things worse, which is a lesson usually learned expensively.

nodes.name: Risk
nodes.desc: What could go wrong, how likely, and what it would cost. Insurance, reserves and diversification are three answers, and knowing which risks you are keeping is the point.

nodes.name: Structures & Contracts
nodes.desc: The legal form of a venture, what it protects, and what a contract is actually promising. Reading the termination and liability clauses first is the habit worth acquiring.

nodes.name: Negotiation
nodes.desc: Finding the deal both sides prefer to no deal. Knowing your walk-away point beforehand is most of it, and asking what the other side needs beats arguing about what you want.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.desc: Deciding what to do and, harder, what not to. A strategy that does not rule anything out is a list of ambitions with a better name.

nodes.name: Compounding
nodes.desc: Growth on growth, which is unremarkable for five years and startling over forty. Every other idea in this tree is a footnote to how much the time in the market matters.

nodes.name: Inflation
nodes.desc: Money losing purchasing power quietly. Cash under a mattress is not a neutral choice; it is a small guaranteed loss every year, which reframes what "safe" means.

nodes.name: Risk & Return
nodes.desc: Higher expected returns come with a wider range of outcomes, including bad ones. Anything advertising the first without the second is either misunderstood or misrepresented.

nodes.name: Time Horizon
nodes.desc: When the money is actually needed, which decides almost everything else. Money required in two years and money required in thirty are two different problems with different answers.

nodes.name: Emergency Fund
nodes.desc: Several months of expenses somewhere boring and immediately reachable. It exists so that an unexpected bill does not force a sale at the worst possible time.

nodes.name: Asset Classes
nodes.desc: Shares, bonds, property, cash and the rest, each with a different shape of return and risk. Understanding what an asset actually is, and who pays you, comes before any decision about it.

nodes.name: Shares
nodes.desc: Part-ownership of a business, with a claim on what is left after everybody else is paid. That last clause is why they return more on average and fall further when things go wrong.

nodes.name: Bonds
nodes.desc: Lending money for a fixed return, where the risks are default and rates moving. Their price falls when interest rates rise, which surprises people who bought them for safety.

nodes.name: Diversification
nodes.desc: Spreading holdings so no single failure matters much. It is the one thing in investing that reduces risk without reducing expected return, which is why it gets called the only free lunch.

nodes.name: Funds & Index Tracking
nodes.desc: Buying a slice of hundreds of holdings in one purchase. Tracking a whole market cheaply beats most active management over long periods, and the evidence for that is not close.

nodes.name: Fees & Costs
nodes.desc: Percentages that sound trivial and compound exactly like returns do, in the wrong direction. One percent a year over a working life is a substantial fraction of the final total.

nodes.name: Tax-Efficient Saving
nodes.desc: Accounts and wrappers that change what is owed on growth and income. Using the allowance you already have is usually worth more than any change to what is held inside it.

nodes.name: Pensions & Retirement
nodes.desc: Money locked away for decades, often with an employer contribution and tax relief attached. Declining a matched contribution is turning down part of your salary.

nodes.name: Property
nodes.desc: A large, illiquid, borrowed-against, undiversified asset that people also live in. The leverage cuts both ways and the transaction costs make it a poor short-term holding.

nodes.name: Insurance
nodes.desc: Paying a small certain cost to avoid a rare catastrophic one. Insure what would be unrecoverable and self-insure what would merely be annoying.

nodes.name: Behavior
nodes.desc: Not selling in a crash and not buying at a peak. Investor returns lag fund returns, and the gap is entirely this node rather than any question of selection.

nodes.name: Asset Allocation
nodes.desc: The split between kinds of asset, which drives most of the variation in outcomes. Deciding it in advance is also the mechanism that makes rebalancing possible.

nodes.name: Rebalancing
nodes.desc: Selling what has grown and buying what has not, on a schedule rather than on a feeling. It enforces the discipline of buying low precisely when it feels wrong.

nodes.name: Scams & Red Flags
nodes.desc: Guaranteed returns, urgency, complexity and anything that resists a simple question. The pitch is always about the upside; the tell is what happens when you ask about liquidity.

nodes.name: A Financial Plan
nodes.desc: Goals, timescales, contributions and the rules you will follow when markets move. Written down in advance, because the point of a plan is that it exists before it is needed.

nodes.name: Scarcity & Choice
nodes.desc: Limited means against unlimited wants, which makes every choice a choice against something. The whole subject is the study of that trade-off at different scales.

nodes.name: Opportunity Cost
nodes.desc: The value of the best thing you did not do. It is the concept that changes how decisions are made once it really sinks in, and the one most often quoted without being used.

nodes.name: Incentives
nodes.desc: People respond to what they are rewarded for, including in ways nobody intended. Most policy failures are a rule that was obeyed exactly as written.

nodes.name: Supply & Demand
nodes.desc: Two schedules of willingness meeting at a price. It is a model rather than a law, and its value is in predicting the direction of a change rather than the level of anything.

nodes.name: Elasticity
nodes.desc: How much quantity responds to a change in price. It decides who really pays a tax, which is rarely the person the tax is written against.

nodes.name: Market Structures
nodes.desc: From many small sellers to one, and what changes about price and quantity along the way. Competition is a spectrum, and almost nothing real sits at either end.

nodes.name: Market Failure
nodes.desc: Where prices leave something out: pollution, public goods, information nobody shares. Most economic arguments about policy are arguments about whether one of these is present.

nodes.name: Behavioral Economics
nodes.desc: What people actually do, as opposed to what a perfectly rational agent would. Losses looming larger than equivalent gains is the finding with the widest reach.

nodes.name: Game Theory
nodes.desc: Decisions where the outcome depends on what somebody else decides. The prisoner dilemma is the standard example because individually sensible choices produce a jointly worse result.

nodes.name: Measuring an Economy
nodes.desc: Output, income and expenditure as three routes to one total. What the headline figure excludes (unpaid work, depletion, distribution) is as informative as what it counts.

nodes.name: Growth
nodes.desc: More output per person over time, driven mainly by productivity rather than by effort. Small differences in rate compound into enormous differences in living standards within a lifetime.

nodes.name: Employment
nodes.desc: Who is working, who is looking, and who has stopped looking. The headline rate omits the last group, which is why it can improve while things get worse.

nodes.name: Money & Banking
nodes.desc: What money is, and the fact that most of it is created by commercial banks lending. That mechanism is the part that surprises people the first time.

nodes.name: Inflation
nodes.desc: A general rise in prices, from demand, from costs, or from expectations feeding themselves. Its costs are unevenly distributed, which is why it is politically explosive at low levels.

nodes.name: Monetary Policy
nodes.desc: A central bank moving interest rates and the quantity of money to steer demand. It acts with a long and variable delay, which is what makes it so hard to get right.

nodes.name: Fiscal Policy
nodes.desc: Government spending and taxation as levers on the economy. Debt matters relative to the size of the economy and the rate on it, not as an absolute number.

nodes.name: International Trade
nodes.desc: Comparative advantage, and why two countries can both gain even when one is better at everything. The aggregate gain is real and so is the fact that it is not shared evenly.

nodes.name: Development
nodes.desc: Why some countries are rich and others are not, and what actually changes it. Institutions, geography and history all compete for the explanation, and the honest answer uses all three.

nodes.name: Inequality
nodes.desc: How income and wealth are distributed and how that changes over generations. Wealth is far more concentrated than income everywhere, and mobility is what makes the difference bearable or not.

nodes.name: Economic Data
nodes.desc: Finding the series, checking how it is constructed, and noticing revisions. Most confident economic claims in public are made about a number nobody has read the definition of.

nodes.name: Thinking Like an Economist
nodes.desc: Asking about incentives, margins and what the alternative was, while remembering the models are simplifications. The discipline is useful precisely to the degree it stays aware of what it left out.

nodes.name: The Problem You Solve
nodes.desc: What somebody was struggling with before this existed. Marketing that starts from features rather than from that struggle is a description rather than a reason to buy.

nodes.name: Audience
nodes.desc: Who specifically, in enough detail to know where they already spend their attention. Everybody is not an audience; it is the phrase that precedes a campaign that reaches nobody.

nodes.name: Customer Research
nodes.desc: Asking people about their behavior rather than their intentions. What somebody did last month predicts far better than what they say they would do.

nodes.name: Positioning
nodes.desc: The space you occupy in the mind of a buyer, relative to the alternatives, including doing nothing. Being second-best at everything loses to being clearly first for a narrower group.

nodes.name: Messaging
nodes.desc: Saying the thing in words your audience already uses. Clarity beats cleverness reliably, and the test is whether a stranger can repeat what you do after one reading.

nodes.name: Brand
nodes.desc: The set of associations people carry about you, built by consistency over time. A logo is the smallest part of it and the part most often mistaken for the whole.

nodes.name: Copywriting
nodes.desc: Words that get one specific action taken. Lead with the benefit, keep the sentences short, and cut every phrase that would survive being deleted.

nodes.name: Content
nodes.desc: Being useful before asking for anything. It compounds slowly and it is the only channel that keeps working after you stop paying for it.

nodes.name: Search
nodes.desc: Being found by people already looking for the answer. Intent is what makes search traffic valuable, and matching the page to the question is most of the work.

nodes.name: Social Channels
nodes.desc: Platforms where attention is rented rather than owned, and where the rules change without notice. Pick the one your audience is on rather than all of them badly.

nodes.name: Email & Owned Audience
nodes.desc: A list you can reach without an intermediary deciding whether to show it. The most durable asset in marketing, and the one that survives every platform change.

nodes.name: The Funnel
nodes.desc: The path from never having heard of you to buying, and the drop at each step. Fixing the worst step beats adding traffic to the top, and it is usually far cheaper.

nodes.name: Landing Pages
nodes.desc: One page, one audience, one action. Everything that is not helping somebody take that action is competing with it, including navigation you added out of habit.

nodes.name: Paid Advertising
nodes.desc: Renting attention, measured against what a customer is worth. It scales what already works and reliably accelerates the failure of what does not.

nodes.name: Analytics
nodes.desc: Deciding which numbers actually indicate progress and watching those. Traffic and impressions flatter; activation, retention and revenue per visitor tell you something.

nodes.name: Testing
nodes.desc: Comparing two versions properly, with enough traffic to tell them apart. Most reported wins are noise called early, which is worse than not testing at all.

nodes.name: Retention
nodes.desc: Keeping the customers you already have, which costs a fraction of finding new ones. A leaking bucket makes acquisition an expensive way to stand still.

nodes.name: Pricing & Offers
nodes.desc: What to charge, how to package it and when to discount. Price communicates as much as it collects, and cutting it is the fastest way to change what you are understood to be.

nodes.name: Ethical Persuasion
nodes.desc: The line between making something easy to choose and making it hard to refuse. Manufactured urgency and awkward cancellation work in the short run and are how trust is spent.

nodes.name: Marketing Strategy
nodes.desc: A coherent plan across positioning, channels and budget, with a stated view of who you are not for. The tactics are interchangeable; the choice of which battle to fight is not.

nodes.name: Managing Yourself
nodes.desc: Reliable follow-through on your own commitments before asking anybody to rely on you. A manager who drops things teaches the team that dropping things is acceptable.

nodes.name: Listening
nodes.desc: Hearing what somebody actually said, including the part they were reluctant to say. Most management problems are visible weeks earlier to somebody who was asked and listened to.

nodes.name: Setting Expectations
nodes.desc: Saying what good looks like and by when, before the work starts. A surprising share of underperformance is a person doing exactly what they understood was wanted.

nodes.name: One to Ones
nodes.desc: A regular, protected conversation that belongs to the other person. Canceling it repeatedly says more about your priorities than anything you would say in it.

nodes.name: Feedback
nodes.desc: Specific, timely and about the work. Saved for a review six months later it is no longer feedback, it is a verdict on something nobody could still fix.

nodes.name: Delegation
nodes.desc: Handing over the outcome and the authority, not the task and the instructions. Keeping the interesting work is the most common way a new manager stalls both the team and themselves.

nodes.name: Prioritising
nodes.desc: Deciding what the team will not do this quarter. A list where everything is important is a list that has not been prioritized, whatever order it is in.

nodes.name: Planning Work
nodes.desc: Breaking an objective into work with owners and dates that somebody actually believes. Estimates are ranges, and treating one as a commitment is how a plan becomes a fiction.

nodes.name: Running Meetings
nodes.desc: A purpose, the right people and a decision at the end. The best improvement most teams can make is deleting half of them and writing the update instead.

nodes.name: Decision Making
nodes.desc: Knowing which decisions are reversible and moving fast on those. Saying who decides, before the discussion, prevents the meeting that ends with everybody assuming somebody else will.

nodes.name: Hiring
nodes.desc: Defining the role, running a fair process and testing for the work itself. A slow hire is expensive and a wrong hire is far more expensive, mostly to the people around them.

nodes.name: Onboarding
nodes.desc: The first month deciding whether somebody becomes effective or quietly disengages. A first task that ships, and one named person to ask anything, does most of the work.

nodes.name: Coaching & Growth
nodes.desc: Helping somebody get better at what they want to be better at, which may not be what you want from them. Asking beats telling, and the payoff is longer than any one quarter.

nodes.name: Conflict
nodes.desc: Two people who both have a point, addressed early and in person. Avoided, it does not fade; it becomes a fact about the team that new joiners inherit.

nodes.name: Performance Problems
nodes.desc: Naming the gap, agreeing what changes, and following through either way. Handled clearly it is a kindness; left alone it is unfair to the person and to everybody covering for them.

nodes.name: Trust & Safety
nodes.desc: A team where bad news travels upward quickly. It is built by how you react the first few times somebody tells you something you did not want to hear.

nodes.name: Process & Systems
nodes.desc: Enough structure that the work does not depend on you remembering. Every process has a cost, and the ones added after a single incident are the ones to review.

nodes.name: Measuring a Team
nodes.desc: Choosing indicators that do not distort behavior when people know they are being measured. Any single number will be gamed eventually, including by well-intentioned people.

nodes.name: Leading Change
nodes.desc: Moving a group to a new way of working while the current one is still running. Explaining why, repeatedly and to individuals, is most of the job.

nodes.name: Leadership
nodes.desc: Setting direction people choose to follow, and being the same person under pressure as when things are calm. Authority comes with the title; this does not.

nodes.name: Finding a Problem
nodes.desc: Starting with something people really struggle with. Good businesses solve real problems people will pay to fix.

nodes.name: Talking to Customers
nodes.desc: Asking people about their problems before you build anything. Listen way more than you pitch.

nodes.name: Money Basics
nodes.desc: Revenue, costs and profit. Know how much each sale actually puts in your pocket.

nodes.name: Testing an Idea
nodes.desc: Cheap tests like a sign-up page or a pre-sale. Find out if people will pay before you build.

nodes.name: A Simple First Version
nodes.desc: The smallest product that solves the problem. Ship it fast, then make it better.

nodes.name: Pricing
nodes.desc: Charging what it is worth to the customer. Most first-time founders charge too little.

nodes.name: Brand & Name
nodes.desc: A name, a logo and a message people remember. Simple and clear wins over clever every time.

nodes.name: Getting the Word Out
nodes.desc: Social media, word of mouth and flyers. Go where your customers already hang out.

nodes.name: Selling
nodes.desc: Asking for the sale and handling a no. Every no teaches you something about the pitch.

nodes.name: Running Operations
nodes.desc: Making, delivering and supporting your product reliably. Good systems free up your time.

nodes.name: Legal Basics
nodes.desc: Permits, taxes and when a parent needs to sign. Minors have extra rules, so check yours early.

nodes.name: Building a Team
nodes.desc: Finding co-founders and helpers who fill your gaps. Agree on roles and splits early.

nodes.name: Pitching
nodes.desc: Telling your story in two minutes to judges or investors. Problem, solution, traction and the ask.

nodes.name: Tracking Growth
nodes.desc: Customers, revenue and repeat buyers. Pick a few numbers and check them every week.

nodes.name: Pitch Competitions
nodes.desc: DECA, FBLA and youth startup contests. They are great for feedback, connections and prize money.

nodes.name: Funding
nodes.desc: Bootstrapping, grants and investors. Most student businesses don't need outside money at all.

nodes.name: Pivoting
nodes.desc: Changing direction when the data says so. Lots of big companies started out as something else.

nodes.name: Scaling Up
nodes.desc: Growing beyond what you can do yourself. Hire, delegate and build systems that don't need you.

nodes.name: What Accounting Is For
nodes.desc: Recording money so owners, banks and the government can trust the numbers. Every business decision leans on it.

nodes.name: The Accounting Equation
nodes.desc: Assets equal liabilities plus equity, always. Every transaction keeps both sides in balance.

nodes.name: Types of Accounts
nodes.desc: Assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses. Sort each one before you record anything.

nodes.name: Debits & Credits
nodes.desc: Left side and right side, and which accounts each one grows. It's backwards from your bank app at first, then it clicks.

nodes.name: Journal Entries
nodes.desc: Recording each transaction with a date, accounts and amounts. Debits always equal credits.

nodes.name: The General Ledger
nodes.desc: Posting entries into T-accounts and finding balances. It shows where every dollar sits.

nodes.name: Trial Balance
nodes.desc: Checking that total debits match total credits. A mismatch means something got posted wrong.

nodes.name: Adjusting Entries
nodes.desc: Accruals, deferrals and depreciation at the end of a period. They match revenue and expenses to the right month.

nodes.name: Income Statement
nodes.desc: Revenue minus expenses equals profit or loss. It shows how a business did over a stretch of time.

nodes.name: Balance Sheet
nodes.desc: What a business owns and owes on a single day. It always balances, because it's built to.

nodes.name: Cash Flow Statement
nodes.desc: Where cash actually came from and went. A profitable business can still run out of cash.

nodes.name: Inventory
nodes.desc: FIFO, LIFO and the cost of goods sold. The method you choose changes reported profit.

nodes.name: Payroll
nodes.desc: Wages, withholding and employer taxes. Your own paycheck stub makes a great example.

nodes.name: Financial Ratios
nodes.desc: Margins, liquidity and debt ratios to compare businesses. One ratio alone can mislead, so use a few together.

nodes.name: Accounting Software
nodes.desc: QuickBooks, spreadsheets and how they automate the cycle. Knowing the manual steps makes the software make sense.

nodes.name: Accounting Paths
nodes.desc: Bookkeeping, CPA, auditing and FBLA accounting events. Strong accounting skills open doors in every business field.

nodes.name: What Law Does
nodes.desc: Rules that keep order, settle fights and protect rights. Laws come from constitutions, legislatures, courts and agencies.

nodes.name: Civil vs Criminal Law
nodes.desc: Criminal cases are the state against a person, and civil cases are disputes between people. The burden of proof differs a lot.

nodes.name: The Court System
nodes.desc: Trial courts, appeals courts and supreme courts, state and federal. Most cases never leave the state system.

nodes.name: Your Rights
nodes.desc: Speech, search and seizure and the right to remain silent. Students have rights at school too, with some limits.

nodes.name: How a Case Moves
nodes.desc: Arrest or filing, pretrial, trial and appeal. Most cases end in a plea deal or a settlement.

nodes.name: Contracts
nodes.desc: Offer, acceptance and consideration. Minors can usually cancel contracts, with some exceptions.

nodes.name: Torts
nodes.desc: Negligence, defamation and other harms you can sue over. Duty, breach, cause and damages is the checklist.

nodes.name: Criminal Law
nodes.desc: Elements of a crime, intent and defenses. Prosecutors must prove every element beyond a reasonable doubt.

nodes.name: Reading Cases
nodes.desc: Facts, issue, rule, analysis and conclusion. Briefing a case is how every law student starts.

nodes.name: Legal Reasoning
nodes.desc: Applying rules to new facts and arguing from precedent. Good lawyers find the case that fits best.

nodes.name: Rules of Evidence
nodes.desc: Relevance, hearsay and when to object. Knowing these rules is half of doing well in mock trial.

nodes.name: Openings & Closings
nodes.desc: Telling the jury the story you will prove, then showing that you did. Plain words beat legal jargon.

nodes.name: Direct & Cross
nodes.desc: Open questions on direct and short leading ones on cross. Never ask a question on cross you do not know the answer to.

nodes.name: Mock Trial
nodes.desc: Playing attorneys and witnesses in a full trial against another school. It is great for confidence and college apps.

nodes.name: Law & Justice
nodes.desc: Wrongful convictions, sentencing and reform debates. Fair laws can still be applied unfairly.

nodes.name: Paths Into Law
nodes.desc: Pre-law majors, the LSAT and jobs that use legal skills. Many people with law degrees never become trial lawyers.

nodes.name: Capture
nodes.desc: Writing everything down the moment it appears, in one place you trust. The value is not the list; it is that nothing is being held in working memory where it costs attention all day.

nodes.name: Tasks Worth Writing
nodes.desc: A task that names a physical next action rather than a topic. "Sort out the insurance" sits untouched for weeks; "find the renewal email" gets done in four minutes.

nodes.name: Deciding the Day
nodes.desc: Choosing a small number of things for today, in the morning or the night before. A list of thirty is not a plan; it is a way of guaranteeing the day ends in a sense of failure.

nodes.name: Prioritising
nodes.desc: Separating what is urgent from what actually matters, and doing the second before the first has finished shouting. Most days are spent entirely on urgent items belonging to other people unless this is deliberate.

nodes.name: Estimating Time
nodes.desc: Guessing how long something will take and then checking. Everybody underestimates, consistently, and the only fix is a record of how wrong you were last time.

nodes.name: Time Blocking
nodes.desc: Putting work in the calendar rather than on a list, so it has to compete with everything else for actual hours. A list pretends time is infinite; a calendar refuses to.

nodes.name: Batching
nodes.desc: Grouping similar work so the setup cost is paid once. Email four times a day rather than continuously is the standard example, and the one with the largest effect.

nodes.name: Starting
nodes.desc: Getting past the first two minutes, which is where most procrastination actually lives. Shrinking the first step until it is faintly ridiculous is the reliable trick.

nodes.name: Procrastination
nodes.desc: Usually avoidance of a feeling rather than laziness: the task is ambiguous, or the outcome is frightening. Naming which one it is suggests the fix, and discipline alone rarely does.

nodes.name: Habits
nodes.desc: Behavior that no longer requires a decision, built with a cue, a small action and a consistent time. Starting far too small is what makes one stick.

nodes.name: Energy & Rhythms
nodes.desc: Matching demanding work to the hours you are actually sharp. Scheduling analytical work into your worst two hours daily is a hidden and enormous tax.

nodes.name: The Weekly Review
nodes.desc: An hour to empty the inbox, look at every commitment and choose the coming week. It is the maintenance that keeps a system trustworthy, and the first thing dropped when things get busy.

nodes.name: Notes & Reference
nodes.desc: Somewhere to put things you will want later but do not have to act on. Keeping reference material out of the task list is what stops the list becoming unreadable.

nodes.name: Goals
nodes.desc: A small number of outcomes with a date and a defined finish. Goals without a next action are wishes, and goals without a review are forgotten by February.

nodes.name: Projects
nodes.desc: Anything that takes more than one action, broken down far enough that the next step is obvious. A stalled project is nearly always one whose next action was never defined.

nodes.name: Saying No
nodes.desc: Declining early and clearly rather than agreeing and delivering late. Every yes is a no to something with less of a voice, usually your own work.

nodes.name: Tools
nodes.desc: The smallest set of tools that supports the habits. Reorganizing the system is itself a satisfying form of procrastination, and switching apps has never once been the problem.

nodes.name: Reflection
nodes.desc: Looking back at what worked and what did not, on purpose and in writing. Without it, the same week is repeated with more effort applied to it.

nodes.name: A System You Trust
nodes.desc: Everything captured, reviewed regularly, and reliable enough that nothing is being remembered. That trust is the point of the whole tree: it is what makes it possible to work on one thing without the rest of it nagging.

nodes.name: How Attention Works
nodes.desc: A limited resource that refills with rest and is spent by switching. Understanding that switching has a cost, rather than believing in multitasking, is what makes the rest of this tree worth doing.

nodes.name: Naming Distractions
nodes.desc: Keeping a note of what pulled you away for a week. It is nearly always a shorter and more specific list than expected, which makes it fixable.

nodes.name: Environment
nodes.desc: A place where the default is work: the phone in another room, the browser closed, the door shut. Changing the surroundings beats resisting them every time.

nodes.name: Notifications
nodes.desc: Turning off everything that is not a person needing an answer now, which is almost all of it. Each interruption costs far longer than it takes, because attention has to be rebuilt.

nodes.name: Focus Sessions
nodes.desc: A fixed block with one task and a timer running. The length matters less than the commitment not to switch inside it, and twenty-five minutes is a starting point rather than a rule.

nodes.name: Single-Tasking
nodes.desc: One thing until it is finished or the block ends. It feels slower and finishes more, which is unintuitive enough that most people need to measure it once to believe it.

nodes.name: Starting Rituals
nodes.desc: A short, repeated sequence that signals work is beginning. Same place, same time, same first action removes the negotiation about whether to start.

nodes.name: Deep Work
nodes.desc: Ninety minutes or more on something cognitively demanding, with nothing else touched. Almost all really hard work is produced in blocks like this and almost nobody schedules them.

nodes.name: Shallow Work
nodes.desc: Email, admin and coordination, which are necessary and expand to fill whatever space is left. Giving them a fixed window is what stops them eating the day.

nodes.name: Context Switching
nodes.desc: The cost of picking up a different task, which is paid in minutes of reloading state. It is why five projects in one day gets less done than two, with more effort.

nodes.name: Flow
nodes.desc: The state where the work carries itself, reached when difficulty roughly matches skill. It cannot be forced and it can be arranged for: clear goal, no interruptions, the right level of hard.

nodes.name: Tolerating Boredom
nodes.desc: Not reaching for a phone in a queue. Attention trained to expect stimulation at every gap will not sit still for two hours of hard work when it is asked to.

nodes.name: Digital Minimalism
nodes.desc: Deciding what each tool is for and removing the rest. Applications are designed by large teams to hold attention, and treating that as a fair fight is the mistake.

nodes.name: Breaks
nodes.desc: Real breaks between blocks, away from a screen. A break spent scrolling restores very little, which is why people finish a day of them still feeling drained.

nodes.name: Working with Energy
nodes.desc: Putting the hardest work where your attention is best and admin where it is not. Most people have two or three really sharp hours, and spend them on email.

nodes.name: Handling Interruptions
nodes.desc: Capturing the thing and returning, rather than following it. Telling somebody when you will be free is more effective than being unreachable and less costly than stopping.

nodes.name: Protecting the Calendar
nodes.desc: Defending contiguous hours from being sliced into unusable fragments. Four meetings spread across a day cost far more than four in a row, and only one of those is negotiable.

nodes.name: Rebuilding Attention
nodes.desc: Extending how long you can concentrate, deliberately and gradually, as a trainable capacity. Reading a long book is unfashionable and remains the most effective exercise for it.

nodes.name: Measuring Focus
nodes.desc: Recording hours of real concentration rather than hours at a desk. The number is always lower than expected, and it is the only one that correlates with output.

nodes.name: A Focused Working Life
nodes.desc: Structuring weeks around the work that needs depth rather than fitting it into the gaps. It is a set of arrangements defended repeatedly, not a personality trait somebody has.

nodes.name: Reliability
nodes.desc: Doing what you said by when you said, or saying early that you cannot. It is unglamorous and it is the reputation everything else is built on.

nodes.name: Email & Messages
nodes.desc: Writing so the reader knows what is wanted from them in the first two lines. A message that buries the request under context gets answered late or not at all.

nodes.name: Writing at Work
nodes.desc: Documents that survive being skimmed: conclusion first, headings, and a summary somebody could act on alone. Most workplace writing is read by people looking for one thing.

nodes.name: Meetings
nodes.desc: Knowing why you are there, contributing, and leaving with an owner and a date attached to anything decided. A meeting with no decision should have been a message.

nodes.name: Following Up
nodes.desc: A short written record of what was agreed, sent afterwards. It takes five minutes and it is what prevents the most common failure mode of collaborative work.

nodes.name: Working with Others Remotely
nodes.desc: Writing things down, being explicit about status, and not assuming everybody saw the thread. Distributed work fails on unstated assumptions rather than on technology.

nodes.name: Presenting
nodes.desc: One clear message, slides that support rather than duplicate you, and a rehearsal out loud. Reading your own slides aloud is the most common and most avoidable failure.

nodes.name: Asking Good Questions
nodes.desc: Saying what you tried, what you expected and what happened. It respects the time of whoever answers and usually solves the problem while you are writing it.

nodes.name: Receiving Feedback
nodes.desc: Listening, asking for specifics, and separating the work from yourself. Getting defensive is normal and expensive, because it teaches people to stop telling you things.

nodes.name: Making Work Visible
nodes.desc: Keeping a record of what you did and its effect, and sharing progress without being asked. Good work that nobody knows about is indistinguishable from no work at review time.

nodes.name: Working Across Teams
nodes.desc: Understanding what other groups are measured on, which explains most of what looks like obstruction. Finding the shared interest is faster than escalating.

nodes.name: Managing Your Workload
nodes.desc: Being explicit about what will slip when something is added. Silently absorbing everything ends in missed commitments, and by then the choice has been made for you.

nodes.name: Deliberate Skill Growth
nodes.desc: Choosing what to get better at rather than absorbing whatever the job happens to teach. Time at a desk is not experience; repeated practice on hard things is.

nodes.name: Professional Relationships
nodes.desc: Staying in touch with people you worked well with, before you need anything. Most jobs arrive through weak connections rather than through applications.

nodes.name: CV & Portfolio
nodes.desc: What you did, at what scale, with what result. Responsibilities describe a job description; outcomes describe you doing it.

nodes.name: Job Searching
nodes.desc: A targeted small number of applications beats a hundred generic ones. Reading the posting properly and answering it specifically is most of what gets a reply.

nodes.name: Interviewing
nodes.desc: Structured answers with a situation, what you did and what resulted. Prepared stories beat improvisation, and questions you ask them are assessed as closely as your answers.

nodes.name: Negotiating an Offer
nodes.desc: Knowing the range, asking once, politely and specifically. The conversation is uncomfortable for a few minutes and compounds for years, in both directions.

nodes.name: Changing Direction
nodes.desc: Moving to different work by finding the overlap and building the missing piece publicly. Sideways moves inside a place you are known are usually the cheapest route.

nodes.name: Deciding What You Want
nodes.desc: Working out what you actually want from work. The conditions, not the title. It is the question this whole tree is in service of and the one most easily deferred indefinitely.

nodes.name: Finding a Job
nodes.desc: Restaurants, stores, tutoring, lifeguarding and babysitting. Ask around, since lots of teen jobs never get posted.

nodes.name: Work Permits & Paperwork
nodes.desc: Work permits, ID, tax forms and bank info. The rules for teens vary by state, so look yours up.

nodes.name: Your First Resume
nodes.desc: School, activities, volunteering and skills. You don't need job experience to have a good resume.

nodes.name: Applying
nodes.desc: Filling out applications and dropping off a resume. Show up in person when you can, and dress neatly.

nodes.name: Job Interviews
nodes.desc: Being on time, smiling and having a few examples ready. Practice the common questions out loud.

nodes.name: Your First Week
nodes.desc: Learning the ropes, asking questions and writing things down. Everyone expects you to be new.

nodes.name: Being Reliable
nodes.desc: Showing up on time and covering the shifts you agreed to. Reliability gets you more hours and good references.

nodes.name: Customer Service
nodes.desc: Staying friendly with difficult people. Stay calm, listen and grab a manager when you need one.

nodes.name: Balancing School
nodes.desc: Keeping your hours low during busy school weeks. Tell your manager about exams early.

nodes.name: Understanding Your Paycheck
nodes.desc: Taxes, withholding and hourly math. Your take-home pay will be lower than you expect.

nodes.name: Saving What You Earn
nodes.desc: Splitting each paycheck into saving and spending. A savings habit started now grows huge over time.

nodes.name: Working With Coworkers
nodes.desc: Getting along with people of all ages. Help out without being asked and people notice.

nodes.name: Talking to Your Boss
nodes.desc: Asking for time off, more hours or feedback. Be specific and give plenty of notice.

nodes.name: Your Rights at Work
nodes.desc: Minimum wage, breaks, hour limits for teens and safety rules. Know them so nobody takes advantage of you.

nodes.name: Asking for a Raise
nodes.desc: Showing what you've done and asking at the right time. Back it up with real examples.

nodes.name: Leaving Well
nodes.desc: Giving two weeks' notice and asking for a reference. You never know when you'll need that boss again.

nodes.name: Using Your Experience
nodes.desc: Turning job skills into resume lines and essay stories. A cashier job shows responsibility colleges value.

nodes.name: What Internships Are
nodes.desc: Short-term work to learn about a field. Paid, unpaid, research and virtual ones all count.

nodes.name: Finding Openings
nodes.desc: Counselors, summer programs, LinkedIn and cold emails. High school internships often come through people you know.

nodes.name: Resume & Cover Letter
nodes.desc: Tailoring both to each opening. Mention the company's actual work so it doesn't read like a form letter.

nodes.name: Cold Emailing
nodes.desc: Short, polite emails to professors or companies. Say who you are, why them and what you're asking for.

nodes.name: LinkedIn Profile
nodes.desc: A photo, a headline and a short summary. Connect with the people you meet along the way.

nodes.name: Applying
nodes.desc: Applying widely and keeping a tracker. Expect plenty of no's, so cast a wide net.

nodes.name: Internship Interviews
nodes.desc: Behavioral questions with the STAR method, plus your own questions for them. Research the company first.

nodes.name: Technical Interviews
nodes.desc: Coding problems or case questions for some fields. Practice them out loud, since thinking aloud is part of the test.

nodes.name: Starting Strong
nodes.desc: Learning names, tools and expectations in week one. Ask lots of questions early, while it feels natural.

nodes.name: Professional Habits
nodes.desc: Emails, meetings, dress code and deadlines. Act like a real employee from day one.

nodes.name: Owning a Project
nodes.desc: Finishing something real you can talk about later. Ask for meaningful work if nobody offers it.

nodes.name: Finding a Mentor
nodes.desc: Someone who guides you during the internship and after. Ask for quick coffee chats with people on the team.

nodes.name: Asking for Feedback
nodes.desc: Checking in at the midpoint so there's still time to improve. Ask what one thing you should do differently.

nodes.name: Networking
nodes.desc: Meeting people across the company, beyond your own team. Stay in touch after the internship ends.

nodes.name: Final Presentation
nodes.desc: Sharing what you did and what you learned. Show results with numbers when you can.

nodes.name: Return Offers & References
nodes.desc: Turning a good summer into an offer or a strong letter. Thank everyone who helped you.

nodes.name: Leading Yourself
nodes.desc: Keeping your own promises first. People follow those who do what they say they will.

nodes.name: Listening
nodes.desc: Hearing people out fully before you answer. Most team problems start with someone not feeling heard.

nodes.name: Leading by Example
nodes.desc: Doing the hard jobs yourself. Your team copies what you do much more than what you say.

nodes.name: Clear Communication
nodes.desc: Saying what needs to happen, by when and why. Repeat important things more than feels necessary.

nodes.name: Setting Goals
nodes.desc: Goals your group can actually reach and track. Make them specific, with a date on each one.

nodes.name: Running Meetings
nodes.desc: An agenda, a time limit and clear next steps. Bad meetings drain clubs faster than anything.

nodes.name: Delegating
nodes.desc: Giving people real jobs and trusting them to do them. Trying to do everything yourself burns you out.

nodes.name: Motivating People
nodes.desc: Recognizing effort and connecting the work to a purpose. Thank people in public.

nodes.name: Including Everyone
nodes.desc: Making sure quiet members get a voice. Different views lead to better decisions.

nodes.name: Handling Conflict
nodes.desc: Talking to people privately and finding common ground. Deal with problems while they are still small.

nodes.name: Giving Feedback
nodes.desc: Feedback that is specific, kind and on time. Praise in public and correct in private.

nodes.name: Making Decisions
nodes.desc: Getting input, then choosing and explaining why. Putting off a decision is a choice too.

nodes.name: Planning Events
nodes.desc: Budgets, timelines and roles for big events like fundraisers. Plan backwards from the date.

nodes.name: Leading Under Pressure
nodes.desc: Staying calm when plans fall apart at the last minute. Your mood spreads to the whole team.

nodes.name: Setting a Vision
nodes.desc: Where the group should be a year from now. A clear vision helps people make choices without you.

nodes.name: Growing New Leaders
nodes.desc: Training people to take over after you. Great leaders make themselves easy to replace.

nodes.name: Reflecting on Leadership
nodes.desc: Looking back at what worked and what didn't. Write it down for college essays and interviews.

nodes.name: Observation
nodes.desc: Drawing what is there rather than what you know is there. The symbol your hand wants to produce for an eye is the single largest obstacle, and defeating it is most of learning to draw.

nodes.name: Shape & Proportion
nodes.desc: Getting the big relationships right before any detail. Measuring by comparison (this is twice that) fixes more work than any amount of careful rendering.

nodes.name: Line
nodes.desc: Confident marks that vary in weight and say something. A line drawn quickly from the shoulder reads better than one assembled from hesitant strokes, even when it is less accurate.

nodes.name: Value & Light
nodes.desc: Light and dark, which do far more work than color does. Squinting collapses a scene into a few values, and a picture that works in those will work in anything.

nodes.name: Form & Volume
nodes.desc: Making a flat mark look like a solid object under a light. Once you can see the planes turning away from the source, shading stops being guesswork.

nodes.name: Perspective
nodes.desc: Depth on a flat surface, built from a horizon and vanishing points. The rules are simple and unforgiving: one wrong eye level makes an entire drawing feel off without anybody being able to say why.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.desc: Arranging things inside the frame so the eye goes where you want and stays. It is decided in the first thirty seconds with thumbnails, not rescued in the last hour.

nodes.name: Color
nodes.desc: Hue, saturation and value as three separate dials. Nearly every muddy result is a saturation problem, and nearly every flat one is a value problem wearing color.

nodes.name: Materials
nodes.desc: What pencil, ink, paint or pixels each do well and badly. Learning one medium properly teaches more than sampling six, because the limits are what force decisions.

nodes.name: Gesture
nodes.desc: Catching the movement and weight of a subject in seconds. Timed studies teach it, and the point is not to produce a good drawing but to stop drawing outlines.

nodes.name: Anatomy
nodes.desc: The structure under the surface: what a shoulder actually does and where a hip sits. Knowledge is what makes a figure convincing when reference is not available.

nodes.name: Depth & Atmosphere
nodes.desc: Contrast, detail and color dropping off with distance. It is the difference between a scene that has air in it and a set of objects at different sizes.

nodes.name: Stylization
nodes.desc: Choosing what to exaggerate and what to leave out. Convincing stylization is a deliberate departure from something understood, which is why it comes after the observational nodes.

nodes.name: Critique
nodes.desc: Assessing your own work against what you intended, and hearing somebody else do it. Turning the piece upside down or looking in a mirror shows what your eye has stopped seeing.

nodes.name: Working from Reference
nodes.desc: Using photographs and life as material rather than as something to copy. Several references combined and understood beats one traced, and it shows immediately.

nodes.name: Sketch to Finish
nodes.desc: Thumbnails, then a value study, then color, then detail. Working in that order means the expensive mistakes are found while they cost minutes.

nodes.name: A Body of Work
nodes.desc: Enough finished pieces for the consistencies to become visible. Style is noticed in retrospect across a body of work rather than chosen in advance for a single piece.

nodes.name: Mileage
nodes.desc: Drawing regularly and badly for long enough that the hand catches up with the eye. Nothing else in this tree substitutes for it, and everybody who can draw did this part.

nodes.name: Mark Control
nodes.desc: Straight lines, smooth curves and ellipses that close, drawn from the shoulder. Dull warm-up exercises that quietly determine whether everything later looks confident or scratchy.

nodes.name: Construction
nodes.desc: Building a subject from simple solids before refining it. Drawing through the forms, including the parts you cannot see, is what keeps an object coherent from any angle.

nodes.name: Sight Measuring
nodes.desc: Using a pencil at arm length to compare angles and lengths. It feels mechanical and it is how accurate drawings get made without tracing.

nodes.name: Still Life
nodes.desc: Objects that hold still under a light you control. The ideal training ground precisely because nothing moves and every error is yours.

nodes.name: Shading
nodes.desc: Turning form with value: core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow. The edge between light and shadow tells the viewer more about the surface than the darkness does.

nodes.name: Texture & Surface
nodes.desc: Making a thing look like metal, cloth or skin. It is mostly about how sharp the highlights are and how quickly value changes, not about drawing every detail.

nodes.name: Figure Drawing
nodes.desc: The human body from life, starting with gesture and ending with structure. Weight, balance and where the ribcage sits relative to the pelvis carry the whole drawing.

nodes.name: Portraits
nodes.desc: Likeness, which lives in proportion and placement rather than in careful features. Get the skull and the spacing right and the face appears; get them wrong and no eyelash saves it.

nodes.name: Hands & Feet
nodes.desc: The parts everybody hides behind pockets. Simplified into a box for the palm and wedges for the fingers, they become drawable rather than a wall.

nodes.name: Perspective in Practice
nodes.desc: Putting constructed objects into a believable space, including the ones at odd angles. Establish the horizon first; everything else is measured against it.

nodes.name: Environments
nodes.desc: Landscapes and interiors, where the subject is space rather than an object. Depth comes from overlapping shapes and falling contrast far more than from detail.

nodes.name: Ink & Line Work
nodes.desc: Committing without an eraser, and building value from hatching. The discipline of no undo teaches decisiveness faster than any other medium.

nodes.name: Paint Handling
nodes.desc: Mixing, loading a brush and laying down an edge you meant. Most early painting problems are consistency and brush pressure rather than color choice.

nodes.name: Color Mixing
nodes.desc: Getting a specific color from a limited palette, and keeping it clean. A restricted palette produces more harmonious work than a full set, and teaches faster.

nodes.name: Painting from Life
nodes.desc: Working outdoors or in front of the subject with the light changing. The time limit forces simplification, which is the lesson rather than a nuisance.

nodes.name: Digital Painting
nodes.desc: Layers, brushes and undo, which speed everything up and remove the pressure that taught decisiveness. Fundamentals transfer completely; the shortcuts do not replace them.

nodes.name: Composing a Picture
nodes.desc: Deciding what the picture is of and removing everything competing with it. Thumbnail several arrangements before committing hours to the first idea.

nodes.name: Master Studies
nodes.desc: Copying good work to find out how a decision was made. Analytical copying (asking why an edge is soft there) teaches what admiring never will.

nodes.name: Finished Work
