nodes.desc: Scrolling that leaves you feeling worse. Mute, unfollow and set time limits that you keep.

nodes.name: Talking It Out
nodes.desc: Sharing with friends, family or a school counselor. Saying it out loud makes it smaller.

nodes.name: Saying No
nodes.desc: Protecting your time and energy. You can't do everything, and that's completely fine.

nodes.name: Making Time for Fun
nodes.desc: Hobbies and hanging out, on purpose and on the calendar. Rest makes you better at the hard stuff.

nodes.name: Letting Go of Perfect
nodes.desc: Good enough is often good enough. Perfectionism slows you down and wears you out.

nodes.name: Getting Help
nodes.desc: When stress won't go away, talk to a counselor, doctor or adult you trust. In a crisis in the US, call or text 988.

nodes.name: Your Stress Toolkit
nodes.desc: A short list of what works for you, written down. Reach for it before things get bad.

nodes.name: Bouncing Back
nodes.desc: Getting through hard times and learning from them. Every rough patch you survive is proof you can handle the next.

nodes.name: Ball Handling
nodes.desc: Dribbling with both hands without looking down. Daily drills make the ball feel like part of your hand.

nodes.name: Footwork
nodes.desc: Pivots, jump stops and triple threat. Good footwork stops travels and makes space for your shot.

nodes.name: Passing
nodes.desc: Chest, bounce and overhead passes. Throw it to the spot your teammate is running to.

nodes.name: Shooting Form
nodes.desc: Balance, elbow in and a full follow through. Start close to the hoop and move out as it gets automatic.

nodes.name: Layups
nodes.desc: Both hands, both sides and the right footwork. Practice your weak-hand layups twice as much.

nodes.name: On-Ball Defense
nodes.desc: Stance, slides and staying between your player and the hoop. Good defense is mostly effort and focus.

nodes.name: Rebounding
nodes.desc: Boxing out and going hard after the ball. Most rebounds go to whoever wants them more.

nodes.name: Free Throws
nodes.desc: The same routine every single time you step up. Shoot 50 a day and track how many you make.

nodes.name: Dribble Moves
nodes.desc: Crossovers, hesitations and spins. Changing speed beats defenders more often than fancy moves.

nodes.name: Moving Without the Ball
nodes.desc: Cuts, screens and spacing. Most points come from players moving when they do not have the ball.

nodes.name: Team Defense
nodes.desc: Help side, rotations and talking the whole time. A quiet defense is a beaten defense.

nodes.name: Shooting Range
nodes.desc: Adding the three-pointer without wrecking your form. Strength comes first, then range.

nodes.name: Running Plays
nodes.desc: Learning your team's sets and why they work. Know what every position is supposed to do.

nodes.name: Basketball IQ
nodes.desc: Reading the defense and making the right play. Watch game film to start seeing the patterns.

nodes.name: Conditioning
nodes.desc: Sprints, agility work and lasting all four quarters. Tired players make bad decisions.

nodes.name: Mental Game
nodes.desc: Shaking off mistakes and staying confident when shots miss. Next play, every time.

nodes.name: Making Varsity
nodes.desc: Tryouts, coach feedback and off-season work. What you do in the summer decides your season.

nodes.name: First Touch
nodes.desc: Controlling the ball so it drops exactly where you want it. A good first touch buys you time.

nodes.name: Dribbling
nodes.desc: Close control with both feet at speed. Use the inside, outside and sole of your foot.

nodes.name: Passing
nodes.desc: Inside-foot passes with the right weight. Pass to your teammate's foot that's away from the defender.

nodes.name: Shooting
nodes.desc: Laces for power and the inside of the foot for placement. Aim low and to the corners.

nodes.name: Weak Foot
nodes.desc: Training your other foot until defenders can't force you one way. Fifteen minutes a day really works.

nodes.name: Defending
nodes.desc: Jockeying, staying patient and timing your tackles. Don't dive in, make them make the move.

nodes.name: Positioning
nodes.desc: Knowing where to be with and without the ball. Good team shape wins more games than talent.

nodes.name: Scanning
nodes.desc: Looking around before the ball arrives. Top players check over their shoulder all the time.

nodes.name: Heading
nodes.desc: Hitting it with your forehead using safe technique. Youth rules limit heading, so check yours.

nodes.name: Combination Play
nodes.desc: Give-and-gos, overlaps and third-man runs. Quick passing breaks down even good defenses.

nodes.name: Set Pieces
nodes.desc: Corners, free kicks and throw-ins. A big share of goals come from dead-ball situations.

nodes.name: Pressing
nodes.desc: Winning the ball back as a team. Press together or hold your shape, never halfway.

nodes.name: Soccer Fitness
nodes.desc: Sprints and quick recovery for a full match. Interval runs match what the game asks of you.

nodes.name: Tactics & Formations
nodes.desc: A 4-3-3, a 4-4-2 and what each one asks of you. Know your job in every system your coach uses.

nodes.name: Goalkeeping Basics
nodes.desc: Catching, diving and positioning. Every field player should know the basics in a pinch.

nodes.name: Mental Toughness
nodes.desc: Bouncing back after mistakes and handling big games. Put all your focus on the next action.

nodes.name: Club & College Soccer
nodes.desc: Showcases, highlight videos and emailing coaches. Start early and keep your grades up.

nodes.name: A Weekly Rhythm
nodes.desc: Fixed days for the recurring things, so they stop being decisions. Laundry on a day rather than when the basket overflows is the difference between maintenance and crisis.

nodes.name: Tidying
nodes.desc: Everything having a place, and going back to it. Ten minutes at the end of a day prevents the state where tidying becomes a project requiring a free afternoon.

nodes.name: Cleaning
nodes.desc: What actually needs doing weekly against monthly, and the small number of products that cover it. Cleaning a tidy room takes a quarter of the time, which is why the order matters.

nodes.name: Laundry
nodes.desc: Sorting, temperatures and what quietly ruins fabric. The step everybody skips is putting it away, which is where the whole system usually breaks.

nodes.name: Decluttering
nodes.desc: Owning less so that tidying is quick. Storage solutions are usually a way of keeping things you have already decided not to use.

nodes.name: Shopping & Stock
nodes.desc: A list built from what you plan to eat, and a small set of staples always in. One considered trip beats four improvised ones for money, time and what gets thrown away.

nodes.name: Errands
nodes.desc: Grouping the things that need leaving the house into one route. Kept as a running list rather than remembered, because an errand forgotten costs a second trip.

nodes.name: Household Money
nodes.desc: Knowing the fixed costs, when they leave and what the variable ones average. Most household financial stress is timing rather than total, and a calendar fixes timing.

nodes.name: Admin
nodes.desc: Renewals, appointments, forms and the documents you need once a year. A single folder and a calendar reminder converts a recurring panic into a ten-minute task.

nodes.name: Repairs & Maintenance
nodes.desc: Basic fixes, and knowing which jobs need somebody qualified. Anything gas, structural or on a consumer unit does. Small maintenance done on time is the cheapest money in a home.

nodes.name: Home Safety
nodes.desc: Alarms tested, a first aid kit, and knowing where the stopcock and the fuse box are. Ten minutes of preparation that is worth an enormous amount on one unlikely day.

nodes.name: Plants & Garden
nodes.desc: Light, water and the patience to leave things alone. Most houseplants die of overwatering, which is the one problem more attention makes worse.

nodes.name: Time with People
nodes.desc: Seeing family and friends on purpose rather than when it happens. Relationships decay quietly without contact, and the fix is a recurring arrangement rather than better intentions.

nodes.name: Hosting
nodes.desc: Having people over without it costing a weekend. Simple food prepared beforehand, and accepting that nobody remembers what was served, only whether you were with them.

nodes.name: Occasions & Gifts
nodes.desc: Birthdays in a calendar with a reminder that leaves time to post something. The thought people register is that you knew, rather than what arrived.

nodes.name: Digital Housekeeping
nodes.desc: Backups that exist in two places, a password manager, and photographs that are not only on a phone. The cost of neglecting this is zero until it is total.

nodes.name: Waste & Repair Culture
nodes.desc: Buying less, mending what breaks and disposing of the rest properly. Usually cheaper, occasionally slower, and the only part of this tree with effects outside the house.

nodes.name: A Home That Runs Itself
nodes.desc: Standing orders, recurring reminders and shared lists, so nothing depends on one person remembering. Invisible when it works and immediately obvious when it does not.

nodes.name: Kit & Kitchen Setup
nodes.desc: A sharp knife, a heavy pan, a board and a way to measure. Six good pieces beat a drawer of gadgets, and a blunt knife is the most dangerous thing in most kitchens.

nodes.name: Knife Skills
nodes.desc: A grip that is safe, a claw with the other hand, and pieces of an even size. Even sizing is not neatness; it is the difference between everything cooking at the same rate and half of it burning.

nodes.name: Heat Control
nodes.desc: Knowing when a pan is hot enough, and that most home cooking happens too cool and too crowded. Browning needs space and real heat, and it is where most of the flavor comes from.

nodes.name: Salt & Seasoning
nodes.desc: Seasoning throughout rather than at the end, and tasting as you go. The most common reason home food is flat is that it was salted once, off the heat, from a shaker.

nodes.name: Acid, Fat & Balance
nodes.desc: Something sharp to lift richness, and enough fat to carry flavor. A dish that tastes heavy or dull is usually one squeeze of lemon or a spoon of vinegar from being finished.

nodes.name: Preparation
nodes.desc: Everything chopped and to hand before the pan goes on. It looks fussy and it is what stops the garlic burning while you are still peeling the onion.

nodes.name: Eggs
nodes.desc: Scrambled, fried, boiled and folded, which are four exercises in gentle heat. They are cheap, fast and unforgiving, which makes them the best practice available.

nodes.name: Vegetables
nodes.desc: Roasting, steaming, sauteing and knowing what each does to texture and sweetness. Most people undercook roasted vegetables by ten minutes and underseason them throughout.

nodes.name: Rice, Pasta & Potatoes
nodes.desc: The base of most cheap meals, each with one thing that matters: ratio, salted water, and starting potatoes cold. Getting those three right covers an enormous amount of ground.

nodes.name: Meat, Fish & Alternatives
nodes.desc: Dry surface, hot pan, do not move it, and rest it afterwards. Cooking to temperature rather than to time is the single change that most improves results.

nodes.name: Sauces
nodes.desc: Deglazing a pan, emulsifying, and thickening without lumps. A handful of mother sauces underlie hundreds of dishes, and the pan you just cooked in is where most of them start.

nodes.name: Soups, Stews & Braises
nodes.desc: Slow, forgiving cooking that turns cheap cuts and old vegetables into the best meals in the repertoire. Brown properly first; the difference between a browned base and a boiled one is enormous.

nodes.name: Herbs & Spices
nodes.desc: Which go in early, which at the end, and why blooming whole spices in fat changes them. Hardy herbs cook and delicate ones are stirred in off the heat.

nodes.name: Baking
nodes.desc: Chemistry with a timer, where measuring by weight actually matters. Bread rewards patience and temperature control more than technique, and the first several loaves are supposed to be dense.

nodes.name: Batch Cooking
nodes.desc: Cooking once and eating three times, with things that improve rather than degrade. It is the single most effective habit for eating well during a busy week.

nodes.name: Meal Planning
nodes.desc: Deciding the week before shopping, with meals that share ingredients. It cuts waste, cost and the daily question of what to eat, which is the expensive part.

nodes.name: Leftovers & Waste
nodes.desc: Turning what is left into something that is not obviously yesterday. Fried rice, soup and a frittata will absorb almost anything in a fridge.

nodes.name: Food Safety
nodes.desc: Temperatures, separate boards and how long things actually keep. Unglamorous, occasionally the most important node on this tree.

nodes.name: Cooking Without a Recipe
nodes.desc: Opening the fridge and building something from what is there. It arrives once technique replaces instructions, and it is the point at which cooking stops being a chore.

nodes.name: Cooking for People
nodes.desc: Several dishes finishing at once, for more people than usual, while remaining good company. Timing is the whole skill, and it is learned by getting it wrong in front of friends.

nodes.name: Deciding the Trip
nodes.desc: What this trip is for (rest, seeing people, or seeing places) because those three want different plans. Trips that disappoint are usually ones asked to be all three at once.

nodes.name: Budgeting a Trip
nodes.desc: Transport, beds, food and the daily spending that nobody counts. The last one is where budgets are broken, and estimating it per day beats hoping.

nodes.name: Documents
nodes.desc: Passport validity, visas and the entry rules of the country you are actually landing in. Several countries require six months of remaining validity, which surprises people at check-in.

nodes.name: Booking
nodes.desc: Flights, trains and rooms, and what each is actually cancellable for. Flexibility costs money and is occasionally the best money in the whole trip.

nodes.name: Insurance & Health
nodes.desc: Cover that includes what you will actually do, plus vaccinations and any prescriptions in their original packaging. The scenario it exists for is rare and financially unbounded.

nodes.name: Packing
nodes.desc: Less than feels right, in a bag you can carry up stairs. Everybody wears roughly a third of what they bring, and almost everything can be bought where you are going.

nodes.name: Planning the Route
nodes.desc: How many places, and how long in each. Fewer stops for longer is the single most reliable improvement to a trip that people resist until they have done it once.

nodes.name: Getting Around
nodes.desc: Local trains, buses, apps and what a taxi should cost. Working out the route from the airport before you land removes the most expensive decision of most trips.

nodes.name: Money Abroad
nodes.desc: Cards that do not charge for being used, some local cash, and knowing where tipping is expected. Airport exchange desks are the worst rate you will be offered all trip.

nodes.name: Language for Travel
nodes.desc: Twenty phrases and the willingness to use them badly. Greetings and thank you in the local language change how you are treated far out of proportion to the effort.

nodes.name: Local Customs
nodes.desc: Dress, greetings, queueing, tipping and what is rude. Ten minutes of reading beforehand prevents most of the ways visitors cause offense without noticing.

nodes.name: Staying Safe
nodes.desc: Copies of documents, sensible habits with valuables, and knowing the local emergency number. Most trouble is opportunistic and most of it is avoided by ordinary caution.

nodes.name: Eating Away
nodes.desc: Finding food where locals eat, and knowing what is worth being careful about. Busy stalls with high turnover are usually safer than quiet restaurants with laminated menus.

nodes.name: Traveling Alone
nodes.desc: Complete freedom and nobody to share the decisions or the dull evenings. Hostels, walking tours and eating at the bar are the standard ways of not spending two weeks silent.

nodes.name: Traveling with Others
nodes.desc: Agreeing beforehand on money, pace and time apart. Almost every travel argument is one of those three, and all three are easier to settle at home.

nodes.name: Slow Travel
nodes.desc: Staying long enough to have a routine somewhere. Weeks rather than days change the trip from looking at a place to briefly living in one.

nodes.name: Working Away
nodes.desc: Time zones, connectivity and the rules about where you are allowed to work. It is neither a holiday nor a normal week, and treating it as either is how both go badly.

nodes.name: Traveling Responsibly
nodes.desc: Where the money goes, what the trip costs in emissions, and what pressure it puts on the place. Fewer, longer trips and local spending are the two levers that matter most.

nodes.name: When It Goes Wrong
nodes.desc: Missed connections, lost bags and illness away from home. Knowing your rights, having the documents accessible and building slack into the schedule turns a disaster into a delay.

nodes.name: Coming Home
nodes.desc: A buffer day, the washing done and the photographs actually looked at. The trip is finished properly here, and skipping it is why some holidays leave people more tired than before.

nodes.name: Rules of the Road
nodes.desc: Signs, signals and right of way from your state's driver handbook. Everything on the permit test is in there.

nodes.name: Learner's Permit
nodes.desc: Studying, passing the written test and handling the paperwork. Bring every document the DMV lists.

nodes.name: Car Controls
nodes.desc: Mirrors, seat, pedals, lights and wipers. Adjust everything before you start the engine.

nodes.name: Starting & Stopping
nodes.desc: Smooth acceleration and braking in an empty parking lot. Smooth inputs feel safer for everyone in the car.

nodes.name: Steering & Turns
nodes.desc: Hand-over-hand turns and looking where you want to go. The car follows your eyes.

nodes.name: Scanning & Mirrors
nodes.desc: Checking each mirror every few seconds and looking far ahead. See problems coming before they happen.

nodes.name: Parking
nodes.desc: Straight, angle and parallel parking. Practice with cones or trash cans before the road test.

nodes.name: Lane Changes
nodes.desc: Signal, mirror, shoulder check, then move over. Never skip the shoulder check, ever.

nodes.name: Intersections
nodes.desc: Stop signs, lights and left turns. Left turns cause a lot of teen crashes, so take your time.

nodes.name: Highway Driving
nodes.desc: Merging, speed and following distance. Match the speed of traffic as you merge in.

nodes.name: Night & Bad Weather
nodes.desc: Rain, fog, snow and darkness. Slow down, turn on your lights and leave a lot of extra space.

nodes.name: No Distractions
nodes.desc: Phone away, no texting and few passengers. The text can wait, and you only get one life.

nodes.name: Defensive Driving
nodes.desc: Expecting other drivers to mess up and planning for it. Always leave yourself a way out.

nodes.name: The Road Test
nodes.desc: What examiners check and the most common fails. Rolling through a stop sign is a classic.

nodes.name: Car Care
nodes.desc: Gas, tire pressure, oil and warning lights. Know what to do when you get a flat.

nodes.name: Insurance & Costs
nodes.desc: Insurance, gas and repair costs add up. Good grades can lower teen insurance rates.

nodes.name: If Something Happens
nodes.desc: What to do after a crash or when you get pulled over. Stay calm, stay safe and know what info to swap.

nodes.name: How the Pieces Move
nodes.desc: Every piece, plus castling, en passant and promotion. Learn the special moves early so they never surprise you.

nodes.name: Piece Values
nodes.desc: Pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. Don't trade down without a good reason.

nodes.name: Opening Principles
nodes.desc: Control the center, develop your pieces and castle early. Principles matter more than memorized lines.

nodes.name: Basic Checkmates
nodes.desc: Queen and rook mates against a lone king. Practice until you can finish them fast.

nodes.name: Tactics
nodes.desc: Forks, pins, skewers and discovered attacks. Doing puzzles every day is the fastest way to improve.

nodes.name: Blunder Checking
nodes.desc: Before every move, ask what your opponent is threatening. Most beginner games are lost to blunders.

nodes.name: Opening Repertoire
nodes.desc: A few openings you know well as white and as black. Understand the ideas behind the moves.

nodes.name: Middlegame Plans
nodes.desc: Finding a plan when nothing is forced. The pawn structure usually tells you where to play.

nodes.name: Endgames
nodes.desc: King and pawn endings, opposition and rook endings. Plenty of games get decided right here.

nodes.name: Pawn Structure
nodes.desc: Doubled, isolated and passed pawns. Pawns can't move back, so think hard before you push.

nodes.name: Calculation
nodes.desc: Seeing several moves ahead clearly. Check forcing moves first, meaning checks, captures and threats.

nodes.name: Clock Management
nodes.desc: Using your time wisely in rated games. Saving time is pointless if it costs you the position.

nodes.name: Analyzing Your Games
nodes.desc: Going over every game you play, especially the losses. Find the exact moment it turned.

nodes.name: Positional Play
nodes.desc: Good and bad pieces, weak squares and open files. Small edges add up over a long game.

nodes.name: Tournament Play
nodes.desc: Notation, etiquette and rated games. Scholastic tournaments are a great place to start.

nodes.name: Studying Masters
nodes.desc: Playing through classic games move by move. Try to guess the next move before you look.

nodes.name: Running a Chess Club
nodes.desc: Starting or leading a club at school. Teaching others makes you a better player too.
